Education_Notes: Studied mathematics and medicine at Jena from 1677 to 1680 under Georg Wolfgang Wedel, a physician interested in iatrochemistry. Fellow students included Friedrich Hoffmann and Georg Ernst Stahl. After a brief period at Erfurt, returned to Jena and graduated in 1682 with a thesis on lymph circulation and catarrhs. Traveled through France, Italy, and possibly Holland in connection with this work. Worked at University of Leipzig from 1684 to 1688 under Johannes Bohn, who influenced him to develop a critical attitude toward iatrochemistry.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Chief work is Physiologia medica (1701), a comprehensive treatment of physiological functions based on recent discoveries in anatomy, physics, and chemistry. Emphasized iatromechanics and Cartesian corpuscular theory. Discussed blood circulation, nerve function, muscle contraction, and respiration. Wrote approximately fifty treatises on various medical and physiological topics. Opponent of Galenism, Paracelsianism, and Stahlian animism.
Means_of_Support_Notes: From 1688 worked at University of Wittenberg as assistant professor, then from 1689 as third-ranking professor of anatomy and botany. In 1693 assumed the chair of pathology. In 1697 appointed physician in ordinary by Friedrich August I, king of Poland and Saxony. From 1730 served as consiliarius aulae, senior of the entire university.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed physician in ordinary in 1697 by Friedrich August I, king of Poland and Saxony. Held senior university administrative position from 1730.

Awarded Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1931 with Karl Bosch.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Qualified as university lecturer in Hannover in 1909; established private laboratory for independent research; became head of research laboratory at Goldschmidt Company in Essen in 1914; sold patent rights to Badische Anilin- und Sodafabrik in 1925; founded company in Madrid after World War II; scientific adviser to Argentine government from 1947.
Patronage_Notes: Karl Goldschmidt, owner of the Goldschmidt Company, was an enthusiastic friend and promoter who provided laboratory and experimental plant facilities.

Education_Notes: Received conventional early education in classical subjects at Skara with private instruction in natural history. Entered Uppsala University in 1752, graduated in 1756 after studying mathematics, philosophy, physics, and astronomy. Gained doctorate in 1758 with thesis De interpolatione astronomica.

Early work in entomology on insect larvae and winter moths; astronomical observations including discovery of Venus's atmosphere during 1761 transit; physical geography treatise.

Instruments_Notes: Gave comprehensive account of the blowpipe in De tubo feruminatoria (1779), documenting its use for qualitative mineral analysis with various fluxes and distinguishing oxidizing and reducing flames.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Awarded prize by Stockholm Academy of Science in 1762 for research on winter moths. Delivered inaugural address to the Academy in 1764 on preventing harmful effects of lightning.

Father_Notes: Father was Michael Bergson, a Polish musician and composer.

Published over 400 papers on fungi.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in experimental physiology and environmental physiology. Patronage_Notes: Supported by Claude Bernard as student and collaborator. Received apparatus and support from French physician Denis Jourdanet for high-altitude pressure experiments. Government positions and ministerial appointment provided institutional backing.
Instruments_Notes: Constructed pressure chambers for experimental study of physiological effects of atmospheric pressure, building on apparatus designed by Denis Jourdanet. Father_Notes: Jacques Martin Berthelot came from a family of ironsmiths in the Orléans region and studied medicine in Paris. He spent most of his life as a physician in the poorer districts of Paris, gaining prominence only through his work during the 1832 cholera epidemic. His income was modest.
Education_Institution: Collège Henri IV; University of Paris, Faculty of Science; Collège de France; École de Pharmacie
Education_Notes: Entered Collège Henri IV at age eleven, excelling in Latin verse. Won first prize for philosophy in 1846 among lycée pupils throughout France. Became a boarder at fourteen and met Ernest Renan. Obtained bachelor's degree in letters (bachelier ès lettres) in 1847, then attended courses at the Paris Faculty of Medicine and Faculty of Science, graduating from the latter in July 1849. Studied practical chemistry in the private laboratory of chemist Pelouze. Became demonstrator to Balard at the Collège de France in February 1851. Defended his doctoral thesis on 24 June 1854. Studied further at the École de Pharmacie, graduating as a pharmacist on 29 November 1858. Deliberately avoided the École Polytechnique and École Normale. Visited Italy and Germany during his studies.

Religion_Notes: Raised Roman Catholic by his parents but questioned the validity of religion through his philosophy studies, becoming a skeptic. Influenced by Ernest Renan and his republican sympathies, as the Catholic Church opposed radical thought in mid-nineteenth-century France. Later attacked clerical influence, particularly in education.
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Organic Chemistry; Physical Chemistry; Thermochemistry; Analytical Chemistry; Agricultural Chemistry; History of Chemistry; Alchemy; Pharmacology; Physiology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of organic synthesis, demonstrating that organic compounds could be synthesized from inorganic materials, refuting vitalism. Major contributions to the synthesis of hydrocarbons, alcohols, esters, and aromatic compounds. Developed thermochemistry as a discipline, introducing exothermic and endothermic terminology and the principle of maximum work. Studied esterification equilibrium with Péan de Saint-Gilles, anticipating the law of mass action. Investigated explosives, nitrogen fixation, and animal heat. Conducted extensive historical studies of alchemy and ancient chemistry. Published approximately 1,600 papers across inorganic, organic, physical, analytical, technical, agricultural, and physiological chemistry.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed to a chair of organic chemistry at the École de Pharmacie on 2 December 1859. Given a chair of organic chemistry at the Collège de France on 8 August 1865, where he conducted daily laboratory research until his death. Practiced as a physician. Served in the Senate from 1871, appointed to permanent senatorship in July 1881. Served as minister of education from 11 December 1886 to 30 May 1887 and as foreign minister in 1895 for five months.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed to War Ministry commissions on explosives in 1874 and 1878 (president of the latter). Presided over a commission on laicization of primary education in 1886. Served as minister of education and foreign minister under republican governments.
Instruments_Notes: Developed improved calorimetric apparatus including a water calorimeter with platinum or glass reaction chamber, mechanical stirrer, and precision thermometer. Introduced the bomb calorimeter for determining heats of combustion of gases with high accuracy. Constructed an ozonizer based on Brodie's design for studying silent electric discharge reactions.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie de Médecine in 1863 and to the Académie des Sciences in 1873 after three unsuccessful attempts. Made permanent secretary of the Académie des Sciences in 1889. Elected to the Académie Française in 1901. Member of a large number of foreign academies.

Father_Notes: Samuel was a teacher at the Linköping Gymnasium; died when Jöns was four years old.
Education_Notes: Attended Linköping Gymnasium from 1793. Began medical studies at Uppsala in 1796, interrupted by financial need to work as a tutor; received a three-year scholarship in 1798 to continue studies. Received medical degree in 1802 with a doctoral thesis on the effects of galvanic current on patients. Self-taught in chemistry, learning from Girtanner's textbook and through independent experimentation.
Education_Locations: Linköping, Unknown, Sweden, 1793, Unknown; Uppsala, Unknown, Sweden, 1796, 1802
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Analytical Chemistry; Inorganic Chemistry; Organic Chemistry; Mineralogy; Physics; Electrochemistry
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in analytical chemistry and atomic weight determination; developed dualistic electrochemical theory of chemical affinity; established law of constant proportions through systematic analysis of salts; discovered selenium and thorium; proposed concepts of isomerism, allotropy, and catalysis; developed chemical notation system using element symbols with numerical subscripts; created mineral classification system based on chemical composition; investigated organic acids and animal chemistry, though remained a vitalist opposed to mechanistic organic chemistry.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as tutor (1794, 1798–1800) to support himself during studies. Served as unpaid assistant to professor of medicine and pharmacy at College of Medicine in Stockholm after 1802. Physician to the poor in Stockholm districts with low salary. Appointed professor of medicine and pharmacy in 1807 with increased salary and laboratory access. When Medical College became Karolinska Institutet in 1810, devoted most time to chemistry. Elected secretary of Swedish Academy of Science in 1818, which doubled his income and provided excellent laboratory.
Patronage_Notes: Sven Hedin, chief physician at Medevi mineral springs, took him as assistant in 1800 and later arranged his appointment at College of Medicine. Wilhelm Hisinger, wealthy mine owner, provided laboratory access and collaboration. Swedish Academy of Science provided institutional support and secretarial position.
Instruments_Notes: Built voltaic pile from sixty pairs of zinc disks and copper coins for electrochemical experiments. Became especially skillful with blowpipe, which he popularized through a published book. Designed and built most laboratory apparatus needed for his analytical work, including new forms that became standard equipment worldwide. Developed combustion apparatus for analyzing carbon compounds, though it required extensive time per analysis.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member in 1808; became president in 1810; elected secretary in 1818.

Father_Notes: Civil servant in Minden.
Education_Notes: Attended Gymnasium in Minden for four years before leaving to become a merchant's apprentice. Self-taught in astronomy and mathematics through independent study and professional journals. Awarded doctorate by University of Göttingen without further formalities on Gauss's proposal in 1809.
Education_Locations: None
Scientific_Disciplines: Astronomy; Astrometry; Mathematics; Geodesy; Physics; Geophysics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Founder of the German school of practical astronomy, emphasizing precision instruments and careful reduction of observations. Major contributions to stellar astrometry, determination of stellar parallax, and the theory of astronomical instruments. Developed Bessel functions in treatment of planetary perturbations. Conducted geodetic surveys and triangulation in East Prussia.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Apprentice to mercantile firm Kulenkamp in Bremen (1799–1806), becoming financially independent through proficiency in calculation and accounting. Assistant at Schröter's private observatory in Lilienthal (1806–1810). Director and professor of astronomy at Königsberg Observatory from 1810 until his death. Commissioned by Prussian government for geodetic surveys and triangulation work.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed director of Königsberg Observatory on recommendation of Humboldt by Friedrich Wilhelm III of Prussia. Encouraged and mentored by Heinrich Olbers, who recognized his talent and facilitated his transition from merchant apprentice to professional astronomer. Corresponded with Gauss, Schumacher, and other leading scientists.
Instruments: Heliometer; Meridian Circle; Transit Instrument; Sextant
Instruments_Notes: Used Fraunhofer heliometer for first accurate determination of stellar parallax of 61 Cygni. Employed Reichenbach-Ertel meridian circle (acquired 1819), Fraunhofer-Utzschneider heliometer (1829), and Repsold meridian circle (1841) for precise stellar position measurements. Designed new measuring apparatus for base-line determination in geodetic work.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member of Berlin Academy of Sciences in 1812. Awarded Lalande Prize of Institut de France in 1811 for tables of refraction.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Walter Fricke. Original works: Abhandlungen von Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel, Rudolf Engelmann, ed., 3 vols. Father_Notes: Adnah Bessey was a schoolteacher of Huguenot ancestry.
Education_Institution: Michigan Agricultural College; Harvard University; Harvard University
Education_Notes: Certified to teach at seventeen; entered Michigan Agricultural College in July 1866 and graduated from the scientific course in 1869. Studied under Albert Nelson Prentiss and William James Beal. Visited Harvard in 1872 at Asa Gray's invitation to study morphology and cell structure; returned to Harvard in 1875 to study mycology under William Farlow.

Scientific_Disciplines: Botany; Plant Systematics; Mycology; Plant Anatomy; Plant Physiology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of angiosperm phylogeny and plant classification; developed influential dicta for angiosperm systematics based on floral part reduction and specialization. Introduced cryptogamic botany and physiological plant anatomy to American colleges. Published seminal works on plant phylogeny and taxonomy; authored over 150 papers and reviews.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant in horticulture at Michigan Agricultural College; inaugurated botany and horticulture at Iowa Agricultural College, Ames (fifteen years); professor of botany at University of Nebraska from 1884. Lectured at University of California in 1875 and University of Minnesota in 1881. Associate editor of American Naturalist (1880–1897) and Science (1897–1915).
Instruments_Notes: Used a single Tolles compound microscope in his first botany laboratory course at Iowa Agricultural College in 1871; borrowed compound microscopes from Iowa Agricultural College for the first laboratory course in botany at University of Minnesota in 1881.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: American Association for the Advancement of Science; American Microscopical Society; State Teachers' Association of Nebraska; Iowa Academy of Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: President of American Association for the Advancement of Science in 1910; president of American Microscopical Society in 1903 and 1908. Belonged to approximately twenty organizations. President of State Teachers' Association of Nebraska in 1888. Encouraged the launching of the Iowa Academy of Sciences.

Demonstrated Betti's theorem in elasticity (1878). Pioneered analysis situs in hyperspace, originating the term Betti numbers.

Served as rector of the university and director of the teachers college in Pisa. Member of Parliament in 1862 and senator from 1884. Briefly served as undersecretary of state for public education in 1874.

Father_Notes: Born into a substantial old Berlin merchant family.
Education_Notes: Entered Berlin University at age sixteen to study natural sciences, especially mineralogy under Christian Samuel Weiss. Transferred to University of Bonn in 1834, where Goldfuss inspired him to specialize in paleontology. Received Ph.D. from Berlin University in 1837 with a Latin dissertation on goniatites of the Rhenish Schiefergebirge, influenced by Leopold von Buch.
Education_Locations: Berlin, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1834; Bonn, Unknown, Germany, 1834, 1837
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialized in paleontology and geology throughout his life. Major contributions to stratigraphic classification, particularly the definition and subdivision of the Oligocene epoch. Conducted extensive paleontological studies of north German Tertiary formations and Paleozoic strata. Investigated vertebrate and invertebrate fossils across multiple geological periods. Pioneered geological cartography in Prussia using 1:25,000 topographic maps as the basis for geological mapping.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed privatdozent at Berlin University in 1841, associate professor in 1846, and full professor in 1865, where he spent the rest of his life. Made custodian of geological collections of the Prussian Mining Administration in 1855 and taught mining students from 1857. Appointed scientific director of the Königliche Geologische Landesanstalt und Bergakademie in 1873 and director of the Museum of Natural History in the same year. Commissioned by the Prussian Mining Administration in 1842 to conduct geological survey of Silesia and officially commissioned in 1867 to organize geological mapping operations in Prussia and Thuringia.
Patronage_Notes: Recommended to eminent geologists and paleontologists by Leopold von Buch and Alexander von Humboldt. Commissioned by the Prussian Mining Administration for geological surveys. One of the founders of the German Geological Society in 1848 and its president from 1872 to 1895.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Prussian Academy of Sciences; German Geological Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected full member of the Prussian Academy of Sciences in 1853. One of the founders of the German Geological Society in 1848 and served as its president from 1872 to 1895.

Education_Notes: No formal institutional education is recorded. Likely trained within a scholarly family tradition; his son Laksmīdhara was made chief of the Panditas and his grandson Can̄gadeva served as chief astrologer to the Yādava king Singhana.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Major contributions to polarization of light, for which he received the Rumford Medal in 1840. Also worked on refraction, atmospheric phenomena, sound velocity, heat conduction, electricity, magnetism, geodesy, and meteorites. Authored comprehensive physics textbooks.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of mathematics at École Centrale of Oise (Beauvais) from 1797; entrance examiner for École Polytechnique from 1799; professor of mathematical physics at Collège de France from 1800; assistant astronomer at Bureau des Longitudes from 1806; professor of astronomy at Paris Faculté des Sciences from 1808; dean of the Faculty from 1840 to 1849.
Patronage_Notes: Patronage of Laplace, who encouraged his experimental investigations and secured his position at Bureau des Longitudes. Ordered by Chaptal, minister of the interior, to investigate the meteorite fall at l'Aigle in 1803.
Instruments_Notes: Used the newly invented spherometer by Cauchoix for precise measurement of crystal plates in polarization research. Designed one of the first polariscopes for measuring optical rotation in liquids and solutions.

Elected to Académie des Inscriptions et Belles Lettres in 1841 for research on Egyptian, Babylonian, and Chinese astronomy. Elected to Académie Française in 1856.

Postdoctoral study at University of Leipzig 1880–1881 under Ludwig and Gaule, where he learned paraffin sectioning technique.

Instruments_Notes: Devised the pyrlimnometer, a delicate thermocouple capable of recording light delivered by the sun to different lake depths; later equipped with filters to study light penetration of different wavelengths.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early work on stellar brightness fluctuations in β-Lyra and α-Cassiopeia. Conducted barometric measurements and atmospheric research under Herschel's direction, discovering atmospheric waves. Systematic observations of sunspots and solar rotation. Principal work in selenography: lunar mapping, crater analysis, and study of tint variations on the moon's surface, particularly in Plato crater. Developed notation for lunar features and a twenty-four-shade homo-chromoscope for classifying lunar brightness.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Employed as assistant to Sir John Herschel from 1839 to 1843 for barometric measurement reduction. Conducted electrical measurements at Kew Observatory. Maintained private observatory in Waltham's Town, Essex, equipped with a seven-and-one-half-inch equatorial reflector.
Patronage_Notes: Employed and supported by Sir John Herschel from 1839 to 1843. Worked at Dr. John Lee's observatory at Hartwell, Bedfordshire, between 1861 and 1866.
Instruments_Notes: Built and used a seven-and-one-half-inch equatorial reflector at his private observatory. Designed a homo-chromoscope consisting of twenty-four shades of a single pigment to aid in classifying the brightness of lunar markings.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Astronomical Society on 14 January 1859. First president of the Selenographical Society. Secretary of the Lunar Committee for Mapping the Surface of the Moon, established by the British Association in 1865.

Involved in the water controversy regarding the composition of water.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as secretary of the Royal Society from 1784; medical officer in the British Army from about 1776 to 1780; assistant to Cavendish from about 1782 to 1789, supported by an annuity and legacy from Cavendish.
Patronage_Notes: Knighted in 1792. Close friend of Joseph Banks and Henry Cavendish; supported by Cavendish through annuity and legacy. Associated with French scientists including Berthollet.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1772; served as secretary from 5 May 1784.

Alt_Name: Henri Ducrotay de Blainville; Marie Henri Ducrotay de Blainville
Father_Notes: Pierre Ducrotay; family belonged to lesser Norman nobility with considerable pride and patrimony.
Education_Notes: Early schooling interrupted by French Revolution; resumed in Rouen and Paris studying music, art, and literature before turning to medicine. Received M.D. from Paris in 1808. Worked in Cuvier's laboratory and became a comparative anatomist. From about 1810 began formal instruction as Cuvier's deputy at various Parisian institutions.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1808, 1808
Religion_Notes: Believing and practicing Roman Catholic. Developed a Christian philosophy integrating faith and knowledge, viewing natural order as unfolding of Creator's design. Religion aimed at understanding God's plan of creation rather than spiritual experience.
Scientific_Disciplines: Anatomy; Zoology; Natural History; Paleontology; Physiology; Malacology; Osteology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Outstanding comparative anatomist who lectured and published on descriptive and taxonomic invertebrate zoology, particularly malacology and comparative osteology. Conducted valuable paleontological research supporting the scale of being. Developed physiological theories based on sensibilité as organizing principle of life.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked in Cuvier's laboratory; from about 1810 gave formal instruction at Athénée, Collège de France, and Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle. Named professor at the Muséum in 1830 and appointed to Cuvier's chair of comparative anatomy in 1832.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1825.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted anatomical dissection and study of an Indian elephant (1706); contributed to understanding of plant sexuality and was an ovulist; described pyloric stenosis in 1717; worked on medicinal properties of plants and compiled the Pharmaco-Botanologia.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced as a surgeon in Dundee, Scotland for several years; elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1712.

Father_Notes: Gian-Alberto Blanc was a distinguished naturalist and professor at the University of Rome; the family was affluent, owning extensive property.
Education_Institution: University of Pisa; University of Rome
Education_Notes: Distinguished himself as a student at the universities of Pisa and Rome; no degree is named in the source.
Education_Locations: Pisa, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Rome, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: The Blanc family were Catholic; Cardinal Tisserant accompanied them on field excavations.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Focused on the Quaternary era and human paleontology. Discovered the Monte Circeo Neanderthal skull and approximately fifty prehistoric deposits in Italy. Developed theories of ethnolysis and cosmolysis concerning the evolution of ethnic groupings, species, and the cosmos. Published 164 works over twenty-six years.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed in 1938 to teach geology at the University of Pisa; called to the University of Rome in 1939 to teach ethnology and human paleontology; appointed to the chair in paleoethnology in 1957.
Patronage_Notes: Cardinal Tisserant accompanied the family on field excavations in search of prehistoric remains.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: International Union of Prehistoric and Protohistoric Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of numerous academies and scientific societies; elected president of several international commissions and of the Sixth Congress of the International Union of Prehistoric and Protohistoric Sciences; moving spirit behind the magazine Quaternaria.

Father_Notes: None

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of regional geography based on field research; creator of French Alpine geography; produced important studies of cities combining site analysis with urban development; studied mountains through field observation and structural analysis.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed lecturer at University of Grenoble in 1905, later became professor; appointed dean of Faculty of Liberal Arts in 1940, taught until retirement in 1948. Instructor at Harvard in 1917, full professor 1928–1936; also taught at Chicago, Columbia, and universities in Montreal and Laval.

Father_Notes: Josef Blaschke (1852–1917) was professor of descriptive geometry at the Landes-Oberrealschule at Graz. He influenced Wilhelm's interest in Steiner's geometry and instilled in him a feeling for history and openness to foreign cultures.
Education_Institution: Technische Hochschule Graz; University of Vienna; University of Pisa; University of Göttingen; University of Bonn; University of Greifswald
Education_Notes: Began studies at Technische Hochschule of Graz; earned doctorate from University of Vienna in 1908. Traveled extensively through Europe for more than a decade, studying with leading geometers including Luigi Bianchi at Pisa, Felix Klein and David Hilbert at Göttingen, and Eduard Study at Bonn.
Education_Locations: Graz, Unknown, Austria, Unknown, Unknown; Vienna, Unknown, Austria, Unknown, 1908; Pisa, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Bonn, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Greifswald, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Geometry; Differential Geometry; Integral Geometry; Kinematics; Topology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Leading geometer who centered research on differential and integral geometry and kinematics. Developed kinematic mapping as a central tool in kinematics. Investigated isoperimetric properties of convex bodies. Originated topological differential geometry studying differentiable mappings. Made contributions to affine differential geometry, projective differential geometry, and geometrical probability.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Privatdozent at Bonn (1910); extraordinary professor at Deutsche Technische Hochschule Prague (1913); professor at University of Leipzig (1915); full professor at University of Königsberg (1917); full professor at University of Hamburg (1919–1953). Held visiting professorships at Johns Hopkins, University of Chicago, University of Istanbul, and Humboldt University Berlin.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected corresponding or honorary member of about a dozen European scientific academies.

Alt_Name: Biagio Pelacani da Parma; Blasius Parmensis
Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Took his doctorate at the University of Pavia, perhaps in 1374. Studied in Paris, where he absorbed ideas of the Parisian Scholastics, as mentioned in an explicit to his Questio de tactu corporum duorum.
Education_Locations: Pavia, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1374; Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: In 1396 compelled to recant unspecified transgressions against the Church; held materialist and determinist views condemned at Paris in 1277, including denial of the separability and immortality of the intellective soul, but capitulated and repudiated these views in lectures at Pavia during 1396–1397.
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural Philosophy; Physics; Optics; Mechanics; Astronomy; Astrology; Logic
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Wrote independent treatises on optics (Quaestiones perspectivae, influenced by Ibn al-Haytham), statics (Tractatus de ponderibus, drawing on Jordanus de Nemore), and intension and remission of forms (including both English and French versions of the mean speed theorem). Discussed impetus theory, Bradwardine's function, motion, vacuum, and celestial influence. Initially a materialist and determinist; later attacked astrological determinism while accepting astrology itself.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught logic, philosophy, and astrology at the University of Bologna (1379–1380, 1387–1388); natural philosophy at the University of Florence (1388–1389); mathematics and both philosophies at the University of Pavia (1390s, 1403–1407); and philosophy and astrology at the University of Padua (1384, 1407–1411). Dismissed from Padua in October 1411 due to lack of students and infirmities of old age.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Rose from enserfed peasantry to become a merchant.
Education_Notes: Graduated from Smolensk Gymnasium in 1888 and from the Physics and Mathematics Faculty of Moscow University in 1892.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Primary focus on variable stars, particularly the periodic variation of periods and light curves in RR Lyrae-type stars (the Blazhko effect). Also conducted meteor spectroscopy, solar photography, and investigations of eclipsing binary stars, developing methods for determining orbital elements of Algol-type systems.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant at Moscow Observatory (1894–1915), astronomer observer (1915–1918), professor of astronomy at Moscow University (1918–1953), director of Moscow Observatory (1920–1931), and director of the university's Scientific Research Institute of Astronomy and Geodesy (1922–1931). Also taught at Women's Pedagogical College (1900–1918) and A. L. Shanyavsky People's University (1909–1919).
Patronage_Notes: Elected associate member of the Academy of Sciences of the U.S.S.R. in 1929; received title Honored Scientist of the R.S.F.S.R. in 1934; twice awarded Order of Lenin and Order of the Red Banner of Labor.
Instruments: Equatorial Camera; Photoheliograph; Spectrograph; Blink-Microscope; Meridian Circle Magnifying Glass
Instruments_Notes: Built or designed several instruments including a star spectrograph, blink-microscope, special magnifying glass for reading meridian circle divisions, and a device for eliminating stellar magnitude equation from transit times. Used an equatorial camera (built in Germany to V. K. Cerasky's design) for systematic sky photography and a photoheliograph for solar observations.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Academy of Sciences of the U.S.S.R.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Belonged to numerous astronomical societies, both Russian and foreign; elected associate member of the Academy of Sciences of the U.S.S.R. in 1929.

Father_Notes: Erhard Christoffer Laurentius Blichfeldt, a farmer descended from a long line of ministers; unable to afford his son's university education in Denmark.
Education_Notes: Passed university entrance examinations with honors in Denmark but could not attend due to family finances. After emigrating to the United States at age fifteen, worked as a laborer and surveyor for six years before entering Stanford University in 1894. Studied under Sophus Lie at the University of Leipzig, receiving his doctorate summa cum laude in one year with dissertation on groups of transformation in three-dimensional space.
Education_Locations: Palo Alto, California, United States, 1894, 1897; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, 1897, 1898
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Lifework devoted to group theory and number theory, covering diophantine approximations, orders of linear homogeneous groups, geometry of numbers, finite collineation groups, and characteristic roots. Published Finite Collineation Groups and coauthored Theory and Applications of Finite Groups. His contributions in group theory and Lie groups are now of considerable importance in scientific applications.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Instructor at Stanford University from 1898; promoted to full professor in 1913; chairman of the mathematics department from 1927 to 1938; visiting professor at the University of Chicago (summer 1911) and Columbia University (summers 1924, 1925); professor emeritus at Stanford until his death.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: American Mathematical Society; National Academy of Sciences; National Research Council
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Extremely active in the American Mathematical Society, giving numerous talks on group theory and number theory; elected vice-president of the American Mathematical Society in 1912. Elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1920. Member of the National Research Council from 1924 to 1927.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: University of Chicago; University of Göttingen
Education_Notes: Enrolled at University of Chicago in 1893, one year after its opening. Received bachelor's degree in 1897, master's in 1898, and doctorate in 1900. Initially studied mathematical astronomy under F. R. Moore but turned to pure mathematics. Instructors included E. H. Moore, Oskar Bolza, and H. Maschke. Postgraduate work at University of Göttingen from 1902 to 1903.
Education_Locations: Chicago, Illinois, United States, 1893, 1900; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, 1902, 1903
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Devoted his career to the calculus of variations and analysis, with special emphasis on basic existence theorems. Worked on transformation of Clebsch, Jacobi condition, multiple integrals, and boundary value problems. Applied Weierstrass methods to problems in calculus of variations. Authored foundational texts establishing theoretical foundations of the field.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Mathematics instructor at University of Minnesota (1900–1902) and University of Chicago (1903–1904). Assistant professor at University of Missouri (1904–1905) and Princeton (1905–1908). Associate professor at University of Chicago from 1908 to 1913, professor from 1913 to 1941, and professor emeritus from 1941. Chairman of mathematics department at Chicago from 1927. Martin A. Ryerson distinguished professor from 1933 to 1941.

Associate editor of Transactions of the American Mathematical Society from 1909 to 1916. Member of awards committee for National Research Fellowships in mathematics from 1924 to 1936. Elected to American Philosophical Society in 1926. Fellow of American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1935. Chairman of editorial committee for Mathematical Association of America's Carus Monographs series.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered photometric units of measurement and the oscillograph. Means_of_Support_Notes: Held naval engineering posts 1640–1652; tutor to Loménie de Brienne's son 1652–1655; lecturer in mathematics at the Collège Royal from 1655; commissioner general of the navy; professor and director of the Royal Academy of Architecture from 1671; mathematics tutor to the dauphin from 1673; put in charge of public works for Paris from 1672.
Patronage_Notes: Sponsored by Loménie de Brienne (secretary of state for foreign affairs) as tutor and for diplomatic missions 1652–1662. Scientific_Societies_Notes: Attended informal scholarly meetings in Paris from 1640; admitted to the Royal Academy of Sciences as a geometer (topographer) in 1669; appointed professor and director of the Royal Academy of Architecture in 1671.

Father_Notes: Heinrich Blumenbach was assistant headmaster at the Gymnasium Ernestinum in Gotha. Mother was Charlotte Eleonore Hedwig Buddeus, daughter of a high government official and granddaughter of a Jena theologian.
Education_Institution: Gymnasium Ernestinum; University of Jena; University of Göttingen
Education_Notes: Completed Gymnasium studies in 1769. At Jena attended lectures of mineralogist Johann Ernst Immanuel Walch on fossils. At Göttingen studied under Christian W. Buttner, who lectured on natural history and encouraged his anthropological work. Received M.D. in 1775.

Religion_Notes: Born into a cultured, wealthy Protestant family.
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural History; Anthropology; Comparative Anatomy; Geology; Paleontology; Zoology; Botany
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Founded scientific anthropology as a discipline; first reliable survey of human racial characteristics and distribution. Pioneered comparative anatomy lectures and textbooks in Germany. Developed ideas on fossil morphology and geological dating; recognized extinct groups of organisms. Contributed to evolutionary theory through recognition of nature's historicalness. Studied parasites, plant and animal variability, and domestication.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed curator of the natural history collection and extraordinary professor at Göttingen in 1776; named full professor of medicine in 1778; appointed professor primarius of the Faculty of Medicine in 1816. Renowned as a teacher.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Königliche Societät der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen; Institut de France; Royal Society; Linnean Society of London; Königliche Akademie zu Berlin; Imperial Academy of St. Petersburg; American Philosophical Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of Königliche Societät der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen from 1776; permanent secretary from 1812. Regular or corresponding member of more than seventy academies and scientific organizations. Carried on extensive correspondence with Albrecht von Haller, Peter Camper, and Charles Bonnet.

Father_Notes: Native of Norfolk; died in 1820 when Edward was ten years old.
Education_Notes: Attended Dr. Fennell's school at Wimbledon from 1820; frequently truant for scientific expeditions. In 1825 studied chemistry in London with Mr. Keating, whom he found unsatisfactory. No formal degree recorded.
Education_Locations: Wimbledon, Unknown, England, 1820, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Established reputation as diligent and accurate naturalist through contributions to scholarly journals, especially The Magazine of Natural History (1833–1841). Edited and annotated works on mammals, reptiles, and birds. Curator of the Royal Asiatic Society of Bengal (1841–1862), publishing numerous reports and monographs on Indian fauna with emphasis on mammals and birds. Conducted detailed observations on variation, sexual selection, and natural selection in nature; corresponded extensively with Darwin on species questions.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Invested in a small druggist's business in Tooting, Surrey, which failed due to his indifference. Established reputation through journal contributions while barely managing to exist. Appointed curator of the Royal Asiatic Society of Bengal (1841–1862) at 250 rupees per month; later received government pension of £150 per year. Contributed articles to Land and Water and The Field after returning to England in 1862.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Asiatic Society of Bengal; Zoological Society of London; scientific academies in Turin, Norway, Batavia, Moselle, Philadelphia
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected honorary member of the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1865; corresponding member of the Zoological Society of London and various other scientific academies and societies.

Father_Notes: Meier Boas was a moderately successful merchant; mother Sophie Meyer founded a Froebel-type kindergarten in Minden.
Education_Institution: Gymnasium; University of Heidelberg; University of Bonn; University of Kiel
Education_Notes: Studied mathematics and physics at the Gymnasium in Minden, then pursued graduate work in physics at Heidelberg, Bonn, and Kiel, receiving a doctorate at age twenty-three. Influenced by naturalist Alexander von Humboldt and geographer Theobald Fischer toward anthropology. Received anthropometric training from Rudolf Virchow in Berlin.
Education_Locations: Minden, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Heidelberg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Bonn, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Kiel, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Experienced discrimination and insults because of his Jewish origins while in Germany, which influenced his decision to remain in the United States.
Scientific_Disciplines: Anthropology; Ethnology; Linguistics; Folklore; Physical Anthropology; Natural History; Geography
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in reorienting anthropology toward historical and scientific methods from 1890 to 1925. Made significant contributions to human growth studies, linguistics, folklore, art, and ethnology of Northwest Coast Indians. Developed the historical method in anthropology and emphasized the plasticity of human types and the independence of race, language, and culture.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant editor of Science (1887); lecturer in anthropology at Clark University (until 1892); anthropological assistant and curator of exhibits for the Columbian Exposition; curator of anthropology at the Field Museum; curator of ethnology and somatology at the American Museum of Natural History (1896); lecturer in physical anthropology at Columbia University (1896) and professor (1899–1937); curator of anthropology at the American Museum (1905–1905).
Patronage_Notes: F. W. Putnam provided crucial mentorship and arranged positions at Clark University, the Columbian Exposition, the Field Museum, and the American Museum of Natural History. Adolf Bastian and Rudolf Virchow offered encouragement and training in Berlin.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: American Anthropological Association; New York Academy of Science; American Folklore Society; American Association for the Advancement of Science; Bureau of American Ethnology
Scientific_Societies_Notes: President of the American Anthropological Association (1907, 1908), New York Academy of Science (1910), American Folklore Society (1931), and American Association for the Advancement of Science (1931). Honorary philologist to the Bureau of American Ethnology (1901–1919). Editor of the Journal of American Folk-Lore (1908–1924) and the Handbook of American Indian Languages (1911–1941). Founded and edited the International Journal of American Linguistics (1917 until his death).

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal contributions to geometry through studies of successive polars of curves and algebraic surfaces, reciprocal polars, and projective geometry methods. Work in mechanics included studies of catenaries, equilibrium of chains on curved surfaces, and the principle of virtual velocities. Kinematics work included theorems on plane motion and the Bobillier construction for centers of curvature.

Patronage_Notes: Appointed director of the Carte de France project after Camus's death; elected honorary member of the Académie des Sciences in 1779.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected honorary member in 1779; financed publication of Laplace's Théorie du movement et de la figure élliptique des planètes.

Father_Notes: Ferdinand Bôcher was the first professor of modern languages at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Education_Notes: Specialized in mathematics and natural science at Harvard under W.E. Byerly, B.O. Pierce, and J.M. Pierce. Elected to Phi Beta Kappa upon graduation. Studied at Göttingen as a traveling fellow, auditing lectures of Felix Klein, Schönflies, Schur, Schwarz, and Voigt. Doctoral dissertation completed in 1891, published as a book in 1894 with introduction by Klein.
Education_Locations: Boston, Massachusetts, United States, 1883, 1888; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, 1888, 1891
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Prolific contributor to mathematical journals on the theory of differential equations and related questions. Research included systems of linear differential equations of the first order, singular points of functions satisfying partial differential equations of the elliptic type, boundary problems, Green's functions for linear differential and difference equations, and oscillation theorems of Sturm and Klein.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Instructor in mathematics at Harvard from 1891, rising through the ranks to professor in 1904. Exchange professor at the Sorbonne for three months beginning November 1913.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: National Academy of Sciences; American Philosophical Society; American Academy of Arts and Sciences; American Mathematical Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Vice-president of the American Mathematical Society in 1902 and president in 1909 and 1910. Chairman of the American Committee on Graduate Work in Universities under Felix Klein's leadership of the International Commission on the Teaching of Mathematics. Invited speaker at the St. Louis Congress of Mathematicians in 1904 and the Fifth International Congress of Mathematicians in Cambridge, England, in 1912.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as a master cobbler in Görlitz from 1599 until 1613, when he entered the cloth trade. Later years clouded by financial distress from inflation and the Thirty Years' War.
Patronage_Notes: Visited spiritual friends among the nobility of the region.

Education_Notes: Studied theology and philosophy at Leiden from 1684; earned philosophy degree in 1690 with thesis on mind-body distinction. Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of clinical teaching and bedside observation; synthesized iatromechanical theories; introduced exact quantitative methods to chemistry using temperature measurement and precision balances; founder of physical chemistry; contributor to pneumatic chemistry and biochemistry. First to obtain urea and discover its diuretic properties. Extensive work on botanical classification and garden curation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lecturer in medicine at University of Leiden from 1701; professor of botany and medicine from 1709; professor of chemistry from 1718. Gave private lectures on medicine and mathematics for student fees. Practiced medicine in Leiden. Held three of five chairs in the Faculty of Medicine simultaneously for ten years.

Alt_Name: Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius; Boethius of Rome
Father_Notes: Manlius Boethius, consul for 487, may have been his father; a prefect of the praetorium for 454 may have been his grandfather. The family belonged to the eminent Anicii, one of the more prominent families of Roman aristocracy.
Education_Notes: No formal institutional education is documented. The entry debates whether he studied in Athens or Alexandria; the most likely view is that he obtained Greek philosophical texts and knowledge indirectly through intermediaries and written sources rather than direct study abroad. He may have learned from his father-in-law Symmachus and from fourth-century Roman intellectual circles.
Education_Locations: None
Religion_Notes: Embedded in Christian Roman culture; wrote theological treatises on the Trinity and Christology. Executed under Theodoric the Ostrogoth, later venerated as a martyr.
Scientific_Disciplines: Philosophy; Logic; Mathematics; Theology; Music; Natural Philosophy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Translated and commented extensively on Aristotle and Porphyry, especially logical works. Wrote on the quadrivium (arithmetic, music, geometry, astronomy). Composed the Consolation of Philosophy, a synthesis of Neoplatonic cosmology and Christian doctrine. Contributed to medieval logic, the problem of universals, and rational theology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held the honorific title of consul in 510 and the high office of magisterium officiorum in the Gothic kingdom, giving him control over state affairs. Wrote commentaries and translations while engaged in public service.
Patronage_Notes: King Theodoric flattered him for his learning and sought his advice on technical matters (a harper, a water clock, a sundial). Theodoric appointed him to high office, though the entry notes uncertainty whether this was for his abilities or to strengthen the king's hold on the Roman nobility. Theodoric later ordered his imprisonment and execution in 522.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at Riga Polytechnic Institute from 1895, holding the rank of professor from 1900. Accompanied the institute when evacuated to Moscow during World War I. Returned to Riga in 1919 and was appointed professor at the University of Latvia.

Education_Notes: Studied medicine in Jena and Leipzig; received doctorate from the medical school of Leipzig around 1665. Traveled through Denmark, Holland, England, Switzerland, France, and possibly Italy from 1663 to 1665.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Named professor of anatomy and surgery at Leipzig in 1668; became municipal physician in 1690; appointed professor of practical medicine in 1691.

Father_Notes: Father was the distinguished physiologist Christian Bohr; mother was daughter of prominent financier, politician, and philanthropist D. B. Adler.

After master's examination, studied with Landau in Göttingen. Also studied at Cambridge and Oxford with Hardy and Littlewood. Obtained doctor's degree in 1910.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Leading analyst of his time. Major contributions include application of Cesàro summability to Dirichlet series, theory of Dirichlet series and distribution of function values, Bohr-Landau theorem (1914) on zeros of the Riemann zeta-function, and most significantly the theory of almost-periodic functions, which found central place in contemporary mathematics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Joined faculty of University of Copenhagen after obtaining doctor's degree in 1910. Appointed professor at College of Technology in 1915, a position retained until 1930 when he returned to University of Copenhagen to head the newly founded Institute of Mathematics.

Father_Notes: Co-proprietor of a wine business at Cognac; family belonged to ancient Protestant nobility of Poitou and Angoumois, though wealth had declined from earlier prosperity due to religious persecutions.
Education_Notes: No formal schooling. Self-taught through study of École Polytechnique course books and experiments in a home laboratory equipped by his uncle.
Education_Locations: None
Religion_Notes: Family belonged to the ancient Protestant nobility of Poitou and Angoumois.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of spectroscopic methods for elementary analysis. Discovered gallium (1875), the first of Mendeleev's predicted elements to be isolated, confirming the periodic classification. Conducted extensive spectral examinations of thirty-five elements and identified rare earth elements including samarium, dysprosium, terbium, europium, and gadolinium through spectroscopic and phosphorescent analysis.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked for the family wine business at Cognac from age twenty, traveling on business throughout the Continent and England. As business prospered, devoted increasing time to scientific research. Later conducted research in Wurtz's laboratory in Paris.
Instruments_Notes: Developed refined spectroscopic methods for elementary analysis and spectral examination of elements.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Corresponding member of the chemistry section of the French Academy of Sciences; foreign member of the Chemical Society of London.

Father_Notes: Thomas Kast Boltwood graduated from Yale College in 1864 and Albany Law School in 1866; died in 1872 when Bertram was young.

Education_Notes: Attended Albany Academy from 1879 to 1889 in preparation for Yale. Entered Yale's Sheffield Scientific School in 1889, majoring in chemistry and completing the three-year course with highest honors. Pursued two years of advanced study at Ludwig-Maximilian University in Munich under Alexander Krüss in analytical methods and rare earths. Returned to Yale in 1894 as laboratory assistant and graduate student under Horace L. Wells; spent a semester at University of Leipzig in 1896 studying physical chemistry under Ostwald. Received Ph.D. from Yale in June 1897.
Education_Locations: Amherst, Unknown, United States, 1879, 1889; New Haven, Connecticut, United States, 1889, 1892; Munich, Unknown, Germany, 1892, 1894; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, 1896, 1896; New Haven, Connecticut, United States, 1894, 1897
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in radiochemistry and the study of radioactive decay series. Confirmed the disintegration theory through measurement of radium-uranium ratios in minerals. Identified ionium as the parent of radium and developed the lead-uranium method for radioactive dating of rocks. Made major contributions to understanding the uranium decay series and brought precision analytical techniques to radioactivity research.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Instructor in analytical and physical chemistry at Yale's Sheffield Scientific School from 1894 to 1900. Established private consulting laboratory in New Haven in 1900 and partnered with Joseph Hyde Pratt as Pratt and Boltwood, Consulting Mining Engineers and Chemists, analyzing ore samples. Appointed assistant professor of physics at Yale College in 1906 and full professor of radiochemistry in 1910. Appointed director of Yale College chemical laboratory in 1918.
Instruments_Notes: Devised a simple automatic Sprengel pump and a new form of water blast. Used a gas-light gold-leaf electroscope to measure radium emanation activity and confirm the proportionality between radium and uranium in mineral samples.

Education_Notes: Early education from his father in Marosvásárhely; studied at the Evangelical-Reformed College 1815–1818 where his father taught; entered the imperial engineering academy in Vienna 1818–1822 for military education. No university degree is recorded.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed non-Euclidean (absolute) geometry, constructing a consistent geometry without the parallel axiom. Scientific_Societies_Notes: Participated in the Jablonow Society prize contest in 1837 but did not win.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: Gymnasium; University of Berlin; University of Strasbourg; University of Göttingen; University of Freiburg; University of Göttingen
Education_Notes: Studied languages and comparative philology at Gymnasium in Freiburg; entered University of Berlin in 1875 to study physics under Kirchhoff and Helmholtz; switched to pure mathematics in 1878 under Weierstrass; studied at Berlin, Strasbourg, and Göttingen from 1878 to 1880; prepared for and passed the Staatsexamen from 1880 to 1883; worked on doctoral dissertation at University of Freiburg from 1883 to 1885; received doctorate from Göttingen in June 1886 for dissertation on hyperelliptic integrals; completed year's private seminar with Felix Klein at Göttingen.
Education_Locations: Freiburg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Berlin, Unknown, Germany, 1875, 1880; Strasbourg, Unknown, France, 1878, 1879; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, 1879, 1880; Freiburg, Unknown, Germany, 1883, 1885; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, 1886, 1887
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Calculus of Variations; Elliptic Functions; Hyperelliptic Functions
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal investigations covered reduction of hyperelliptic integrals and calculus of variations. Worked on third- and fourth-degree transformations and elliptic theory. Published Lectures on the Calculus of Variations (1904) synthesizing contributions of Weierstrass, Kneser, and Hilbert. Most significant contribution was unification of Lagrange and Mayer problems into the Problem of Bolza, establishing the fifth classical necessary condition for a minimum. Extended existence theorems for implicit functions and differential equations.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Reader in mathematics at Johns Hopkins University from January 1889; associate professor at Clark University from October 1889; associate professor at University of Chicago from 1 January 1893, advanced to full professor in 1894; left University of Chicago in 1910 with title of nonresident professor; honorary professor at University of Freiburg upon return to Germany; returned to lecturing at University of Freiburg from 1929 to 1933.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Marneck); Meister Eckehart als Mystiker (Munich, 1938); articles in Mathematical Annals, American Journal of Mathematics, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society, and other journals 1887–1935. Secondary: G. A. Bliss, 'Oskar Bolza—In Memoriam,' Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society, 50 (1944), 478–489.
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Ronald S. Calinger.

Father_Notes: Italian immigrant art dealer; widely read with active social conscience; helped found an orphanage in Prague.
Education_Notes: Attended Piarist Gymnasium 1791–1796; studied philosophy, physics, and mathematics at University of Prague from 1796; entered theological faculty after 1800; took holy orders in 1804. No formal degree is named.
Education_Locations: Prague, Unknown, Czechoslovakia, 1791, 1796; Prague, Unknown, Czechoslovakia, 1796, 1804
Religion_Notes: Reconciled religion with ethical views through his professor's doctrine that faith yielding moral profit justifies belief. Charged with heresy in 1816; repeatedly refused to recant; action ended in 1825 through intervention of J. Dobrovsky.
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Logic; Philosophy; Natural Philosophy; Geometry
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in rigorous mathematical foundations; developed theory of real numbers (1832–1835) and continuous functions; proved early version of Jordan curve theorem; advanced logic as formal discipline in Wissenschaftslehre (1837); contributed to methodology of science.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Chair in philosophy of religion at University of Prague from 1805; dean of philosophical faculty 1818; dismissed 24 December 1819 and forbidden to publish; lived on estate of friend J. Hoffmann 1823–1842; continued studies until death.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed to chair by Emperor Franz I of Austria in 1805 as part of Catholic restoration policy.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member in 1815.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by B. van Rootselaar. Father_Notes: Father Antonio Mazzoli (alias Bombelli) was a wool merchant who moved to Bologna and married Diamante Scudieri, daughter of a tailor.
Education_Notes: Studied under Pier Francesco Clementi of Corinaldo, an engineer-architect. University of Bologna attendance suggested but considered unlikely given family background and profession.
Education_Locations: None
Religion_Notes: Inferred from Italian context and employment by papal officials; no explicit statement in entry.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Author of a comprehensive five-book treatise on algebra written between 1557 and 1560, published in part in 1572. Made significant contributions to handling imaginary numbers in the irreducible case of cubic equations and developed innovative algebraic notation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Spent most of his working life as an engineer-architect in service of Monsignor Alessandro Rufini, employed on the reclamation of the Val di Chiana marshes. Also engaged in mathematical instruction and writing.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by Monsignor Alessandro Rufini, a Roman nobleman, cameriere and favorite of Pope Paul III, later bishop of Melfi. Rufini employed Bombelli on major engineering projects and provided the villa in Rome where Bombelli wrote his algebra treatise.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Alt_Name: Charles Lucien Bonaparte; Prince Charles Louis Bonaparte
Father_Notes: Son of Lucien Bonaparte, Napoleon's younger brother; mother was Alexandrine de Bleschamp. Married his cousin Zénaïde Charlotte Julie, daughter of the king of Naples and Spain, in 1822; had twelve children.
Education_Notes: No formal education recorded; became a naturalist through self-directed study and field work in the United States beginning in the 1820s.
Education_Locations: None
Religion_Notes: Member of Pope Pius IX's party upon his accession; later joined the Radical party and participated in Roman republican politics in 1848–1849.
Scientific_Disciplines: Zoology; Ornithology; Ichthyology; Herpetology; Mammalogy; Botany; Natural History
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in systematic zoological classification; critical of Cuvier's system; reclassified Insectivora, Rodentia, Chiroptera, and Primates; elevated Batrachia to subclass rank; unified Reptilia; developed new ichthyological sections (Physostomi and Physoclisti) based on air-bladder anatomy; published numerous synopses, catalogs, and monographs on European and North American fauna; advocated for study of local fauna and creation of a natural history museum gallery.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Supported by family wealth as a member of the Bonaparte family; conducted naturalist work in the United States in the 1820s; held no formal academic post but was deeply engaged with museums and scientific institutions; after 1850 devoted himself exclusively to scientific work.
Patronage_Notes: Member of the Bonaparte family; son of Lucien Bonaparte and cousin of the royal house of Naples and Spain through his wife; supported by family connections and wealth.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Philadelphia Academy of Natural Sciences; Academy of Sciences and Literature of Baltimore; Academy of Sciences of Berlin; Royal Academy of Turin; Académie des Sciences de Paris
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected corresponding member of the Académie des Sciences de Paris on 18 March 1844 (defeated Agassiz by one vote in 1839); member of major European and American scientific academies; maintained friendships with Audubon in the United States and with J. C. Temminck and H. Schlegel in Leiden.

Father_Notes: Officer in the army of the duke of Urbino; also a poet.
Education_Notes: Educated in Rome with Francesco Maria della Rovere from age eighteen; continued studies at Urbino in Greek mathematics and natural philosophy. No degree is named.

Religion_Notes: Inferred from cultural context; son Pietro became bishop of Cesena.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal works on meteorology and winds, defending Aristotelian and Theophrastean theories against modern interpreters. Translated Ptolemy's work on fixed stars with commentary. Also wrote on medical subjects.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Supported by the duke of Urbino after his father's death in 1565; served as Urbino's ambassador to several European courts.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by the duke of Urbino, particularly after Duke Francesco Maria II's accession in 1574.

Father_Notes: Luigi Boncompagni, prince of Piombino; family of considerable wealth and standing.
Education_Notes: Student of Barnaba Tortolini, a noted mathematician. No formal degree is named in the source.
Education_Locations: None
Religion_Notes: Among the first thirty members of the Pontifical Academy of the New Lincei, founded by Pope Pius IX in 1847.
Scientific_Disciplines: History of Mathematics; History of Physics; Mathematics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Initially published mathematical analyses in Crelle's Journal (1843), then concentrated on the history of mathematics and physics. Produced major works on the development of physics in sixteenth and seventeenth-century Italy, and on medieval mathematicians and translators including Fibonacci, Bonatti, Plato of Tivoli, and Gerard of Cremona.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Supported by inherited wealth as prince of Piombino. Established and financed his own printing plant for forty years at full personal expense. Founded and financed the Bullettino di bibliografia e di storia delle scienze matematiche e fisiche (1868–1887), and published the Pontifical Academy's transactions at his own expense.
Patronage_Notes: Pope Pius IX appointed him among the first thirty members of the Pontifical Academy of the New Lincei (1847). Boncompagni also provided generous patronage to needy scholars and students, employing them in transcription and translation work.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Pontifical Academy of the New Lincei
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected among the first thirty members in 1847; published the Academy's transactions (volumes XXIV–XLVII) at his own expense; remained faithful to the Academy after the Italian government established the secular Lincei Academy.

Father_Notes: William Cranch Bond, first director of Harvard Observatory; collaborated closely with George on astronomical observations.
Education_Notes: Grew up in an environment focused on Harvard Observatory; began scientific collaboration with his father at an early age; no formal degree is mentioned.
Education_Locations: None
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Discovered Saturn's satellite Hyperion at age twenty-three and Saturn's crepe ring two years later. Conducted comprehensive observations with Harvard Observatory's 15-inch refractor. Investigated the Orion Nebula intensively. Pioneered stellar photography and celestial photography, producing the first photograph of a star (Vega) and advancing wet collodion photographic techniques. Reported on comparative brightness of celestial bodies, contributing the concept of 'Bond albedo' to astronomical vocabulary.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Director of Harvard Observatory from 1859 until his death in 1865; succeeded his father in this position.
Instruments_Notes: Conducted principal observations with Harvard Observatory's 15-inch refractor, one of the largest in the world until 1862. Pioneered daguerreotype work from 1847 to 1851, producing the first photograph of a star. Experimented with wet collodion photography from 1857 onward, achieving significant success in celestial photography.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Awarded the gold medal of the Royal Astronomical Society in 1865, the first ever given to an American, for his monograph on Donati's Comet of 1858.

Father_Notes: William Bond, a Cornishman who emigrated to Massachusetts in 1786; initially engaged in lumber export but the business failed; subsequently opened a clock-making shop in Boston.
Education_Notes: Left school at an early age due to family poverty; acquired mechanical skills through apprenticeship in his father's clock-making shop, where he constructed a chronometer at age fifteen.
Education_Locations: None
Religion_Notes: Described as deeply religious; specific denomination not stated.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted elaborate observational studies of the Orion Nebula and Saturn using the 15-inch refractor; pioneered the use of daguerreotype photography for stellar observation; designed and constructed precision astronomical instruments including an observing chair and chronograph regulating device.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as astronomical observer to Harvard University from 1839 (initially without salary); earned livelihood as an expert clockmaker, rating chronometers for longitude-determination expeditions.
Patronage_Notes: Commissioned by Harvard in 1815 to examine European instruments and observatories; invited by Harvard in 1839 to transfer his equipment to Dana House and serve as astronomical observer.
Instruments_Notes: Constructed a chronometer at age fifteen; designed and built the dome and observing chair for the 15-inch refractor mounted at Harvard in 1847; developed a regulating device that made the chronograph a precision instrument.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Pierre Bonnet, whose family held an estate at Thônex near Geneva; opposed his son's early interest in natural sciences and directed him toward law.
Education_Notes: Educated by private tutor Dr. Laget, who stimulated his early interest in natural sciences. Studied law at his father's insistence and received a doctorate in law in 1744.
Education_Locations: Geneva, Unknown, Switzerland, Unknown, 1744
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural History; Biology; Entomology; Botany; Physiology; Philosophy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of experimental entomology and plant physiology; discovered parthenogenesis in aphids; demonstrated regeneration in worms and other organisms; investigated photosynthesis, leaf nutrition, and plant movement; developed theory of preformation and palingenesis; influential theoretician of biology whose work shaped naturalists of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Retired to his wife's estate at Genthod near Geneva in 1756 after marriage; maintained correspondence with leading scientists and published extensively; appointed corresponding member of the Academy of Sciences of Paris.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Appointed corresponding member of the Academy of Sciences of Paris on Bernard de Fontenelle's recommendation following his discovery of aphid parthenogenesis; maintained extensive correspondence with nearly all major scientists of his time.

Father_Notes: Father was Pierre Bonnet, a banker (commis-banquier).
Education_Institution: Collège of Montpellier; École Polytechnique; École des Ponts et des Chaussées
Education_Notes: Attended the Collège of Montpellier; entered the École Polytechnique in Paris in 1838 and studied at the École des Ponts et des Chaussées. No degree is named in the source.

Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Geometry; Differential Geometry; Geodesy; Cartography
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal work in differential geometry of curves and surfaces, introducing geodesic curvature and torsion; proved the Gauss-Bonnet theorem. Means_of_Support_Notes: Became répétiteur at the École Polytechnique in 1844, augmented income by private tutoring, taught at the École Normale Supérieure, obtained a chair at the Sorbonne in 1878, and served as director of studies at the École Polytechnique from 1871.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to membership in the Académie des Sciences in 1862 to replace Biot; succeeded Liouville as a member of the Bureau des Longitudes in 1883.

Father_Notes: Rev. Thomas Bonney was headmaster of Rugeley grammar school.
Education_Notes: Graduated from St. John's College, Cambridge, as Twelfth Wrangler in the Mathematical Tripos in 1856 and obtained a second-class in the Classical Tripos. Self-taught in geology until becoming college lecturer in the subject in 1868.
Education_Locations: Cambridge, Unknown, England, Unknown, 1856
Religion_Notes: Ordained a priest; served as honorary canon of Manchester and Whitehall Preacher at the Chapel Royal.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Leading figure in early British petrography; lifelong interest in glaciology and valley glaciers; authority on Archaean rocks and metamorphic rocks; pioneering work in microscopic analysis of sedimentary rocks; chairman of the Coral Reef Committee of the Royal Society.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Mathematics master at Westminster School for five years; college tutor and lecturer in geology at St. John's College, Cambridge from 1861; Yates-Goldschmidt professor of geology at University College, London from 1877 to 1901; regular writer for the newspaper the Standard from 1901 to 1905; also served as Hulsean and Rede's lecturer at Cambridge.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Geological Society of London; Mineralogical Society; British Association for the Advancement of Science
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1878; served as secretary and president of the Geological Society of London; president of the Mineralogical Society; secretary of the British Association for the Advancement of Science from 1881; president of its Geological Section; president of the British Association in 1910.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at the École Normale in Paris before succeeding to the chair of botany at the Sorbonne in 1887; founded and directed the Laboratoire de Biologie Végétale at Fontainebleau in 1889.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Demonstrated through microscopic observation that scabies is caused by mites, not a consequence of the disease; proved mites reproduce by eggs and penetrate skin with oral apparatus; established scabies as a contagious infection transmitted by mites and developed local therapeutic treatment targeting the parasites.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as physician in the galleys of Grand Duke Cosimo III based at Leghorn; appointed physician to the grand duke's daughter Anna Maria Luisa in April 1691, accompanying her to Düsseldorf until late 1694 or early 1695.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed physician to Anna Maria Luisa, daughter of Grand Duke Cosimo III, in April 1691; served the grand duke's galleys.
Instruments_Notes: Employed the microscope, with assistance from Giacinto Cestoni's skill, to observe mites and demonstrate their role in scabies transmission and reproduction.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Family circumstances were comfortable, enabling his university education.
Education_Notes: Attended University of Turin; received degree in medicine on 14 April 1764. Studied chemistry under the guidance of V. A. Gioanetti.
Education_Locations: Turin, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1764
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Analytical Chemistry; Pharmaceutical Chemistry; Mineralogy; Metallurgy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Devoted himself almost entirely to chemistry. Early work on qualitative and quantitative analysis of piedmont minerals, particularly pierre hydrophane. Conducted extensive analytical work on mineral waters, salts, and phosphoric acid isolation. Developed quantitative determination techniques for weight loss in substances. Later focused on rational exploitation of Piedmont mineral resources and mining development.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Admitted to College of Physicians in 1778. From 1800 professor of pharmaceutical chemistry and natural history of drugs at University of Turin. Member and president (1801–1802) of Academy of Sciences of Turin.
Patronage_Notes: Served the Academy of Sciences of Turin under the House of Savoy (1783–1798), placed in charge of the Academy's laboratory and mineral analysis work. During Napoleonic period (1798–1812) continued work on mineral resources and mining development for the state.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Admitted 1783; served as president 1801–1802.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Giorgio Pedrocco. Original works: G. G. Bonino, Biografia medica piemontese, II (Turin, 1825), 593–596 for bibliography; Sulle cagioni recenti della minor produzione in bozzoli e in sete nel Piemonte (Turin, 1802); Elementi di chimica farmaceutica e di storia naturale, 2 vols. (Turin, 1804–1810); Pensieri sulla cura dell'epizozia (Turin, 1805); articles in Mémoire dell'Accademia delle scienze di torino (1793) and Journal des mines (1812). Secondary: A. Garmagnano, Laudatio (Turin, 1812); G. G. Bonino, Biografia medica piemontese, II (Turin, 1825); I. Guareschi, Supplemento annuale alla Enciclopedia di chimica (Turin, 1910), pp. 445–453; I. Guareschi, La chimica in Italia dal 1750 al 1800 (Turin, 1909), pp. 327–378.
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Giorgio Pedrocco.

Alt_Name: Anselmus Boetius De Boodt; Boetius Boodt
Father_Notes: Father was Willem de Boodt; mother was Johanna Voet, daughter of a famous lawyer. The Boodts were a noble Roman Catholic family.
Education_Institution: University of Louvain; University of Heidelberg; University of Padua
Education_Notes: Studied civil and canon law at Louvain, obtaining his first university degree. Later studied medicine under Thomas Erastus at Heidelberg and obtained his M.D. from Padua.
Education_Locations: Louvain, Unknown, Belgium, Unknown, Unknown; Heidelberg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Padua, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: The Boodts were a noble Roman Catholic family. Boodt bequeathed sums to the Jesuits of Bruges in his will.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Made the first systematic description of minerals in his Gemmarum et lapidum historia, dividing minerals by size, rarity, hardness, crystalline form, and other properties. Conducted alchemical experiments but was critical of alchemy and opposed Paracelsus. Drew and painted minerals, animals, and flowers; made mineralogical excursions in Germany, Silesia, and Bohemia.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed canon of St. Donat's Church in Bruges in 1584, holding the post until 1595. Nominated physician in ordinary to Rudolf II in 1604, retaining the position until the emperor's death in 1612. Served as town councillor in Bruges from 1612 until his death.
Patronage_Notes: Served as physician to Rudolf II from 1604 to 1612, under whose influence he began writing his chief work. Appointed canon by ecclesiastical authority.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Włodzimierz Hubicki. Original work: Gemmarum et lapidum historia (Hanau, 1609); 2nd ed. prepared by Adrianus Toll (Leiden, 1636); 3rd ed. prepared by Toll (Leiden, 1649) with supplements by John de Laet and Theophrastus; French translation by Jean Bachou as Le parfict joaillier (Lyons, 1644, 1649).
