Partington, A History of Chemistry II (London, 1961); and others.
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Włodzimierz Hubicki.

Father_Notes: John Boole was a cobbler with interests in mathematics and optical instruments; his business declined, affecting his son's prospects. George assisted his father in instrument-making from an early age.
Education_Notes: Attended elementary school and briefly a commercial school. Self-educated in mathematics, Latin, Greek, French, and German, encouraged by his father and aided by William Brooke, proprietor of a circulating library. Had access to Royal Society publications through the Mechanics Institution reading room in Lincoln, where he studied Newton and Lagrange largely unaided.
Education_Locations: None
Religion_Notes: Entry mentions he considered taking holy orders at age fifteen but pursued teaching instead; no explicit religious affiliation stated.
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Mathematical Logic; Algebra; Analysis; Probability Theory
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of symbolic logic and Boolean algebra. Developed operational calculus with differential and finite-difference operators. Contributed to invariant theory. Applied logical calculus to probability theory. Published approximately fifty papers and two major textbooks on differential equations and finite differences.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Began teaching at age fifteen and established his own school in Lincoln. Appointed professor of mathematics at Queen's College, Cork in 1849, where he taught despite heavy teaching load until his death in 1864.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected Fellow of the Royal Society in 1857. Awarded a Royal Medal in 1844 for papers on operators in analysis. Contributed to Cambridge Mathematical Journal beginning in 1840.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by T. A. A. Broadbent. Original works: 'Researches on the Theory of Analytical Transformations' (Cambridge Mathematical Journal, 1841); 'On a General Method in Analysis' (Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 1844); An Address on the Genius and Discoveries of Sir Isaac Newton (Lincoln, 1835); Treatise on Differential Equations (Cambridge, 1859); Treatise on the Calculus of Finite Differences (Cambridge, 1860); The Mathematical Analysis of Logic (Cambridge, 1847); An Investigation of the Laws of Thought (London, 1854). Secondary: E. V. Huntington, 'Sets of Independent Postulates for the Algebra of Logic' (Transactions of the American Mathematical Society, 1904); W. Kneale, 'Boole and the Revival of Logic' (Mind, 1948); Sir Geoffrey Taylor, 'George Boole, 1815–1864' (Notes and Records of the Royal Society, 1956).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by T. A. A. Broadbent.

Father_Notes: Moritz Borchardt was a wealthy and respected Jewish merchant.
Education_Institution: University of Berlin; University of Königsberg
Education_Notes: Studied under private tutors J. Plücker and J. Steiner. From 1836 studied at University of Berlin with Dirichlet. From 1839 studied at University of Königsberg with Bessel, F. Neumann, and Jacobi. Doctoral thesis completed in 1843 under Jacobi's supervision, dealing with systems of nonlinear differential equations; thesis unpublished and now lost.
Education_Locations: Berlin, Unknown, Germany, 1836, Unknown; Königsberg, Unknown, Germany, 1839, 1843
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Generalized Kummer's result on the secular equation of planetary disturbances using determinants and Sturm's functions. Applied determinant theory to algebraic questions, symmetric functions, elimination theory, and interpolation. Studied the arithmetic-geometric mean and its connection to elliptic integrals, circular functions, and hyperelliptic integrals. Also investigated problems of maxima and elasticity theory.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Privatdozent at University of Berlin from 1848. Member of the Berliner Akademie der Wissenschaften from 1855. Edited Crelle's Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik (Volumes 57–90) from 1856 to 1880 as Crelle's successor.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member in 1855.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Christoph J. Scriba. Borchardt's Gesammelte Werke, ed. G. Hettner (Berlin, 1888), contains 25 papers and short communications. Works listed in Poggendorff, I, 238; III, 162; IV, 158. Secondary: Maurice d'Ocagne, 'C. W. Borchardt et son oeuvre,' Revue des questions scientifiques (Jan. 1890), also separately (Brussels, 1890); Max Steck, Neue deutsche Biographie, II (Berlin, 1955), 456.
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Christoph J. Scriba.

Alt_Name: Jean-Charles de Borda; Chevalier de Borda
Father_Notes: Father Jean-Antoine de Lacroix was of the nobility; parental ancestors had been in the military since the early seventeenth century.
Education_Institution: Collège des Barnabites; College de la Flèche; École du Génie de Mézières
Education_Notes: Studied at the Collège des Barnabites at Dax, then at the Jesuit College de la Flèche. Entered the École du Génie de Mézières in 1758 and completed the two-year course in one year. No degree is named.
Education_Locations: Dax, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; La Flèche, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Mézières, Unknown, France, 1758, 1759
Religion_Notes: Scorned religion, at least in his youth.
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Fluid Mechanics; Mathematics; Hydraulics; Instrumentation
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Major contributions to fluid mechanics, demonstrating that Newton's theory of fluid resistance was untenable and that resistance is proportional to the square of fluid velocity and sine of angle of incidence. Introduced the Borda mouthpiece and calculated the coefficient of fluid contraction. Developed surveying instruments and contributed to standard systems of weights and measures. Worked on calculus of variations and trigonometric tables. Unified calculus and experiment across diverse areas of physics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Attained the rank of capitaine de vaisseau in the French navy. Named inspecteur des constructions et de l'École des Ingénieurs de vaisseau in 1784. Participated in several scientific voyages and the American Revolution. Elected to the Paris Académie des Sciences (1756), Académie de Bordeaux (1767), Académie de Marine (1769), and Bureau des Longitudes (1795).
Patronage_Notes: Served in the French navy under government appointment; named to the position of inspecteur des constructions et de l'École des Ingénieurs de vaisseau in 1784.
Instruments: Cercle de réflexion; Platinum standard meter; Standard seconds pendulum
Instruments_Notes: Developed the cercle de réflexion (circle of reflection), a surveying instrument that contributed to French success in measuring the meridional arc. Designed the platinum standard meter and the standard seconds pendulum for the system of weights and measures.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Paris Académie des Sciences; Institut de France; Académie de Bordeaux; Académie de Marine; Bureau des Longitudes
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Paris Académie des Sciences in 1756 and its successor, the Institut de France. Elected to the Académie de Bordeaux in 1767, the Académie de Marine in 1769, and the Bureau des Longitudes in 1795.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by C. Stewart Gillmor. Original works: memoirs on fluid mechanics in Mémoires de l'Académie des sciences (1763, 1766–1769); Description et usage du cercle de réflexion avec différentes méthodes pour calculer les observations nautiques (Paris, 1787; 4th ed., 1816). Secondary: Jean Mascart, La vie et les travaux du Chevalier Jean-Charles de Borda, Annales de l'Université de Lyon, n.s., 2, Droit, Lettres, fasc. 33 (Lyon-Paris, 1919); S. F. Lacroix, Éloge historique de Jean-Charles Borda (Paris, ca. 1800); R. Dugas, Histoire de la mécanique (Paris, 1950), pp. 292–300.
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by C. Stewart Gillmor.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Outstanding student at the Athenée Royal of Brussels; began research before completing medical studies.
Education_Locations: Brussels, Unknown, Belgium, Unknown, Unknown; Brussels, Unknown, Belgium, Unknown, 1892
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Established the basis of humoral immunity and founded serology. Discovered the complement-fixation reaction (Bordet-Gengou reaction), identified complement (Buchner's alexin), demonstrated antigenic specificity, discovered the whooping cough bacillus, and studied blood coagulation and bacteriophages.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Director of the Institut Pasteur du Brabant (later Institut Antirabique et Bacteriologique) from 1901 to 1940; occupied the chair of bacteriology at the Faculty of Medicine of the Free University of Brussels from 1907 to 1935; lectured annually on immunity at the Institut Pasteur in Paris.
Patronage_Notes: Received a scholarship from the Belgian government in 1894 to work at the Institut Pasteur in Paris.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie royale de médecine de Belgique
Scientific_Societies_Notes: President of the Conseil Scientifique at the Institut Pasteur from 1935.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Jean Vieuchage. Original works: papers published in Annales de l'Institut Pasteur; Traité de l'immunité dans les maladies infectieuses (Paris, 1920, 1939); laboratory notebooks at Musée Jules Bordet, Institut Pasteur du Brabant, Brussels. Secondary: J. Beumer, Journal of General Microbiology 29 (1962); Paul Bordet, Florilège des sciences en Belgique (Brussels, 1968); A. M. Dalcq, Bulletin de l'Académie royale de médecine de Belgique 1 (1961); Volume jubilaire de Jules Bordet, Annales de l'Institut Pasteur 79, no. 5 (1950).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Jean Vieuchage.

Father_Notes: Son and grandson of Béarnese physicians.
Education_Institution: University of Montpellier; University of Paris
Education_Notes: Studied medicine at Montpellier, receiving M.D. on 10 November 1743; returned for further study in 1745; studied at La Charité hospital in Paris from 1746; renewed studies and received second M.D. from Paris Faculty of Medicine on 7 October 1754.
Education_Locations: Montpellier, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1743; Paris, Unknown, France, 1752, 1754
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in hydrotherapy and thermalism; demonstrated double innervation of glands and organs; proved secretory nerves exist; described connective tissue (mucous tissue) and its role in nutrition and mechanical equilibrium; advanced semeiology through pulse examination and diagnostic methods; precursor to endocrinology; contributed to vitalism through organ-based theory of life.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced medicine in Pau from 1749 and in Paris from 1752 onward, building a large practice; held posts as intendant and superintendent of mineral waters of Aquitaine; attending physician at La Charité hospital; corresponding member of Royal Academy of Sciences from 1747.
Patronage_Notes: Cared for important persons including Madame Du Barry.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Academy of Sciences of Paris
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Appointed corresponding member in 1747; won full membership through anatomical research on facial bone articulations.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Louis Dulieu. Original works: Chylificationis historia (Montpellier, 1742); De sensu generice considerato (Montpellier, 1742); Recherches anatomiques sur les articulations des os de la face (Paris, 1747); Recherches anatomiques sur les différentes positions des glandes et sur leur action (Paris, 1752); Recherches sur le tissu muqueux (Paris, 1767); Recherches sur les maladies chroniques (Paris, 1775). Complete works ed. A. Richerand, 2 vols. (Paris, 1818). Secondary: E. Forgue, Théophile de Bordeu, fondateur de l'hydrologie (Paris, 1937); J. J. Gardane, Éloge historique de Bordeu (Paris, 1777); F. Grand, Un médecin du XVIIIe siècle aux conceptions biologiques modernes (Montpellier, 1964); P. Roussel, Éloge historique de Théophile de Bordeu (Paris, 1778); Lucien Cornet, Théophile de Bordeu (Bordeaux, 1922) and numerous articles in regional journals.
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Louis Dulieu.

Father_Notes: Protestant village pastor; father of an artisan.
Education_Notes: Entered lycée at Montauban in 1882. In Paris as a scholarship student preparing for university, entered the family circle of G. Darboux. In 1889 won first place in the École Polytechnique, École Normale Supérieure, and general competitions, choosing the École Normale as the gateway to teaching and research. First in the class of 1893.
Education_Locations: Montauban, Unknown, France, 1882, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, 1889, 1893
Religion_Notes: Embraced an agnostic, scientific, and rational outlook.
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Analysis; Measure Theory; Probability; Set Theory; Complex Analysis; Game Theory
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered modern theories of functions of a real variable, measure, divergent series, nonanalytic continuation, and probability. Proved the Heine-Borel covering theorem and that a denumerable set has measure zero. Introduced probability on a denumerable set of events. First to define games of strategy and mixed strategies; proved minimax theorem for three players and conjectured general case in 1927, a year before von Neumann.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at University of Lille (1893–1896), then returned to École Normale. Occupied chair of theory of functions at the Sorbonne from 1909 for thirty-two years. Vice-director of École Normale (1910–1914). Served as mayor of Saint-Affrique, councillor of Aveyron district, member of Chamber of Deputies (1924–1936), and minister of the navy (1925). Director of Institut Henri Poincaré from 1928 until death.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Academy in 1921; served as president in 1934.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Kenneth O. May. Complete scientific bibliography to 1939 in Selecta. Jubilé scientifique de M. Émile Borel (Paris, 1940), extended to 1956 in biographies by Collingwood and Fréchet. Borel's Notice sur les travaux scientifiques (Paris, 1912) and Supplément (1921). Key works: thesis, Annales de l'École Normale 3rd ser. 12 (1895); Leçons sur la théorie des fonctions (Paris, 1898); Mémoire sur les séries divergentes, Annales de l'École Normale 3rd ser. 16 (1899); papers on game theory in Comptes rendus (1921–1927); Les nombres inaccessibles (Paris, 1952). Secondary: Collingwood, Journal of the London Mathematical Society 34–35 (1959–1960); Fréchet, Enseignement mathématique 2nd ser. 11 (1965); L. de Broglie, Notices et discours de l'Académie des Sciences 4 (1957).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Kenneth O. May.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Studied at the University of Montpellier and received his M.D. in 1641.
Education_Locations: Montpellier, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1641
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Practiced medicine and made original contributions including the statement that cataract is a darkening of the crystalline lens, recommendation of concave mirrors for diagnostic examination of nose and throat, and first description of brain concussions. Studied chemistry and alchemy, assembling a major collection of hermetic and chemical manuscripts and books. Conducted microscopic observations and studied the history of the telescope and optical instruments. Compiled linguistic antiquities and a catalog of medicinal plants.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced medicine in Castres after 1641 and held the title of médecin ordinaire du roy in Paris from late 1653 onward.
Patronage_Notes: Received the title of médecin ordinaire du roy (ordinary physician to the king) upon moving to Paris in late 1653.
Instruments_Notes: Conducted microscopic observations and published an account of a hundred medicophysical observations with the microscope. Studied reports about the telescope and credited Zacharias Janssen (1590) and Hans Lipperhey (1608) as inventors. Described a polemoscope, a 1637 invention designed for looking around corners, useful in warfare.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Eduard Farber. Original works: Catalogue des raretés du cabinet de P. Borel (Castres, 1645); Les antiquités, rareté's plantes, minéraux et autres choses considérables de la ville et comté de Castres (Castres, 1649); Bibliotheca chimica (Paris, 1654); De vero telescopii inventore, cum brevi omnium conspicillorum historia (The Hague, 1655, 1656); Hortus (Castres, 1667); Petri Borelli historiarum et observationum medico-physicarum centuriae IV (Frankfurt-Leipzig, 1676). Secondary: R. P. Niceron, Mémoires pour servir à l'histoire des hommes illustres (Paris, 1736); August Hirsch, Biographisches Lexikon der hervorragenden Ärzte, 2nd ed. (Berlin, 1929); Mme. Puech-Milhau, Revue du Tarn, 4th ser., no. 7 (1936).

Alt_Name: Giovanni Francesco Antonio Borelli; Alphonso Borelli
Father_Notes: Father was Miguel Alonso, a Spanish infantryman stationed at Castel Nuovo in Naples. Miguel was arrested in 1615 on suspicion of conspiracy, tried in secret, found guilty, and sentenced to the galleys; the sentence was later commuted to exile. He was exonerated on appeal and returned to duty in 1617, remaining at Castel St. Elmo until his death in 1624.
Education_Notes: Likely received some medical training at the University of Naples before 1626, though no published records confirm this. Became a student of Benedetto Castelli in Rome, studying alongside Evangelista Torricelli. Exposed himself to mathematics, physiology, and planetary astronomy through his studies and travels.
Education_Locations: Naples, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Astronomy; Celestial Mechanics; Physics; Mechanics; Physiology; Iatromechanics; Epidemiology; Volcanology; Natural Philosophy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal contributions in celestial mechanics, explaining planetary motions through centripetal and centrifugal forces; mechanics of percussion and natural motions; iatromechanics and animal motion (De motu animalium); epidemiology of Sicilian fevers; volcanology of Mount Etna. Also worked on geometry, restoration of classical texts (Euclid, Apollonius), and anatomical investigations.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held public lectureship in mathematics at Messina from 1635 onwards. Taught mathematics at the University of Pisa from 1656 to 1667. Practiced medicine and conducted anatomical research. In his final years taught mathematics at the Scuole Pie in Rome from 1677 until his death.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by Queen Christina of Sweden from 1674 onwards; she agreed to bear printing costs for De motu animalium in 1679. Supported by Prince Leopold of Tuscany, who maintained high regard for Borelli and facilitated his work with the Accademia del Cimento. Mentored by Benedetto Castelli and influenced by Galileo's circle. Corresponded with and was supported by Michelangelo Ricci and other leading scientists.
Instruments_Notes: Used an excellent Campani telescope at the San Miniato observatory (1665) to determine the motions of Jupiter's satellites with extreme accuracy. Designed some instruments of his own. Built a mechanical device to demonstrate comet motion via parabolic curve, though neither the device nor its description survives.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Accademia della Fucina; Accademia del Cimento; Accademia degli Investiganti; Accademia Reale; Accademia dell'Esperienza
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of the Accademia della Fucina in Messina from the 1640s, a forum for political and intellectual discussion. Principal animus of the Accademia del Cimento in Florence (1657–1667), where he conducted extensive experimental work. Associated with the Accademia degli Investiganti in Naples. Appeared twice before Queen Christina's Accademia Reale in 1675. Member of the Accademia dell'Esperienza (Accademia Fisica-matematica) organized in Rome in 1677.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Thomas B. Settle. Original works include Discorso (Messina, 1646); Delle cagioni delle febbri maligne di Sicilia (Cosenza, 1649); Euclides restitutus (Pisa, 1658); Apollonius Pergaeus Conicorum (Florence, 1661); Theoricae mediceorum planetarum (Florence, 1666); De vi percussioni liber (Bologna, 1667); De motionibus naturalibus (1670); Historia et meteorologia incendii Aetnaei (1670); De motu animalium (Rome, 1680–1681). Adelmann, Marcello Malpighi and the Evolution of Embryology (Ithaca, 1966); Alexandre Koyré, La révolution astronomique (Paris, 1961); Max H. Fisch, The Academy of the Investigators (1953).

Father_Notes: Hugh of Lucca, a pioneer of Italian surgery; paternity is contested by some scholars but quite certain according to the entry.
Education_Notes: Learned medicine and surgery under his father Hugh of Lucca's tutelage; became a Dominican friar in 1226 at age nine when the family moved to Bologna.
Education_Locations: Bologna, Unknown, Italy, 1226, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Dominican friar from 1226; appointed papal penitentiary of Pope Innocent IV; bishop of Bitonto (1262) and bishop of Cervia (1266), though he never took possession of Bitonto and resided little in Cervia.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of antiseptic surgery, rejecting the theory of laudable pus; advocated wound cleaning, elimination of dead tissue, proper reapproximation, and protective dressing. Improved techniques for soporific sponges and mercurial ointments. Wrote on mineral salts, arsenic sublimation, falconry, and veterinary science of horses.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught medicine and surgery at the University of Bologna for thirty-three years; practiced surgery in Bologna despite his status as a friar and bishop; held ecclesiastical positions as papal penitentiary and bishop.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed papal penitentiary by Pope Innocent IV; named bishop of Bitonto and bishop of Cervia by ecclesiastical authority.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by William A. Wallace, O.P. Original works: Chirurgia (Venice, 1498, 1499, 1513, 1519, 1546), translated by E. Campbell and J. Colton as The Surgery of Theodoric (New York, 1955, 1960); Practica equorum, ed. G. Sachs (Madrid, 1936). Secondary: H. F. Garrison, An Introduction to the History of Medicine, 4th ed. (Philadelphia, 1929); Adalberto Pazzini, Enciclopedia cattolica (Rome, 1949–1954); Jacques Quétif and Jacques Échard, Scriptores ordinis praedicatorum (Paris, 1719–1721); George Sarton, Introduction to the History of Science, II, pt. 2 (Baltimore, 1931).

Alt_Name: Ignaz Edler von Born; Inigo Born
Father_Notes: Descended from a noble German family.
Education_Notes: Studied with the Jesuits in Vienna at age thirteen and briefly joined their order (about sixteen months); studied jurisprudence in Prague; traveled in Germany, the Low Countries, and France; later took up natural history and mining studies in Prague.
Education_Locations: Vienna, Unknown, Austria, 1755, Unknown; Prague, Unknown, Bohemia, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Joined the Jesuit order briefly as a youth but left after about sixteen months. Active in Freemasonry in Vienna after Joseph II's accession.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering mineralogist and mining scientist; published Lithophylacium Bornianum describing his mineral collection; arranged and described the imperial mineral collection in Vienna; invented an amalgamation process for extracting gold and silver from ores; published works on mining equipment and fossil classification.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Joined the department of mines and the mint in Prague in 1770; appointed counselor of mines in Prague; called to Vienna in 1776 by Empress Maria Theresa to arrange the imperial collection; raised to counselor of the court chamber in the department of mines and the mint in 1779.
Patronage_Notes: Empress Maria Theresa called him to Vienna in 1776 to arrange and describe the imperial mineral collection, having heard of his reputation.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Helped found a literary and philosophical society in Prague that became the forerunner of the Bohemian Scientific Society; admitted to various learned societies throughout Europe following publication of Lithophylacium Bornianum.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by J. B. Gough. Original works incl. Father_Notes: Illegitimate son of an Imeretian prince and the wife of an army doctor; father was a nobleman.
Education_Institution: St. Petersburg Academy of Medicine and Surgery
Education_Notes: Studied at the St. Petersburg Academy of Medicine and Surgery from 1850 to 1856 under the direction of N. N. Zinin. Defended his doctoral thesis in 1858 on the analogy of phosphoric and arsenic acids.
Education_Locations: St. Petersburg, Unknown, Russia, 1850, 1856
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in organic and physiological chemistry. First to obtain fluorine benzol and developed fluorination methods for organic compounds (1861). Developed bromine-producing fatty acid synthesis (1869). Conducted extensive studies on polymerization and condensation of aldehydes (1863–1874), discovering aldol condensation. Developed azotometric method for quantitative determination of urea (1876).
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held a professorship at the Academy of Medicine and Surgery from 1864 and helped found medical courses for women there.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Oluf Clusen was a rector (school headmaster).
Education_Institution: University of Copenhagen; University of Angers
Education_Notes: Studied medicine at University of Copenhagen under Thomas Bartholin, Olaus Worm, and Simon Pauli from 1644. Traveled in Germany, Netherlands, France, England, and Italy from 1660–1664 to prepare for university posts. Received M.D. from University of Angers in 1664.
Education_Locations: Copenhagen, Unknown, Denmark, 1644, Unknown; Angers, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1664
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Alchemy; Botany; Medicine; Philosophy; Natural History
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Renowned for polymath erudition spanning chemistry, alchemy, botany, and philology. Wrote histories of chemistry's development and defended Hermeticism and the authenticity of alchemical texts. Believed chemistry approached divine contemplation and opposed mechanistic critiques of Paracelsian medicine.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor ordinarius of philology and professor extraordinarius of botany and chemistry at University of Copenhagen from 1660 for nearly thirty years. Established large and profitable medical practice; served as royal physician to Frederick III and Christian V. Appointed counselor to Supreme Court of Justice (1686) and Royal Chancellery (1689).
Patronage_Notes: Served as tutor to sons of Joachim Gersdorf, lord high steward (Rigshofmester), from 1655. Royal physician to Frederick III and Christian V. Appointed to state advisory posts (Supreme Court counselor, Royal Chancellery).
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Descended from a long line of distinguished civil servants; on his mother's side related to the Kamp family, owners of the pioneering metallurgical firm Kamp & Harkort.
Education_Institution: Technische Hochschule Karlsruhe; Technische Hochschule Danzig; Technische Hochschule Munich; Technische Hochschule Berlin
Education_Notes: Studied electrical engineering at Karlsruhe, Danzig, and Munich. In 1930 became an assistant to Adolf Wilhelm Matthias at the High-Voltage Institute of the Technische Hochschule in Berlin.
Education_Locations: Karlsruhe, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Danzig, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Munich, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Berlin, Unknown, Germany, 1930, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in electron microscopy from its conception in 1931. Contributed significantly to the design and development of the transmission electron microscope, became an outstanding expert in associated photographic techniques, and extended its use to metallic surfaces by reflection methods. Promoted the introduction of electron microscopy into many fields of research, notably in the life sciences.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant at the High-Voltage Institute of the Technische Hochschule Berlin from 1930. From 1937 worked with Siemens on electron microscope development. After World War II, formed and directed an electron-microscopy institute in Düsseldorf with joint government and private support. From 1953 served as professor of electron optics at the Technische Hochschule in Aachen.
Patronage_Notes: Persuaded Siemens to support the electron microscope project in 1937, giving the firm a lead in the field. After World War II, the Düsseldorf institute received joint government and private support.
Instruments_Notes: Had a leading part in the design of the transmission electron microscope, which he and Ernst Ruska put on the market in 1939. Became an outstanding expert in associated photographic techniques and extended the instrument's use to metallic surfaces by reflection methods.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: German Society for Electron Microscopy; International Federation of Electron Microscope Societies
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Helped found the German Society for Electron Microscopy. Was the principal organizer of the International Federation of Electron Microscope Societies and served as its president from its foundation in 1954 until his death in 1956.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Charles Süsskind. Publications through 1952 in Poggendorff's Biographisch-literarisches Handwörterbuch, VIIa. Alt_Name: Vladislav Josephowitsch Bortkewitsch; Ladislaus Josephowitsch Bortkewitsch
Father_Notes: Joseph Ivanowitsch Bortkewitsch, a member of the gentry from Kovno province; colonel and instructor in artillery and mathematics; author of textbooks on elementary mathematics and works in economics and finance.
Education_Institution: University of St. Petersburg; University of Strasbourg; University of Göttingen; University of Vienna; University of Leipzig
Education_Notes: Graduated from the Faculty of Law at the University of St. Petersburg in 1890; took postgraduate course in political economy and statistics; studied under G. F. Knapp at Strasbourg (1891–1892), W. Lexis at Göttingen (1892), and at Vienna and Leipzig; defended doctoral dissertation in philosophy at Göttingen in 1893.
Education_Locations: St. Petersburg, Unknown, Russia, Unknown, 1890; Strasbourg, Unknown, France, 1891, 1892; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, 1892, 1893; Vienna, Unknown, Austria, Unknown, Unknown; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in mathematical statistics and probability theory; formulated the law of small numbers (law of rare events) and demonstrated its connection to the Poisson distribution; contributed to order statistics, theory of runs, and application of probability to actuarial science and political economy; proponent of connecting statistics with probability theory following Lexis.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Privatdozent and lecturer in actuarial science and theoretical statistics at Strasbourg (1895–1897); clerk in the Railway Pension Committee office in St. Petersburg (1897–1907); taught statistics at Alexandrowsky Lyceum (1899–1900); extraordinary professor of statistics at University of Berlin from 1901; ordinary professor of statistics and political economy from 1920.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Swedish Academy of Sciences; Royal Statistical Society; American Statistical Association; International Statistical Institute
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of four major statistical and scientific societies.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Studied under Salvatore Pincherle at the University of Bologna, receiving his degree summa cum laude in 1889. Completed postgraduate studies in Paris in 1892–1893.
Education_Locations: Bologna, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1889; Paris, Unknown, France, 1892, 1893
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Analysis; Topology; History of Mathematics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early work in topology; later research in analysis including calculus of finite differences, distributive operations, continuous fractions, order of infinity, convergence of infinite algorithms, and asymptotic behavior of series. Extensive historical studies of Paolo Ruffini, infinitesimal analysis of the seventeenth century, Torricelli, Cataldi, Fibonacci, Dal Ferro, Tartaglia, Cardano, Ferrari, Bombelli, and ancient Sumerian, Assyrian, Babylonian, and Egyptian mathematics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: University assistant at Bologna until 1891; professor at the lyceum of Modica, Sicily from 1891; taught in Rome from 1893 to 1900; professor of infinitesimal calculus at the University of Modena from 1900, serving as dean of the Faculty of Science from 1913 to 1919; professor of analytical geometry at the University of Bologna from 1919 until his retirement in 1936.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Self-taught naturalist; by age sixteen was corresponding with established French naturalists; no formal institutional education is recorded.
Education_Locations: None
Scientific_Disciplines: Biology; Botany; Zoology; Natural History; Zoogeography; Anthropology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Leader of botanical collecting expeditions; contributed to theory and knowledge of island faunas and zoogeography of the seas; pioneered biogeographical classification of oceans; studied classification of human races by physical characteristics, dividing mankind into fifteen species in 1827.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Conscripted into the French army in 1799 and remained an officer until retirement in 1840; seconded to Baudin's expedition to Australia in 1801; served in Germany and Spain; entered politics as deputy for Lot-et-Garonne in 1815; edited Dictionnaire classique de l'histoire naturelle from 1822 to 1831; elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1834; led scientific expeditions to the Peloponnese (1829) and Algeria (1840).
Patronage_Notes: Led official French government scientific expeditions to the Peloponnese in 1829 and Algeria in 1840; elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1834.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1834.

Father_Notes: Paul Bosc d'Antic, son of a surgeon from the Tarn, was a master glassmaker and physician acquainted with leading naturalists of his time.

Education_Notes: Attended Collège de Dijon in youth; assiduously followed courses at the Jardin du Roi under Buffon, where Thouin and Antoine-Laurent de Jussieu taught. No formal degree is recorded.
Education_Locations: Dijon, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural History; Botany; Zoology; Entomology; Agronomy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Described numerous insect genera including Ortheziinae, Ripiphorus, and parasitic worms; discovered and named plant species, particularly Gramineae; conducted extensive natural history surveys in the Carolinas; pioneered practical natural history and agricultural science.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Secretary of the Intendance des Postes (1777); postmaster general under the Girondist ministry (1792); vice-consul in Wilmington, Delaware; consul in New York (1797, never took office); inspector of gardens and nurseries (1803); member of the Institute (1806); professor at the Muséum d'histoire Naturelle (1825).
Patronage_Notes: Held various government posts including postmaster general and consul; member of the Institute.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Co-founded the Société Linnéenne de Paris between 1790 and 1792; elected member of the Institute in 1806.

Father_Notes: Opened a gas and plumbing equipment business; encouraged his son's interest in natural sciences and technology.
Education_Notes: Completed training in an ironworks and mechanical engineering before turning to chemistry. Studied chemistry at Leipzig for four years and obtained his doctorate.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered high-pressure chemical synthesis methods. Transformed Haber's laboratory ammonia synthesis into large-scale industrial production through development of suitable catalysts, equipment design, and process engineering. Also worked on urea synthesis, methanol synthesis, carbon hydrogenation, and synthetic rubber production.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Employed by Badische Anilin- und Sodafabrik in Ludwigshafen as a chemist and engineer. Became president of I. G. Farben in 1925.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Studied philosophy, mathematics, and languages at Leipzig; received M.A. in 1727 and joined the philosophy faculty as junior lecturer in mathematics and physics.
Education_Locations: Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1727
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in promoting the study of electricity in Germany from 1742–1745; revived and improved Hauksbee's electrical machine with a prime conductor; his demonstrations inspired the discovery of the Leyden jar condenser; also wrote on eclipses and astronomy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Junior lecturer in mathematics and physics at University of Leipzig from 1727; held the chair of natural philosophy at University of Wittenberg from 1738 to 1760.
Instruments_Notes: Revived and significantly improved Hauksbee's electrical machine by adding a prime conductor that greatly enhanced its power; used it to produce striking demonstrations that advanced the study of electricity.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Alt_Name: Jagadish Chandra Bose; J. C. Bose
Father_Notes: Father was a deputy magistrate.
Education_Institution: St. Xavier's College; University of Cambridge
Education_Notes: Studied at St. Xavier's, a Jesuit college in Calcutta; went to London to study medicine; transferred to Cambridge University on scholarship to Christ's College and graduated in natural science in 1884.
Education_Locations: Calcutta, Unknown, India, Unknown, Unknown; Cambridge, Unknown, England, Unknown, 1884
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted meticulous experiments on quasi-optical properties of short radio waves and improved the coherer; formulated theory of contact-sensitive substances contributing to solid-state physics. Later devoted himself to comparing responses of animal and plant tissues to stimuli, devising sensitive automatic recorders to measure plant growth and microscopic changes caused by various stimuli.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed professor of physics at Presidency College, Calcutta, from 1884 until retirement in 1915. Founded and directed the Bose Research Institute from 1917, supported largely by his own considerable fortune supplemented by private contributions and government of India funding.
Patronage_Notes: Government of India contributed to the Bose Research Institute; private well-wishers also supported the institute. Bose possessed considerable personal wealth.
Instruments: Coherer; Radio Wave Generator; Automatic Recorder
Instruments_Notes: Designed and constructed fine radio wave generating apparatus; made improvements to the coherer, a tube of iron filings used as an early radio detector. Devised extremely sensitive automatic recorders to measure plant growth with great precision.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1920, the first Indian physicist so honored. Papers were rejected by the Royal Society in 1901 and 1904 before his later election.

Father_Notes: Father Nikola Bošković was a merchant of Dubrovnik; mother Paula Bettera was daughter of Bartolomeo Bettera, a merchant from Bergamo. Family of average means but noted for literary interests.
Education_Institution: Jesuit College of Dubrovnik; Sant'Andrea Novitiate; Collegium Romanum
Education_Notes: Began education at Jesuit college of Dubrovnik; entered novitiate of Sant'Andrea in Rome in 1725 at age fourteen; continued at Collegium Romanum where he studied mathematics, physics, astronomy, and geodesy independently. In 1735 began studying Newton's Opticks and Principia. No formal degree recorded.
Education_Locations: Dubrovnik, Unknown, Yugoslavia, Unknown, Unknown; Rome, Unknown, Italy, 1725, Unknown; Rome, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Became a Jesuit; remained in the order until its suppression in 1773. Had discussions with representatives of the Church of England during travels.
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural Philosophy; Mathematics; Astronomy; Physics; Geodesy; Optics; Mechanics; Meteorology; Geology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Polymath whose work spanned instrumental sciences (astronomy, optics, geodesy) and abstract sciences (mathematics, mechanics, natural philosophy). Developed universal law of forces and theory of matter as dynamic configuration of force centers. Advanced methods in astronomical observation, lens improvement, and geodetic measurement. Contributed to geophysics and meteorology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed professor of mathematics at Collegium Romanum in 1740 despite incomplete theological studies. Undertook practical and diplomatic commissions for papal and ecclesiastical authorities, including investigation of St. Peter's cupola and planning drainage of Pontine marshes. Professor of mathematics at University of Pavia from 1763; worked at Scuole Palatine in Milan from 1770. Served as director of optics for French navy in Paris in final years.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by papal government under Benedict XIV for geodetic and hydraulic projects. Represented Republic of Lucca before Hapsburg court in Vienna. Received patronage from French crown and arranged post as director of optics for French navy. Supported by influential friends including aristocratic patrons during travels.
Instruments: Circular Micrometer; Leveler; Micrometric Wedge; Vitrometer; Achromatic Lens
Instruments_Notes: Invented circular micrometer for astronomical observation; designed leveler for verifying astronomical quadrants using water-filled canal; developed micrometric wedge for measuring distances between planes. Worked on improvement of achromatic lenses and optical devices; collaborated with Stephen Conti of Lucca on lens fabrication. Designed various astronomical instruments for Brera observatory.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Academy of Sciences, Paris; Royal Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected corresponding member of Academy of Sciences in Paris following 1738 publication on aurora borealis; correspondent of Dortous de Mairan. Elected fellow of Royal Society on 15 January 1761; dedicated poem on eclipses to the Society.

Education_Notes: Classical course at Dartmouth College; frequented the observatory there and learned to handle astronomical instruments and reduce observations.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work on positions and proper motions of fundamental stars. Developed homogeneous system of stellar declinations; created catalogs of star positions and proper motions; computed orbits of comets; observed transit of Venus.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as clerk in government offices in Washington, D.C.; appointed assistant astronomer for 49th parallel survey (1872–1876); director of Dudley Observatory from 1876 until death; superintendent of weights and measures of New York (1883–1906); associate editor then editor of Astronomical Journal (1897–1909).
Patronage_Notes: U.S. government survey appointment (1872); Carnegie Institution financed major catalog work and established department of meridian astrometry under his direction (1906); elected to National Academy of Sciences (1889), Königlich Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften (1910), and Imperial Academy of Sciences of St. Petersburg.
Instruments: Zenith Telescope; Meridian Circle; Pistor and Martins Meridian Circle
Instruments_Notes: Used zenith telescope for latitude determinations during 49th parallel survey; employed Pistor and Martins meridian circle at Dudley Observatory, investigating its flexure and division corrections to achieve high precision; moved great meridian circle temporarily to Argentina for San Luis observations.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Astronomical Society; National Academy of Sciences; Königlich Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften; Imperial Academy of Sciences of St. Petersburg
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to National Academy of Sciences (1889); elected to Prussian Academy (1910) and Russian Academy; awarded gold medal of Royal Astronomical Society (1905) and Lalande Prize of Paris Académie des Sciences (1911).

Father_Notes: Father was a tailor; mother was Marie Martinet.
Education_Notes: None
Education_Locations: None
Religion_Notes: Inferred from secondary literature reference to La France protestante; no explicit statement in the entry.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed and propagated Desargues's projective geometry and perspective methods; applied perspective to curvilinear surfaces and gnomonics; illustrated scientific works on chemistry, light, and botany.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as a draftsman and engraver in Paris from around 1625; published numerous treatises and illustrated scientific books; received royal patronage for botanical engravings.
Patronage_Notes: Commissioned to engrave botanical plates by order of King Louis XIV for the Recueil des plantes.

Father_Notes: Father Barthélemy Bossut died when Charles was six months old; Charles was raised by a paternal uncle.
Education_Notes: Entered the Jesuit Collège de Lyon at age fourteen as a student of Père Béraud, a mathematician. Took minor ecclesiastical orders and became an abbé until 1792. Aided in professional formation by d'Alembert, Clairaut, and Abbé Charles Étienne Louis Camus.
Education_Locations: Lyon, Unknown, France, 1744, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Took minor ecclesiastical orders and was an abbé until 1792.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Contributed to European scientific education through textbooks on mathematics and mechanics. Conducted experiments on fluid resistance and wrote on mechanics applied to ships and planetary motion. Also wrote a history of mathematics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of mathematics at École du Génie at Mézières from 1752 to 1768, then examiner of students until 1794. Held chair of hydrodynamics at the Louvre from 1775 to 1780. Examiner at École Polytechnique. Supported as an abbé until 1792.
Patronage_Notes: Aided by d'Alembert, Clairaut, and Abbé Camus in his professional formation. d'Alembert took him as a student and sponsored his admission as correspondant to the Académie des Sciences in 1753. Turgot established the chair of hydrodynamics for him at the Louvre.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Academy of Bologna; Academy of Turin; Academy of St. Petersburg; Academy of Lyons; Academy of Toulouse
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Admitted as correspondant to the Académie des Sciences on 12 May 1753; rose to géométre, mécanicien, and mathématicien. Won or shared Academy prizes in 1761, 1762, and 1765 for memoirs on mechanics and planetary motion. Elected to scientific academies of Bologna, Turin, and St. Petersburg; won prizes from academies of Lyons and Toulouse.

Father_Notes: Edinburgh graduate and Liverpool physician; died in 1774 when John was an infant.
Education_Notes: Attended Joseph Priestley's chemical lecture course at Hackney College in 1792; studied with an apothecary and attended Liverpool General Dispensary; studied medicine at Edinburgh University from autumn 1794, where he was elected member and president of the Medical Society; graduated M.D. in 1798 with thesis on secretion of bile.
Education_Locations: Hackney, Unknown, England, 1792, 1792; Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, 1794, 1798
Religion_Notes: Grew up in Liverpool's active Protestant Dissenter community.
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Medical Chemistry; Medicine; Physiology; Natural History
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Primary research interest was medical chemistry with valuable contributions to body fluids and urinary components. Gave first complete description of hay fever. Published extensively on respiration, galvanism, and medical history. Wrote numerous medical and scientific articles for journals and encyclopedias.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Physician to Liverpool General Dispensary after 1798; developed extensive medical and chemical consulting practice; chemical lecturer at Guy's Hospital in London after 1817; edited Annals of Philosophy with A. Aikin; prolific author and journal contributor.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Geological Society; Royal Society; Medico-Chirurgical Society; Linnean Society; Zoological Society; Horticultural Society; Royal Society of Literature
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Secretary of Geological Society (president 1826); council member of Royal Society (vice-president 1832); treasurer of Medico-Chirurgical Society; served on councils of Linnean, Zoological, Horticultural societies and Royal Society of Literature.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Arnold Thackray. Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: University of Pavia; University of Padua
Education_Notes: Studied medicine at Pavia and continued studies at Padua under Gabriele Falloppio.
Education_Locations: Pavia, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Padua, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Military surgeon with expertise in gunshot wounds; contributed to understanding of cardiac anatomy and fetal circulation, though attributions were partly erroneous; described fused kidneys with horseshoe configuration; wrote on medical ethics and skeptical of astrology in medicine.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced medicine in Asti; served as military surgeon with French forces from at least 1544; physician to Charles IX from 1560; served in royal medical service under Catherine de' Medici and the duke of Anjou (later Henry III); temporarily engaged in 1575 to treat Henry I of Lorraine, duke of Guise.
Patronage_Notes: Enjoyed favor and confidence of Catherine de' Medici, queen mother, partly due to shared Italian origin; she arranged his transfer to service the duke of Anjou; treated Henry I of Lorraine, duke of Guise.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Studied physics, mathematics, and chemistry at the University of Berlin from 1908 to 1912. Obtained his doctorate in 1914 under Max Planck for a study of molecular theory of refraction, reflection, dispersion, and extinction.
Education_Locations: Berlin, Unknown, Germany, 1908, 1914
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Nuclear Physics; Atomic Physics; Experimental Physics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in coincidence counting methods and experimental nuclear physics. Major contributions to understanding scattering of alpha and beta rays, cosmic rays, nuclear transmutation, and the discovery of the neutron. Studied electron scattering, Compton effect, and beta and gamma spectra over more than thirty years.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught physics at the University of Berlin from 1920 to 1931. Accepted professorship of physics at Giessen in 1931. Became director of the Max Planck Institute at Heidelberg in 1934, where he remained until his death. Worked at the Physikalische-Technische Reichsanstalt radioactivity laboratory.
Patronage_Notes: Worked under Hans Geiger's invitation at the Physikalische-Technische Reichsanstalt. Directed the Max Planck Institute at Heidelberg. Received the Max Planck Prize and shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Max Born in 1954.
Instruments: Geiger Counter; Van de Graaf Accelerator; Cyclotron
Instruments_Notes: Modified the Geiger counter for use in coincidence experiments, a novel procedure in 1924. Involved in construction of a Van de Graaf accelerator at the Max Planck Institute and planning of a cyclotron completed in 1943.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: None

Pioneering research on osmotic resistance of red blood cells, osmotic pressure of organic liquids across animal classes, and muscle physiology (sarcoplasm and myofibril function). Also conducted research on nutrition physiology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant in physiology at Institute of Higher, Practical, and Postgraduate Studies of Florence (1894); Privatdozent in physiology (1896); director of Institute of Physiology at University of Genoa (1902); director of Institute of Physiology at University of Naples (1905); director of physiology department at Zoological Station, Naples (1915–1923).
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of the Reale Accademia d'Italia.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Entered University of Halle in 1824 to study theology and philosophy; regularly attended chemistry lectures of Johann S. C. Schweigger. Left university in 1828 and continued chemistry research while employed as a tutor. Received doctorate from University of Halle in 1837.
Education_Locations: Halle, Unknown, Germany, 1824, 1828
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Broad interests in chemistry with emphasis on practical applications. Invented electroforming process for reproducing illustrations (1841); demonstrated nickel electroplating (1843) and high-purity iron production by electrolytic deposition (1845); credited with independent discovery of guncotton; introduced improved match heads with red phosphorus mixture (1847). Investigated acetylides, chrome alum, chromic oxide, and chemistry of indium, thallium, and cesium. Devised tests for nitrites and chlorates still in use. Work was mainly qualitative, ingenious, and accurate.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Employed as a tutor after leaving university in 1828. Called to the Physicalischer Verein at Frankfurt am Main in 1835, where he taught physics and chemistry for the remainder of his life.
Instruments_Notes: Invented a kindling apparatus modified from Schönbein's lamp. Developed an electroforming process for reproducing illustrations, widely used in 1841.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Education_Notes: None
Education_Locations: None
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Discovered and excavated evidence of Stone Age cultures at Abbeville, publishing findings in a series of monographs. Work initially rejected locally but later validated by prominent British scientists including Charles Lyell.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Director of the customshouse at Abbeville; pursued archaeology during leisure time.
Patronage_Notes: Work supported and validated by eminent British scientists including Lyell, who visited his excavation sites in 1859.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: His work was rejected by the scientific society of Abbeville.

Father_Notes: Jean-Henri Boué was a shipbuilder and shipowner. Ami's mother, Suzanne de Chapeaurouge, was the daughter of an Alsatian merchant settled in Hamburg.
Education_Notes: Studied medicine at Edinburgh from 1814, where mineralogist Robert Jameson influenced his interest in geology and botany. Continued medical studies in Paris (1818–1819), Berlin (1820), and Vienna (1821), but devoted himself exclusively to geology thereafter.
Education_Locations: Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, 1814, 1817
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in geological mapping and stratigraphy of Europe. Published major works on Scottish, German, Austrian, and Italian geology. Studied botanical geography and fossil stratigraphy, including Cretaceous and Jurassic formations. Synthesized geological knowledge in a global geological map.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Inherited wealth at age twenty allowed him to pursue geology independently. Elected member of the Academy of Sciences of Vienna in 1849. Owned property at Vöslau where he maintained gardens and vineyards.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Co-founded the Société Géologique de France in 1830 with Constant Prevost, Paul Deshayes, and Jules Desnoyers; served as president in 1835. Elected member of the Academy of Sciences of Vienna in 1849.

Father_Notes: Pierre-Yves de Bougainville was a notary; Louis Antoine joined the army to escape this profession.
Education_Notes: Completed schooling and came under the influence of d'Alembert, who guided his early mathematical work. No university degree is named.
Education_Locations: None
Religion_Notes: Inferred from French context and burial in the Panthéon. Despite royalist sympathies, survived the Terror.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early career in mathematics: wrote Traité du calcul-intégral (1754–1756), extending L'Hospital's calculus textbook to integral calculus and updating differential calculus. Achieved greatest fame as an explorer and circumnavigator (1766–1769). Made systematic astronomical observations of longitude during his voyage; discovered islands in the Pacific and confirmed the existence of pouched mammals in the East Indies.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Joined the army to escape his father's profession; saw service with Montcalm in Canada and in North America. Promoted in both army and navy. Elected to the Académie des Sciences and the Royal Society of London. Became a count of the empire under Napoleon and a senator.
Patronage_Notes: Received many honors and promotions from the French crown following his circumnavigation. Became a count of the empire under Napoleon and served as a senator.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Royal Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Royal Society of London in 1756 following publication of his calculus treatise. Associate of the Académie des Sciences, which noticed his mathematical work in January 1753.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Wilma George. Father_Notes: Jean Bouguer was royal professor of hydrography.
Education_Notes: No formal degree recorded. At age fifteen, upon his father's death, Bouguer obtained the professorship of hydrography, indicating early training under his father.
Education_Locations: None
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Optics; Geodesy; Hydrography; Navigation; Astronomy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of photometry and atmospheric optics; conducted geodetic measurements on the Peru expedition (1735–1744); made discoveries in light transmission (Bouguer's law); invented the heliometer; contributed to naval architecture and navigation theory.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Royal professor of hydrography from age fifteen; associate geometrician of the Académie Royale des Sciences (1731), full Academician (1735); participated in state-sponsored Peru expedition.
Patronage_Notes: Sent on the Peru expedition by royal order to measure an arc of the meridian near the equator; supported by the Académie Royale des Sciences through prizes and membership.
Instruments_Notes: Invented the heliometer in 1748. Designed several ingenious kinds of photometers, including a method of goniophotometry, demonstrating considerable instrumental skill.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Associate geometrician (1731); full Academician (1735); won three Academy prizes for essays (1727, 1729, 1731); contributed more than thirty articles to the Mémoires.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by W. E. Knowles Middleton. Father_Notes: Veterinary surgeon; his method of treating cryptorchism in horses and pigs inspired Bouin's interest in testicular physiology.
Education_Notes: Studied at Nancy, where he was attracted to histology by his teacher Auguste Prenant. Received docteur en médecine in 1897 with a thesis on testicular degeneration.
Education_Locations: Nancy, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1897
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in reproductive endocrinology; with Paul Ancel elucidated dual function of testis (gametogenesis and hormone secretion) and corpus luteum physiology. Conducted extensive experimental work on laboratory animals and made significant contributions to understanding secondary sexual characteristics and ovulation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Préparateur d'histologie at Nancy Faculty of Medicine (1892); professeur-agrégé of anatomy/histology (1898); professeur titulaire of histology at Algiers (1907), Nancy (1908), and Strasbourg (1918). Also practiced as a physician.
Patronage_Notes: Received major grant from Rockefeller Foundation in 1927 for construction of Institute of Histology. Promoted by Caisse Nationale des Sciences (forerunner of CNRS) around 1930.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Academy of Sciences of Paris; Académie Nationale de Médecine, Paris; Royal Belgian Academy of Medicine of Brussels
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Membre titulaire of Academy of Sciences of Paris and Académie Nationale de Médecine; honorary foreign member of Royal Belgian Academy of Medicine of Brussels.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Marc Klein. R. Courrier, Notice sur la vie et les travaux de Pol Bouin (Paris, 1962).

Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: Faculty of Sciences of Toulouse; Museum of Natural History
Education_Notes: Enrolled at Faculty of Sciences of Toulouse in 1880; earned licence in natural sciences and licence in physical science over four years. Completed teaching certificate in 1887 at Museum of Natural History in Paris after receiving scholarship in 1886. Received doctorate in natural sciences in 1892.
Education_Locations: Toulouse, Unknown, France, 1880, 1884; Paris, Unknown, France, 1886, 1892
Scientific_Disciplines: Geology; Paleontology; Natural History; Philosophy; Anthropology; Archaeology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Initially focused on stratigraphy and petrography; shifted to paleontology under influence of Gaudry. Central figure in establishing prehistory and paleoanthropology in France. Synthesized geological, archaeological, and zoological approaches to human evolution. Major work: Les hommes fossiles (1921), standard paleoanthropology text for quarter century. Detailed anatomical study of Neanderthal remains from Chapelle-aux-Saints (1911–1913) established influential but later-disputed view of Neanderthals as distinct, non-ancestral species.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Brief teaching assignment at Clermont-Ferrand (1890); préparateur in paleontological laboratory at Museum of Natural History (1892); succeeded Gaudry as professor of paleontology at museum, held until retirement in 1936. Founder and editor of L'anthropologie (1890–1920). Director of Institute for Human Paleontology from 1920 until death.
Patronage_Notes: Institute for Human Paleontology founded in 1920 by Albert I of Monaco, impressed by remains uncovered in his principality; Boule appointed first director.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Founder of L'anthropologie in 1890; editor 1893–1920. First director of Institute for Human Paleontology from 1920; founded its Archives and directed its research program.

Father_Notes: None

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Studied the morphology of the Marne Basin and sedimentary terrains; observed stratification and fossil deposits; developed theories on the universal deluge and the elasticity of the earth's strata as the origin of oceanic distribution.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Joined the army as an engineer; appointed to the Département des Ponts et Chaussées in 1745 as superintendent of works; deputy engineer from 1749; posted to the generality of Paris and later Tours; retired in 1759 with the rank of engineer.

Alt_Name: Bullialdus; Clarissimus Bullialdus; Bouillalds; Boulliaud; Bulliald
Father_Notes: Father shared an early interest in astronomical observation with Boulliau.
Education_Notes: Early studies in law and the humanities; no university degree is named. Resumed interest in astronomical observation upon settling in Paris in 1633.
Education_Locations: None
Religion_Notes: Born to Calvinist parents; converted to Roman Catholicism at age twenty-one and was ordained a priest about four years later.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pursued a predominantly scientific career as an astronomer and mathematician. Made significant contributions to heliocentric theory and the inverse-square hypothesis in astronomy. Published mathematical works on spirals and infinite arithmetic, though these had little influence. Established the periodicity of the variable star Mira Ceti. One of the last reputable scholars to maintain confidence in astrology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Ordained as a priest. Served as librarian to the brothers du Puy, then to de Thou (French ambassador in Holland), and ultimately to the Bibliothèque Royale in Paris.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: In 1663 elected among the first foreign associates to the Royal Society of London. Never elected to the Académie des Sciences, though he participated in the groups that gave rise to it.

Father_Notes: None

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialized in differential and integral calculus, differential geometry, systems of straight lines in space, orthogonal surfaces, and analytic functions. With Briot, clarified Cauchy's analytic methods and studied elliptic functions and differential equations.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor at lycée of Marseilles; professor at Faculté des Sciences of Lyons; taught special mathematics at Lycée Bonaparte (1852–1858) and Lycée Louis-le-Grand (1858–1867); maître de conférences at École Normale Supérieure; répétiteur at École Polytechnique; chair of differential and integral calculus at the Sorbonne (1874–1884).
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1875.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Secondary education in Gray and Dijon; admitted to École Polytechnique in 1850, graduated first in his class in 1852; continued studies at École des Mines in Paris. Defended two theses in celestial mechanics before the Faculté des Sciences in Paris on 3 December 1855.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1850, 1852; Paris, Unknown, France, 1852, 1855
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Analytical Mechanics; Celestial Mechanics; Algebra; Geometry; Infinitesimal Geometry
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal contributions in differential equations in dynamics, composition of movements, and reduction of the three-body problem to the plane case. In infinitesimal geometry, memoir on deformation of surfaces containing theorems on ruled surfaces and minimal surfaces.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Mining engineer and professor of mechanics and mining at École des Mines of Saint-Étienne from July 1855 to end of 1859; lecturer in descriptive geometry at École Polytechnique from 1859; professor at École des Mines and professor of mechanics at École Polytechnique from 1860–1861.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Candidate for membership in the Académie des Sciences in April 1862 but was defeated by Ossian Bonnet. Received the grand prize in mathematics from the Académie des Sciences in 1861 for his paper on the deformation of surfaces.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Completed apprenticeship under master apothecaries in Paris; purchased an apothecary's license from the house of Monsieur (Gaston of Orléans).
Education_Locations: None
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted systematic chemical analysis of plant, animal, and mineral substances; analyzed normal and pathological organic liquids and fresh and salt water. Used distillation to identify phlegm, acids, volatile salts, oils, solid salts, and residues. Advanced experimental methodology and hypothesis-driven research in chemistry.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held two offices in the household of Monsieur (the king's younger brother): assistant apothecary and apothecary to the stable, for approximately twenty years. Became member of the Royal Academy of Sciences in 1666 and conducted research in the Academy's laboratory from 1667 until 1686, continuing experimentation at home until his death.
Patronage_Notes: Purchased apothecary's license from the house of Monsieur (Gaston of Orléans), the king's younger brother, and held two offices in his household. Membership in the Royal Academy of Sciences provided institutional support and access to laboratory facilities.
Instruments_Notes: Installed and equipped the Royal Academy of Sciences laboratory with furnaces and distilling apparatus. Distillation was his principal technique for analyzing plant substances.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member when the Academy was created in 1666. Installed the Academy's laboratory next to the meeting room and conducted research there from March 1667 to end of 1686, then continued work at home until his death.

Father_Notes: Maximilien Michon was a barber-surgeon; the family adopted the name Bourdelot from the mother's side in 1634.
Education_Notes: Began medical studies in Paris around 1629 under the patronage of his uncles Edmé Bourdelot and Jean Bourdelot; passed medical examinations while accompanying Prince Henri II de Condé on campaigns in Spain; earned the title of king's physician by 1642.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1629, 1642
Religion_Notes: Obtained the living of the abbey of Massay in Berry, which gave him the title abbé; no explicit statement of faith in the entry.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Practiced medicine and gained fame for a gout treatment; wrote a history of music published posthumously by his nephews, which has been studied by music historians.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as physician to François de Noailles, Prince Henri II de Condé, Queen Christina of Sweden, and the Great Condé; held the living of the abbey of Massay; maintained a private medical practice with notable patients including Mme. de Sévigné.
Patronage_Notes: Served as physician to Prince Henri II de Condé and his son Louis II; gained marked influence over Queen Christina of Sweden (1651–1653); received patronage from François de Noailles.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Founded the Académie Bourdelot around 1642, which held biweekly meetings attended by nobles, men of letters, philosophers, and scientists including Roberval, Gassendi, and the Pascals. The academy presented vacuum experiments in 1647/1648, resumed in 1664, and continued until 1684. Its Conférences were published in 1672 by Le Gallois.

Father_Notes: Merchant who died in 1830; expected his son to enter business.
Education_Notes: Sent to Nuremberg for two years to learn German; apprenticed in an optician's shop for two years after his father's death in 1830.
Education_Locations: None
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Designed and built steam engines and pressure gauges. Invented the metallic manometer (Bourdon tube), a pressure gauge without mercury, patented 18 June 1849. The Bourdon tube, a metal tube with elliptical cross section, became the most widely used pressure indicator for ranges of 15 to 100,000 pounds per square inch.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Established an instrument and machine shop in 1832 at 71 Faubourg du Temple, Paris, operating until 1872 when his sons took over management. Built approximately two hundred small steam engines and numerous pressure gauges.
Instruments: Bourdon Tube; Pressure Gauge; Steam Engine; Anemometer
Instruments_Notes: Invented the metallic manometer (Bourdon tube), a pressure gauge without mercury, in which a metal tube with elliptical cross section responds to internal pressure. Also designed steam engines with glass cylinders and an anemometer employing a venturi tube.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Presented a model steam engine to the Société d'Encouragement pour l'Industrie Nationale in 1832. Awarded the Legion of Honor in 1851 following the success of his gauges at the London International Exhibition.

Father_Notes: Owner of the Château de Fabert near Metz; formed a large mineralogical collection that stimulated Bournon's early interest in mineralogy.
Education_Notes: No formal institutional education is recorded. His mineralogical knowledge developed through his father's collection and his own research.
Education_Locations: None
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early supporter of Haüy's crystal structure theories; published approximately twenty scientific memoirs on mineralogical species and crystal variations. Major work was the three-volume Traité complet de la chaux carbonatée et de l'arragonite (1808) describing crystal variations of calcite and aragonite. First described the mineral bournonite completely in 1804.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Pursued a military career as lieutenant of the marshals of France; lectured frequently on mineralogy in England; became director general of the mineralogical cabinet of Louis XVIII after the Restoration.
Patronage_Notes: Organized large mineralogical collections for Lord Grenville, Sir Abraham Hume, and Sir John St. Aubyn; appointed director general of the mineralogical cabinet of Louis XVIII.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1802; helped found the Geological Society and served as its first foreign secretary from 1811 to 1814.

Father_Notes: Came from a family of small farmers.
Education_Notes: Attended the small seminary at Montpellier; received the baccalauréat; obtained licence ès sciences in 1851; earned docteur ès sciences in 1867 for his thesis on heat propagation. Self-taught in scientific matters beyond formal study.
Education_Locations: Montpellier, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown

Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Mechanics; Mathematics; Hydraulics; Elasticity; Heat Transfer
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Made important contributions to all branches of mathematical physics except electromagnetism. Studied light waves, heat theory, hydrodynamics, fluid flow, whirlpools, liquid waves, pulverulent masses, and elasticity. Developed asymptotic solutions of differential equations and nonanalytic integrals of hydrodynamic equations.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant master in a private school (non-teaching role); taught at Collège d'Agde, Le Vigan, and Gap; professor at Faculté des Sciences in Lille from 1873; held chairs of physical and experimental mechanics, mathematical physics, and calculus of probabilities in Paris.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences in January 1866; eventually became its dean; at his death was its oldest member.

Father_Notes: None

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted geological and meteorological research in South America (1821–1832). Applied organic analysis to agricultural problems: soil fertility, crop rotation, nitrogen fixation in plants and soil, ammonia in rainwater, and nitrification. Demonstrated legume nitrogen fixation and soil nitrification; identified microorganisms as agents of nitrogen fixation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1839. From 1834 to 1876 conducted field and laboratory research on his farm at Bechelbronn, Alsace.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1839 following recognition from South American research.

Father_Notes: Father was the celebrated French philosopher Émile Boutroux.
Education_Notes: Studied at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris. Published his thesis of licence in 1900 at age nineteen, L'imagination et les mathématiques selon Descartes, but no formal degree is named.

Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; History of Science; Philosophy of Science
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: In pure mathematics, studied multiform functions and singularities of differential equations, extending work of Painlevé, Poincaré, and Picard. Principal contributions were extensions and clarifications of existing ideas rather than formulation of new ones. Major works on history and philosophy of science include Les principes de l'analyse mathématique and L'idéal scientifique des mathématiciens, which examined the evolution of mathematical thought and advocated for integrated history of science rather than narrow technical studies.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lectured in mathematics at University of Montpellier; professor of integral calculus at University of Poitiers from 1908 to 1920; visiting professor at University of Nancy in 1909; lectured at Collège de France on mathematical functions; chair of higher mathematics at Princeton University from 1913 to 1914, also chairing the graduate mathematics department; returned to Collège de France in 1920 as professor of the general history of science.

Father_Notes: Theodor Boveri Sr., a physician of Frankish descent; fell into debt by 1890.
Education_Notes: Attended school in Bamberg (1868–1875) and Realgymnasium in Nuremberg (1875–1881). Entered University of Munich in 1881, initially studying history and philosophy before turning to natural science. Studied anatomy under Carl von Kupffer and received doctorate summa cum laude in 1885 for dissertation on nerve fiber structure. Awarded five-year Lamont-Stipendium fellowship in 1885, renewed for two years. Habilitated in zoology and comparative anatomy in 1887.
Education_Locations: Munich, Unknown, Germany, 1881, 1885
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in cell biology and cytology. Demonstrated chromosome individuality and proved differential value of chromosomes, establishing the physical basis of heredity. Conducted landmark experimental studies on Ascaris and sea urchin eggs. Investigated egg polarity, centrosome function, chromatin diminution, and cytoplasmic influence on nuclear behavior. Proposed early theory linking abnormal chromosome numbers to tumor malignancy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked at Zoological Institute in Munich (1885–1893) under Richard Hertwig, initially as fellow and later as assistant. Became professor of zoology and comparative anatomy and director of the Zoological-Zootomical Institute at University of Würzburg in 1893, remaining there for the rest of his life. Made working visits to Zoological Station at Naples (1888–1914). Declined 1912 invitation to direct Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Biology in Berlin-Dahlem.
Instruments_Notes: Renowned for exceptional powers of observation as a microscopist and for devising illuminating experimental techniques.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
