Father_Notes: Jonathan Ingersoll Bowditch was a Boston merchant. Family was prominent and well-connected; paternal grandfather was mathematician Nathaniel Bowditch; maternal grandfather was Timothy Pickering, secretary of state under George Washington.
Education_Institution: Epes S. Dixwell School; Harvard College; Lawrence Scientific School; Lawrence Scientific School; Harvard Medical School; University of Paris; University of Bonn; University of Leipzig
Education_Notes: Preparatory education at Epes S. Dixwell's school in Boston. Entered Harvard College in 1857, graduated 1861. Studied natural history and chemistry at Lawrence Scientific School, Cambridge. Interrupted by Civil War service 1861–1865. Resumed studies at Lawrence Scientific School in comparative anatomy under Jeffries Wyman. Completed Harvard Medical School requirements; received M.A. in 1866 and M.D. in 1868. Studied in Europe 1868–1871 under Claude Bernard and Louis-Antoine Ranvier in Paris, and under Carl Ludwig in Leipzig.
Education_Locations: Boston, Massachusetts, United States, Unknown, Unknown; Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States, 1857, 1861; Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States, 1861, 1865; Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States, 1865, 1868; Boston, Massachusetts, United States, 1861, 1868; Paris, Unknown, France, 1868, 1869; Bonn, Unknown, Germany, 1869, 1869; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, 1869, 1871
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of experimental physiology in America. Established the first teaching laboratory for physiology in the United States at Harvard Medical School. Conducted fundamental research on cardiac muscle irritability, demonstrating the Treppe and the all-or-none law. Investigated vasomotor reflexes, pulmonary circulation, nervous system function, and anthropometry of growth in children. Developed improvements to physiological apparatus including the kymograph and the Bowditch clock.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant professor of physiology at Harvard Medical School from 1871, appointed full professor in 1876, and first occupant of the George Higginson professorship of physiology from 1903 until retirement in 1906. Taught physiology at Harvard for thirty-five years. Also served as dean of the Harvard Medical Faculty 1883–1893.
Patronage_Notes: Invited to Harvard Medical School by Charles W. Eliot, the new president of the university, in 1871. Studied under Carl Ludwig at Leipzig, one of the most prominent physiological laboratories of the period.
Instruments: Kymograph; Bowditch Clock; Plethysmograph; Induction Apparatus; Artificial Respiration Device; Cannula; Unpolarizable Electrodes
Instruments_Notes: Developed an improvement of Ludwig's kymograph in 1869 for automatically registering time relations of blood-pressure tracings. Invented the Bowditch clock for marking elapsed time periods. Designed or adapted a new plethysmograph for registering changes in organ volume, a new induction apparatus permitting variation of intensity, a device for artificial respiration, a cannula for observing vocal cords, and an arrangement of unpolarizable electrodes. Collected apparatus from German laboratories to establish the first American teaching laboratory for physiology.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: American Academy of Arts and Sciences; National Academy of Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1872 and to the National Academy of Sciences in 1887. Member of many other learned academies in the United States and Europe. One of the principal founders of the American Physiological Society in 1887 and elected its second president in 1888, succeeding S. Weir Mitchell; returned to the presidency 1891–1895.

Father_Notes: Bowditch came from a poor family.
Education_Notes: Self-educated through extensive reading and study. Learned Latin in 1790 to read Newton's Principia and German at age forty-five to access scientific literature. Acquired knowledge of mathematics, astronomy, and physics through independent study and five long sea voyages between 1795 and 1803.
Education_Locations: None
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Corrected errors in mathematical and astronomical writings; published on meteor phenomena, pendulum motion, and celestial mechanics. Translated Laplace's Mécanique céleste with extensive annotations and supplementary material.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Apprenticed to a ship's chandler in youth; participated in five sea voyages between 1795 and 1803, serving as master of a ship on the last voyage to Sumatra. Retired from the sea in 1804 and entered the insurance business, becoming an actuary in Boston.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Royal Society and received other honors based on his published writings before the Mécanique céleste translation appeared.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: Queen's University; Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Education_Notes: Entered Queen's University in 1903; took honors courses in chemistry and mineralogy, awarded M.A. in 1907; entered Faculty of Applied Science and awarded B.S. from School of Mining in 1909. Doctoral studies at Massachusetts Institute of Technology from 1909; worked under direction of A. L. Day at the Geophysical Laboratory of the Carnegie Institution.
Education_Locations: Kingston, Ontario, Canada, 1903, 1909; Cambridge, Unknown, United States, 1909, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal investigator and leader of the magmatist school of geology in the twentieth century. Pioneered experimental petrology and phase-equilibrium studies of igneous rocks. Developed theory of igneous rock evolution through differentiation by crystallization and reaction series. Analyzed behavior of inclusions in magma by physical-chemical methods. Bridged chemistry and geology through skilled experimentation combined with field investigation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Employed by Ontario Bureau of Mines before doctoral studies. Worked for Canadian Geological Survey during summers of 1910 and 1911. Served as professor of mineralogy at Queen's University in 1919. Professor of petrology at University of Chicago between 1937 and 1945. Returned to Geophysical Laboratory of Carnegie Institution in 1920 and again in 1947.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Geological Society of America; Mineralogical Society of America
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Served as president of both the Geological Society of America and the Mineralogical Society of America. Received Penrose Medal from the Geological Society of America in 1941. Active in numerous professional societies and received medals from various professional organizations.

Father_Notes: None

Education_Notes: Attended Repton School from 1868; entered Trinity College, Cambridge in 1874 and obtained a first-class degree. Studied under Julius von Sachs at Würzburg in 1877 for two years, then under Anton de Bary at Strasbourg, where he conducted his first original research on fungi and Fucaceae development.
Education_Locations: Repton, Unknown, England, 1868, 1874; Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1874, Unknown; Würzburg, Unknown, Germany, 1877, 1879; Strasbourg, Unknown, France, 1879, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in comparative plant morphology and vascular cryptogams; major contributions to fern classification and evolutionary arrangement; developed the interpolation theory of alternation of generations; investigated stelar morphology and the relationship between surface and bulk in plant tissues.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant to Daniel Oliver at University College, London; lecturer under T. H. Huxley; worked at the Jodrell Laboratory at Kew; held the Regius chair of botany at the University of Glasgow from 1885 to 1925.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society of London; Royal Society of Edinburgh; British Association

Father_Notes: None

Education_Notes: Advanced education began at St. Johns College, Maryland; completed B.S. at Trinity College, Connecticut, where he earned M.A. in 1907; received C.E. degree from Lehigh University in 1895.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Chief of the Division of Geodesy at the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; pioneered mathematical computation methods in isostasy; conducted gravity anomaly studies and established triangulation controls; published Isostasy (1927), synthesizing work on crustal equilibrium and compensation depths.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lifelong career with the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey beginning July 1895 as junior officer; became chief of the Division of Geodesy in 1909; served over forty years with the Survey.
Patronage_Notes: Employed and promoted by the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey; collaborated with U.S. government and Dutch authorities on gravity measurement expeditions in 1928 and 1931–1932.
Instruments_Notes: Sponsored improvement of theodolites, including substitution of silver circles for bronze to eliminate inaccuracies in triangulation.

Father_Notes: Samuel Cressman Bowman was a farmer of moderate means; his father had been a schoolteacher and farmer.
Education_Institution: Ferris Institute; State Normal School at Ypsilanti; Harvard University; Yale University
Education_Notes: Began teaching in country schools at age seventeen while continuing his own education in summers. Attended Ferris Institute and State Normal School at Ypsilanti, where he was inspired by Mark Jefferson's geographical approach. Studied under William Morris Davis at Harvard, earning B.S. in 1905. Earned Ph.D. from Yale in 1909.
Education_Locations: Big Rapids, Michigan, United States, Unknown, Unknown; Ypsilanti, Michigan, United States, Unknown, Unknown; Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States, Unknown, 1905; New Haven, Connecticut, United States, 1905, 1909
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in physiography and landforms study under William Morris Davis's influence. Published Forest Physiography (1911), a comprehensive account of American relief, climate, soils, and vegetation. Conducted extensive South American expeditions and frontier studies, publishing The Andes of Southern Peru (1916) and Desert Trails of Atacama (1924). Developed influential theories on pioneer fringe and frontier settlement.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Instructor in geology at Yale until 1909, then assistant professor. Director of the American Geographical Society from 1915 to 1935, transforming it into a major research institution. President of The Johns Hopkins University from 1935 to 1948.
Patronage_Notes: Advised American delegation to peace conference 1918–1919 on postwar boundaries. Member of Science Advisory Board established by President Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1933. Chairman of National Research Council 1933–1935. Participated in World Security Conference at Dumbarton Oaks (1944) and United Nations implementation (1945).
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Association of American Geographers; International Geographical Union; American Association for the Advancement of Science
Scientific_Societies_Notes: President of Association of American Geographers in 1931. President of International Geographical Union 1931–1934. President of American Association for the Advancement of Science in 1943.

Father_Notes: John Eddowes Bowman was a banker and naturalist, founding member of the Manchester Geological Society, and member of the Linnean and Geological societies; corresponded with Agassiz, Bewick, and Lyell.
Education_Notes: Attended Hazelwood School in Birmingham under Thomas Wright Hill (1826). Apprenticed to W. A. Betts, house surgeon to Birmingham Infirmary (1832), and studied under surgeon Joseph Hodgson. Attended medical department of King's College, London (1837), where he studied anatomy under Richard Partridge and physiology under Richard Bentley Todd, becoming Todd's prosector in 1838. Undertook European hospital tour in 1838 as mentor to Francis Galton.
Education_Locations: Birmingham, Unknown, England, 1826, Unknown; London, Unknown, England, 1837, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines: Medicine; Anatomy; Physiology; Histology; Ophthalmology; Surgery
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of histological anatomy using microscopy; made detailed descriptions of skin, muscle, nerves, sense organs, kidney, bone, and cartilage. Described Bowman's capsule in the kidney and demonstrated the relationship between anatomical structure and physiological function. Later specialized in ophthalmic surgery; described corneal anatomy including Bowman's membrane and ciliary muscle; developed surgical procedures for artificial pupil and lacrymal duct obstruction; early adopter of ophthalmoscopy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant surgeon to King's College Hospital, London (1840); surgeon to the hospital (1856); maintained expanding private practice. Worked as prosector to Richard Bentley Todd at King's College.
Instruments_Notes: Used compound microscope made by Powell for histological investigations. Designed lacrymal probes for obstructed ducts, still in use; created artificial tubular appearances (Bowman's tubes) by mercury injection. Early adopter of Helmholtz' ophthalmoscope (1851).
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Royal College of Surgeons; Ophthalmological Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1841 at age twenty-five; awarded Royal Medal in 1842. Fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons (1844). Founder-president of the Ophthalmological Society (1880); the Bowman lecture was instituted in his honor.

Father_Notes: Richard Boyle, first earl of Cork, an Elizabethan adventurer of considerable wealth and influence; Robert was the youngest of fourteen children.
Education_Notes: Private tuition at home until age eight; attended Eton for several years; from age twelve traveled on the Continent with his brother, receiving private instruction in polite arts, liberal education, and practical mathematics from a Geneva citizen; encountered Galileo's Dialogue on the Two Chief World Systems in Florence in 1642. No university degree is recorded.
Education_Locations: Eton, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Geneva, Unknown, Switzerland, Unknown, Unknown; Florence, Unknown, Italy, 1642, 1642
Religion_Notes: Devout Catholic; scrupulous in conscience, declining the presidency of the Royal Society in 1680 over concerns about the Test Act; wrote extensively on natural theology and the harmony between religion and science.
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Chemistry; Natural Philosophy; Optics; Pneumatics; Hydrostatics; Analytical Chemistry
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of experimental physics through pneumatic experiments with the air pump, establishing Boyle's law (volume inversely proportional to pressure); major contributor to corpuscular philosophy and mechanical explanations of matter; advanced chemistry through systematic analytical methods, acid-alkali classification, and chemical tests for identification; studied color, light, heat, magnetism, and phosphorus; helped establish the experimental method in multiple branches of science.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Supported by considerable family wealth and aristocratic position; from 1661 governor of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in New England; had connection with the Court; maintained a laboratory and lodgings that became a center for research.
Patronage_Notes: Son of the first earl of Cork; had some connection with the Court after the Restoration; supported by his sister Lady Ranelagh, a strong Parliamentarian and friend of John Milton.
Instruments_Notes: Worked with Robert Hooke to design and construct an improved air pump with a glass receiver that allowed easy insertion of objects; used this instrument to conduct a brilliant series of experiments on the physical properties of air, establishing foundational principles of pneumatics.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: One of the founders of the Royal Society; throughout his life was its most notable and influential fellow; maintained correspondence with Henry Oldenburg and other leading scientists.

Father_Notes: Auguste Brachet was an industrialist; the family was sufficiently prosperous to furnish an office for Albert's medical practice.
Education_Institution: University of Liège; University of Edinburgh; University of Freiburg im Breisgau; University of Breslau
Education_Notes: Studied medicine at University of Liège under the influence of zoologist Edouard Van Beneden; worked in Van Beneden's zoology laboratory (1887–1888) and as histological preparator under anatomist Auguste Swaen. After receiving his M.D. in 1894, undertook postdoctoral study at University of Edinburgh, Ernst Gaupp's laboratory at Freiburg im Breisgau, and Gustav Born's laboratory at Breslau, where he learned the wax-plate embryo-modeling method.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in experimental embryology; made fundamental contributions to understanding gastrulation, early cleavage, and embryonic differentiation in vertebrates and invertebrates; studied organ formation (liver, pancreas, heart, blood vessels, urinary organs); confirmed parthenogenetic development and pioneered in vitro cultivation of mammalian embryos.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant in anatomy at University of Liège (from 1895); professor of anatomy and embryology and director of the Institute of Anatomy at University of Brussels (from 1904); adjunct professor at University of Paris during World War I; rector of University of Brussels (1923–1926).
Patronage_Notes: Received a government traveling fellowship enabling postdoctoral study at Edinburgh, Freiburg, and Breslau.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected corresponding member of the Institut de France after World War I; edited the influential journal Archives de biologie.

Father_Notes: Gabriel Braconnot, a lawyer, died in 1787 when Henri was seven years old.

Education_Notes: Attended Collège de Commercy (Benedictine school) but was removed due to his rebellion against strict discipline. Received private education. Apprenticed to an apothecary in Nancy at age thirteen. Worked as a pharmacist in a military hospital in Strasbourg from approximately 1793 to 1801, studying at the École Centrale du Département du Bas-Rhin. In 1801 attended courses in chemistry, biology, and geology in Paris under Fourcroy and Étienne Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in plant and animal chemistry. Conducted systematic investigations over thirty years into the synthesis of complex organic constituents from simple inorganic substances. Discovered numerous plant and animal substances including fungine, ellagic acid, pectic acid, legumin, populin, pyrogallic acid, and xyloïdine. Studied effects of sulfuric acid on wood, animal substances, and other materials.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as a pharmacist in a military hospital in Strasbourg. Secured the directorship of the Jardin Botanique de Nancy in 1801 through the influence of Fourcroy, a position he held for the rest of his career.
Patronage_Notes: Fourcroy's influence secured his directorship at the Jardin Botanique de Nancy.

Father_Notes: William Bradley's income was limited; James was the third son.
Education_Institution: Northleach Grammar School; Balliol College, Oxford
Education_Notes: Educated at Northleach Grammar School and Balliol College, Oxford, entering in 1711. Received B.A. in 1714 and M.A. in 1717. Upon appointment as astronomer royal in 1742, Oxford awarded him an honorary D.D.
Education_Locations: Northleach, Gloucestershire, England, Unknown, Unknown; Oxford, Unknown, England, 1711, 1717
Religion_Notes: Ordained in 1719 and installed as vicar of Bridstow, Monmouthshire. Resigned his livings in 1721 upon appointment to the Savilian professorship, believing he could not do full justice to two employments.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Discovered the aberration of light (1729), demonstrating the earth's orbital motion and providing the first direct observational proof of Copernican theory. Discovered nutation of the earth's axis (1748). Made extensive observations of stars, planets, comets, and solar system bodies. Improved methods for determining star positions, distances, and stellar motions through refined refraction calculations and instrumental precision. Contributed to navigation through lunar tables and longitude determination.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed Savilian professor of astronomy at Oxford in 1721 with a meager salary of £100 per year. Served as astronomer royal from 1742 until his death in 1762. Previously held the vicar position at Bridstow (1719–1721) with additional sinecure living and chaplaincy.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by his uncle, the Reverend James Pound, who fostered his astronomical interests. Edmund Halley drew the Royal Society's attention to Bradley's abilities in 1717 and wished him to succeed as astronomer royal. The Earl of Macclesfield was his patron and friend, to whom Bradley addressed his nutation paper in 1748.
Instruments: Zenith Sector; Mural Quadrant; Transit Instrument
Instruments_Notes: Used a twenty-four-foot zenith sector made by George Graham at Molyneux's house at Kew for parallax observations (1725). Employed a smaller sector at Wanstead (1727) for extended stellar observations. At Greenwich Observatory after 1750, used two mural quadrants and a transit instrument, all made by John Bird, to conduct a massive program of 60,000+ observations of exceptional accuracy.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Académie Royale des Sciences; Academy of Berlin; Academy of Bologna; Academy of St. Petersburg
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1718 and remained so for over forty years. By 1748, his brilliant discoveries brought him preminence among English and foreign astronomers, leading to election as member of the Académie Royale des Sciences and the academies of Berlin, Bologna, and St. Petersburg.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Studied sap movement in trees and sexual reproduction in plants, particularly through experiments on tulips and hazel. Emphasized pollination, insect fertilization, and cross-fertilization. Prolific botanical writer with over twenty works on gardening and husbandry.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed to the chair of botany at Cambridge University in 1724, which he held until his death. Prolific author of botanical and agricultural works.
Instruments_Notes: Claimed to have invented the kaleidoscope, which he used to design symmetrical patterns for formal gardens, predating David Brewster's claims by approximately ninety years.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society of London on 1 December 1712.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Fellow of Balliol College from August 1321; fellow of Merton College from 1323 until approximately 1335. Degrees earned at Oxford: B.A. by August 1321, M.A. by ca. 1323, B.Th. by 1333, D.Th. by 1348.
Education_Locations: Oxford, Unknown, England, 1321, 1348
Religion_Notes: Held ecclesiastical positions including canon of Lincoln (1333) and archbishop of Canterbury (1349).
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work on the mathematical relation between forces, resistances, and motion (Tractatus de proportionibus velocitatum in motibus, 1328). Developed axiomatic mathematical arguments against atomism in the Tractatus de continuo. Composed elementary mathematical compendia on geometry and arithmetic. Theological works addressed predestination and divine will.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Fellow at Oxford colleges (Balliol and Merton) until ca. 1335. Held ecclesiastical positions: canon of Lincoln (1333), chancellor of St. Paul's, London (1337), chaplain and confessor to Edward III (ca. 1338/1339), archbishop of Canterbury (1349).
Patronage_Notes: Entered the coterie of Richard de Bury, bishop of Durham, ca. 1335. Served as chaplain and possibly confessor to Edward III from ca. 1338/1339; accompanied the king's retinue to France in 1346 and delivered a sermon in the king's presence. Appointed archbishop of Canterbury by ecclesiastical authority.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Robert John Bragg, former officer in the merchant marine.
Education_Institution: King William's College; Trinity College, Cambridge
Education_Notes: Attended King William's College, Isle of Man. At Trinity College, Cambridge, read mathematics under Routh's coaching; came out third wrangler in Part I of mathematical tripos (1884) and obtained first-class honors in Part III (1885). Attended lectures by J. J. Thomson at the Cavendish Laboratory in his final year.
Education_Locations: Isle of Man, Unknown, England, Unknown, 1881; Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1881, 1885
Religion_Notes: Experienced religious fervor as a schoolboy but preserved composure by refusing to take literally the biblical threat of eternal damnation; retained his faith and abhorrence of atheism.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in X-ray physics and crystal structure analysis. Early work on absorption of alpha particles and radioactive decay; developed corpuscular theory of X-rays and gamma rays. With his son William Lawrence, developed X-ray crystallography and the Bragg law (nλ = 2d sin θ), reducing crystal structure analysis to a standard procedure by 1913. Later directed research on organic crystal structures at the Davy-Faraday Laboratory.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of mathematics and physics at University of Adelaide (1886–1908); Cavendish professor of physics at University of Leeds (1908–1915); Quain professor of physics at University College London (1915–1923); head of the Royal Institution (1923–1942). During World War I, served as resident director of research at Naval Experiment Station, working on submarine detection.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by Lord Fisher's Board of Invention and Research during World War I. Knighted (K.B.E., 1920) and made C.B.E. (1917) in recognition of war work and scientific eminence.
Instruments_Notes: Constructed the first X-ray spectrometer in January 1913, initially to investigate spectral distribution of X-rays and later to determine crystal structures by inverting the Bragg relation.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society of London; Deutsche Physikalische Gesellschaft
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Royal Society in 1907 (nominated by Horace Lamb, supported by Rutherford). Delivered the Bakerian lectureship (1915). President of the Royal Society (1935–1940). Member of the Deutsche Physikalische Gesellschaft since before World War I. Member of foreign academies including Paris, Washington, Copenhagen, and Amsterdam.

Father_Notes: Father was Otto Brahe, a Danish nobleman and privy councillor.
Education_Institution: University of Copenhagen; University of Leipzig
Education_Notes: Studied at University of Copenhagen (1559–1562), then at University of Leipzig (winter 1561–62), and traveled to Germany and Italy for further study. No formal degree is recorded.
Education_Locations: Copenhagen, Unknown, Denmark, 1559, 1562; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, 1561, 1562
Religion_Notes: Lutheran, as was standard in sixteenth-century Denmark.
Scientific_Disciplines: Astronomy; Observational Astronomy; Instrumentation; Mathematics; Astrology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering observational astronomer who reformed astronomical practice through systematic, precise naked-eye observations. Designed and built advanced astronomical instruments including sextants and quadrants. Observed and published on the nova of 1572 and the comet of 1577. Developed the Tychonic system of planetary motion as an alternative to both Ptolemaic and Copernican models. Compiled extensive star catalogs and lunar theory.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Supported by Danish crown; established and directed the observatory Uraniborg on the island of Hven (1576–1597). Later moved to Prague under patronage of Emperor Rudolf II. Engaged in astrological practice and teaching.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by Danish King Frederick II, who granted him the island of Hven and funded Uraniborg. Later supported by Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II in Prague.
Instruments: Sextant; Quadrant; Armillary Sphere; Refraction Instrument
Instruments_Notes: Designed and constructed advanced astronomical instruments of unprecedented precision for naked-eye observation. Described his instruments in Astronomiae instauratae mechanica (1598). His instruments enabled the systematic observations that revolutionized astronomy.

Father_Notes: Died in 1591 when Bramer was an infant; Bramer was then taken as a foster son into the household of his sister and her husband Joost Bürgi.
Education_Notes: Tutored by his brother-in-law Joost Bürgi, the court clockmaker, who awakened his passion for mathematics. Accompanied Bürgi to the imperial court at Prague from 1604 to 1609. No formal degree is recorded.
Education_Locations: None
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Published on sine calculation (1614) and geometric instruments for perspective and triangulation. Developed methods for accurate geometrical perspective drawing (1630) and contributed to triangulation instruments (1651). Also investigated the problem of empty space and vacuum.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed master builder of the court in Marburg by Landgrave Moritz of Hesse–Kassel in 1612. From 1620 directed construction of fortifications at Marburg castle and town. Patronage_Notes: Patronized by Landgrave Moritz of Hesse–Kassel, who appointed him master builder in 1612. Also served the count of Solms as consultant.

Contributed to triangulation instruments with semicirculus using an inclined ruler to determine sighted points and inclination (1651).

Means_of_Support_Notes: Lecturer on chemistry and pharmacy at London medical schools from 1808; superintendent of chemical operations at Apothecaries' Hall from 1812; professor of chemistry at the Royal Institution from 1813 to 1852; superintendent of the dies department and later chief officer of the coinage department at the Mint.

Education_Notes: Studied at Uppsala University; arrived in Leiden in 1721 and became a pupil of Boerhaave for three years of intensive study in chemistry; received M.D. from Rheims in 1726; studied mining and smelting in the Harz Mountains on his return to Sweden.

Produced major telescope objectives and mirrors for leading observatories worldwide.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as a mechanic in a Pittsburgh steel mill until 1881; then established the John A. Brashear Company, which manufactured astronomical and physical instruments for half a century.
Patronage_Notes: Encouraged and supported by astronomer Samuel Pierpont Langley; financially backed by William Thaw, a merchant patron, enabling establishment of his workshop in 1881.
Instruments: Telescope; Mirror; Spectroscope; Spectroheliograph; Interferometer; Diffraction Grating
Instruments_Notes: Developed an improved silvering process for glass mirrors; produced concave metal mirrors for Rowland's diffraction gratings; manufactured spectroscopes for major observatories; built optical components for Michelson's interferometer and Hale's spectroheliograph; created numerous telescope objectives culminating in a 72-inch primary mirror for Dominion Observatory.

Father_Notes: Civil servant with scientific interests in mineralogy, physics, and astronomy.
Education_Institution: Karlsruhe Lyceum; University of Heidelberg; University of Munich; University of Tübingen
Education_Notes: After private tutoring, entered Karlsruhe Lyceum in 1816 and published his first paper at age sixteen. Enrolled at University of Heidelberg in 1824, initially studying medicine but focusing on botany. Became close friends with Carl Friedrich Schimper and Louis Agassiz. In 1827 went to University of Munich, attracted by Oken and Schelling. Received doctorate from University of Tübingen in 1829.
Education_Locations: Karlsruhe, Unknown, Germany, 1816, Unknown; Heidelberg, Unknown, Germany, 1824, 1827; Munich, Unknown, Germany, 1827, 1829; Tübingen, Unknown, Germany, 1829, 1829
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Established the doctrine of spiral phyllotaxis with Carl Schimper, explaining the geometric arrangement of leaves on plant stems. Made important contributions to plant morphology, the biology of freshwater algae, and cell theory, opposing Schleiden and Schwann's emphasis on the cell wall and insisting the cell contents were the site of physiological activity. Wrote on rejuvenescence as a distinguishing feature of organic nature, extending Goethe's doctrine of metamorphosis. Believed in teleological transmutation of species and objected to Darwin's natural selection. Developed a natural system of plant classification.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Teacher of botany and zoology at the polytechnic school in Karlsruhe (until 1846); chair of botany at Freiburg im Breisgau (1846–1850); position at Giessen (1850–1851); professor of botany and director of the botanical gardens at University of Berlin (1851–1877).

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Major work in electricity and wireless telegraphy; studied thermodynamics and elastic vibrations. Instruments_Notes: Invented the Braun tube (cathode-ray oscilloscope) in 1897 for studying high-frequency alternating currents; the principle of electron-beam deflection by alternating voltage became fundamental to television. Developed a directional antenna for wireless transmission.

Father_Notes: Dr. Francis Brauner was a lawyer and Czech political leader; family was of comfortable means with extensive education and wide-ranging scientific and political interests.

Education_Notes: Studied at Czech Polytechnical High School; attended chemistry courses at University of Prague with research in metal analysis and organic preparations; trained under Robert Bunsen at Heidelberg; worked under Henry Roscoe at Owen's College, Manchester; received doctorate from University of Prague in 1880.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal work was experimental examination of Mendeleev's periodic law and system, particularly determination of atomic weights and positions of rare earth elements. First to prepare quadrivalent cerium salt and elemental fluorine by chemical method. Studied atomic weights of beryllium, tellurium, lanthanum, praseodymium, neodymium, samarium, tin, and thorium. Investigated position of hydrogen in periodic table and properties of inert gases. Made small contributions to astronomy and physiology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed lecturer in chemistry at Czech branch of Charles University, Prague in 1882; rose to docent in 1885, assistant professor in 1890, and full professor in 1897; retired from academic life in 1925.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Czech Academy of Science; Czechoslovakia's National Research Council

Education_Notes: Completed classical education at Collège Stanislas, Paris (1827), winning honorable mention in mathematics. Failed polytechnical examination in 1828; studied special mathematics at Collège St.–Louis and won first prize in mathematics in the general competitive examination. Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Derived the fourteen possible arrangements of points in space (Bravais lattices), combining periodicity with Haüy's law of rational intercepts. Concentrated on relationships between ideal lattice and material crystal, proposing lattice points at centers of gravity of molecular polyhedra. Conducted extensive observations in astronomy, meteorology, and terrestrial magnetism during Arctic expedition. Studied plant organography with his brother Louis and Charles Martins.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Entered the navy in 1831, becoming first-class cadet and serving in Mediterranean and North African mapping expeditions. Taught astronomy at Faculté des Sciences at Lyons from 1841. Appointed professor of physics at École Polytechnique in 1845. Resigned from École Polytechnique in 1856 and retired from the navy in 1857 due to illness.
Patronage_Notes: Minister of public education entrusted him with a scientific mission in the Alps in 1844.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member of Académie Royale des Sciences, Belles–Lettres et Arts de Lyon in 1844. Admitted to Académie des Sciences in its geography and navigation section in 1854. Studied spectra of cometary heads and tails and applied spectroscopic techniques to astrophysical investigations.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at Moscow University from 1858, becoming ordinary professor in 1865. Worked at Moscow observatory from 1855, becoming director in 1873. Elected academician and director of Pulkovo observatory in 1890, retiring in 1895 for health reasons.
Patronage_Notes: Served as director of Moscow observatory (1873–1890) and Pulkovo observatory (1890–1895), both state institutions. Elected academician of the Russian Academy of Sciences in 1890.
Instruments_Notes: Used spectroscope to observe comets, gaseous nebulae, and solar phenomena. Conducted systematic telescopic observations of comets, Jupiter, Mars, and solar features including the red spot and chromospheric protuberances.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Inherited and expanded the family clockmaking business; from 1833 organized it as a company with partners; became designer-manufacturer to the Bureau des Longitudes; firm produced electrical instruments, telegraph apparatus, batteries, lamps, and dynamos.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Studied astronomy and mathematics from 1883 at universities in Berlin, Munich, London, Paris, and Stockholm. Received doctorate in 1890 for dissertation on perturbation theory applied to latitude disturbances. Habilitated at Greifswald in 1892.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialist in celestial mechanics, particularly mathematical methods for computing perturbations affecting planetary and minor-planet orbits. Means_of_Support_Notes: Extraordinary professor of theoretical astronomy at Göttingen (1898–1907); lecturer in mathematics and insurance mathematics at Academy of Commerce, Frankfurt am Main (1907–1908); director of Frankfurt observatory (1908–1927); ordinary professor at University of Frankfurt and director of its observatory (1914–1927). Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Nonresident medical student in Paris hospitals from 1808, resident student from 1809, and received his doctorate in 1812. Studied under the renowned surgeon Guillaume Dupuytren.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1808, 1812

Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed surgeon and head of anatomical studies at the Hôtel Dieu in 1819, agrégé in 1825, and professor of anatomy at the Faculty of Medicine from 1836. Also practiced as a physician and conducted anatomical research.

Father_Notes: Father was a notary.
Education_Notes: Entered École Polytechnique in November 1800 for civil engineering studies but withdrew due to poor health (October 1802–November 1803) and was removed from the rolls in December 1803. Earned doctorate in sciences on 10 March 1812.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1800, 1803
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialized in analytical geometry of plane surfaces and space, particularly the theory of conics and quadrics. Contributed to algebraic equations, especially the limitation of real roots and the theory of elimination using greatest common divisor of polynomials to establish Bézout's theorem. Also worked on continued fractions and symmetric functions.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of transcendental mathematics at the lycée in Grenoble from 1804; professor at the Faculté des Sciences in Grenoble from October 1811 until his death in 1819.

Father_Notes: Father was a master surgeon; family came from the old bourgeois class.
Education_Notes: Attended École de Santé in Paris from 1795, where he heard clinical lectures by Corvisart. Failed an examination in 1801 and abandoned studies; later completed doctoral thesis and final examinations in 1815 to qualify for his position as chief physician.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1795, 1801
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered the concept of specific inflammation and disease specificity; individualized typhoid fever and diphtheria through analysis of lesions and transmission; demonstrated the localization and cyclic development of typhoid lesions on Peyer's patches; identified diphtheria as a distinct contagious disease with characteristic false membrane; first successful tracheotomy for croup in 1825. Also a first-rate botanist and horticulturist; wrote treatise on plant grafting.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Public health officer in Chenonceaux; chief physician at Tours hospital from approximately 1815; director of the École de Santé in Tours until 1838; thereafter practiced medicine among the poor.
Instruments: Tracheotomy Cannula; Hydraulic Hammer; Barometer; Thermometer
Instruments_Notes: Invented the double cannula for tracheotomy, which he used in the first successful operation on a croup patient in 1825. Also constructed hydraulic hammers, barometers, and thermometers.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Presented papers to the Académie Royale de Médecine on diphtheria (26 June and 6 August 1821) and on typhoid contagion (7 July 1829).

Father_Notes: Leopold Breuer (1791–1872) was a teacher of religion employed by the Jewish community of Vienna; described as belonging to the first generation of Eastern European Jews to emerge from the intellectual ghetto into the Western world.
Education_Notes: Tutored by his father until age eight; attended Akademisches Gymnasium of Vienna, graduating 1858; one year of general university studies; medical school at University of Vienna 1859–1867, completing doctoral examination in 1867.
Education_Locations: Vienna, Unknown, Austria, Unknown, 1858; Vienna, Unknown, Austria, 1859, 1867
Religion_Notes: Skeptic in matters of religion; espoused views of Fechner and Goethe; referred to himself as one of many intellectuals with religious needs unable to satisfy them within popular religion. Requested cremation in his will, contrary to conventional Jewish practice.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted fundamental research on reflex regulation of respiration (Hering–Breuer reflex, 1868) and the function of the labyrinth, including semicircular canals and otolith system. Pioneered cathartic treatment of hysteria and contributed foundational concepts to psychoanalysis, including the discovery that neurotic symptoms arise from unconscious processes and vanish when made conscious.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Entered private medical practice in 1871 after assisting internist Johann Oppolzer; qualified as Privatdozent in internal medicine in 1875 but resigned in 1885 over access to teaching patients. Maintained a large private practice as an internist, treating many medical faculty professors and prominent figures; conducted physiological research privately at home, supported by medical practice fees.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Viennese Academy of Science in 1894 upon nomination of Ernst Mach, Ewald Hering, and Sigmund Exner.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Entered Séminaire St.-Sulpice, Paris in 1897 and was ordained a priest in 1900. Displayed early interest in natural history, geology, and human paleontology. No university degree is named.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1897, 1900

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Leading authority on Paleolithic studies in Europe, China, and South Africa. Made major contributions through painstaking recording and analysis of Paleolithic cave art, including work at Altamira, Font de Gaume, Les Combarelles, Tuc d'Audoubert, Les Trois-Frères, and Lascaux. Reclassified Paleolithic industries in his 1912 Geneva Congress paper. Later work on megalithic art and South African rock paintings proved more controversial.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lecturer in prehistory and ethnography at University of Fribourg (1905–1910); professor of prehistoric ethnography at Institut de Paléontologie Humaine, Paris (1910 onward); professor of prehistory at Collège de France (1929–1947). Supported by ecclesiastical position as ordained priest.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Institute de France; American Academy of Science; Society of Antiquaries of London; nineteen foreign societies and academies
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member of the Institute de France in 1938. Gold medalist of the American Academy of Science and Society of Antiquaries of London. Awarded Huxley Memorial Medal and Prestwich Medal for Geology. Member of nineteen foreign societies and academies. Received honorary degrees from Oxford, Cambridge, Edinburgh, Cape Town, Lisbon, and Fribourg.

Father_Notes: James Brewster was rector of Jedburgh grammar school; David learned physical science from his father's manuscript notes from the University of Aberdeen.
Education_Notes: Entered University of Edinburgh in 1794 and completed prescribed courses but did not take a bachelor's degree. Awarded honorary M.A. in 1800. Licensed to preach in Church of Scotland in 1804 but never ordained. Received LL.D. from Aberdeen in 1807 and D.C.L. from Oxford in 1832.
Education_Locations: Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, 1794, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Evangelical Presbyterian; licensed to preach in Church of Scotland in 1804 but never ordained; became member of Free Church of Scotland in 1843; believed in unity of truth and saw implications of physical theories for religion.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in optical polarization, optical mineralogy, and photoelasticity. Discovered that light could be polarized by oblique refraction and reflection; established laws of polarization; created new field of optical mineralogy by discovering biaxial crystals; studied absorption spectroscopy and challenged Newton's doctrine of colors; defended emission theory of light against undulatory theory.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Private tutor 1799–1807; edited Edinburgh Magazine and Scots Magazine 1802–1806, Edinburgh Encyclopaedia 1807–1830, and scientific journals 1819 onward; authored numerous popular books and articles; principal of United Colleges of St. Salvator and St. Leonard, St. Andrews from 1838; elected principal of University of Edinburgh in 1859 and became vice-chancellor.
Patronage_Notes: Political friends including Henry Brougham (lord chancellor), Charles Grant (Lord Glenelg), and earl of Buchan provided influence and honor; Brougham obtained pensions and knighthood for Brewster in 1832; government appointed him principal of St. Andrews in 1838 to relieve financial worries.
Instruments_Notes: Built telescopes, microscopes, and sundials in youth with encouragement of James Veitch; invented kaleidoscope in 1816 as direct result of studies on polarization by multiple reflections; designed monochromatic microscope illuminator for spectroscopic studies.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society of Edinburgh; Royal Society of London; French Institute
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Fellow of Royal Societies of Edinburgh and London; foreign associateship in French Institute in 1848; leader in establishment of Edinburgh School of Arts (1821), Royal Scottish Society of Arts (1821), and British Association for the Advancement of Science (1831).

Father_Notes: None

Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as a lieutenant in Napoleon's artillery, participating in Peninsular campaigns in Spain and Portugal from 1808 to 1813. Appointed professor at the Artillery School of the Royal Guard in 1818, where he taught until his death.

Father_Notes: Father Leonard Victor Bridges died when Calvin was three years old; the boy was raised by his paternal grandmother.
Education_Notes: Attended high school in Plattsburg, New York, graduating at age twenty. Entered Columbia University as a freshman in 1909 on scholarship and graduated in three years while largely supporting himself and conducting research with Drosophila. Earned Ph.D. from Columbia under T. H. Morgan's direction; doctoral thesis completed in 1916.
Education_Locations: New York, Unknown, United States, 1909, 1912
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in Drosophila genetics and cytology. Proved the chromosome theory of heredity through nondisjunction studies. Means_of_Support_Notes: Research associate of the Carnegie Institution of Washington from 1915. Held position at Columbia University until 1928, then moved to California Institute of Technology where he remained until his death.
Instruments_Notes: Introduced binocular microscopes to replace hand lenses in Drosophila work. Developed dependable temperature controls and played the largest part in improvement and standardization of culture bottles and media for fly rearing.

Father_Notes: Raymond Landon Bridgman was a newspaper correspondent and author of books on public affairs.
Education_Notes: Attended public schools in Newton, Massachusetts. Graduated summa cum laude from Harvard College with rigorous training in physics and mathematics. Remained at Harvard for graduate degrees in physics.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in high-pressure physics, developing techniques and apparatus for pressures up to 400,000 atmospheres. Made discoveries in polymorphism, zone melting, and electrical effects in metal crystals. Developed operational philosophy of science as a critical examination of physics concepts.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Research fellow (1908), instructor (1910), assistant professor (1913), professor (1919), Hollis professor of mathematics and natural philosophy (1926), Higgins university professor (1950), and professor emeritus (1954) at Harvard University.

Instruments_Notes: Developed the free-piston gauge and unsupported area seal (leakproof packing), which became the key innovation enabling high-pressure research. Designed and built much of his own apparatus, including pressure vessels and measuring instruments using electrical bridges and potentiometers.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: American Academy of Arts and Sciences; National Academy of Sciences; American Physical Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Active member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and served on the board of editors of Daedalus. President of the American Physical Society in 1942. Member of the National Academy of Sciences and fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. Foreign member of academies of science in England, Mexico, and India.

Education_Notes: Began medical studies at Edinburgh in 1808; interrupted in second year to serve as naturalist on Mackenzie's Iceland expedition, contributing notes on botany and zoology. Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in clinico-pathological correlation, particularly kidney disease. Contributed to knowledge of nervous system diseases, pancreatic, duodenal, and hepatic disease, abdominal tumors, and appendicitis. Exemplified transition from observation with unaided senses to laboratory-aided medicine.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant physician at Guy's Hospital from 1820; promoted to physician in 1824. Taught medicine and engaged in clinical research for approximately twenty years. From about 1840 until death, absorbed in practice rather than research.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Worked primarily on algebraic functions and algebraic geometry using algebraic methods and avoiding transcendental approaches. Fundamental work with Noether on invariant properties under birational transformations (1874). Papers on three-dimensional algebraic curves (1907) and pseudospherical space (1885). Also wrote on determinants, elimination theory, elliptic functions, curves and surfaces, and theoretical mechanics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Dozent at Giessen 1867–1869; professor at Politechnikum Darmstadt 1869–1875; professor at Politechnikum Munich 1875–1884; professor at University of Tübingen 1884–1918.

Father_Notes: His father was a painter; the family was middle-class.
Education_Notes: Studied at Lycée Condorcet in Paris; passed baccalaureate in 1873; attended École Normale Supérieure 1874–1878. Obtained doctorates in both mathematics and physics in 1881.

Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Mathematics; Thermodynamics; Hydrodynamics; Geophysics; Optics; Crystallography
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Prominent theoretical physicist and skilled experimenter. Research encompassed kinetic theory of gases, liquids, and solids; viscosity and thermodynamics; hydrodynamics and hydraulic problems; electromagnetic phenomena in crystals; quantum theory; and physics of the earth, especially tides. Published over 200 papers and books.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant to physicist Mascart at Collège de France; assistant professor of physics at universities of Nancy, Dijon, and Toulouse; returned to École Normale Supérieure in 1888; professor of mathematical physics at Collège de France from 1900 until retirement in 1931.
Instruments_Notes: Built a new model of the Eötvös balance around 1900 and tested it in the Simplon Tunnel (opened 1906); the improved balance was later used for oil prospecting.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member of the Académie des Sciences de Paris in 1921.

Father_Notes: Johannes Månsson, a farmer.
Education_Notes: Graduated in 1871 from the technical school in Borås. Received an honorary Ph.D. from Uppsala in 1907.
Education_Locations: Borås, Unknown, Sweden, Unknown, 1871
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered the Brinell hardness test, a standard procedure for determining metal hardness using a hardened steel ball pressed under load. Conducted significant research on the metallurgy of steel, particularly changes in internal structure during heating and cooling, and comparative analysis of steel fracture surfaces.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Employed in the Swedish iron industry for approximately fifty years. Chief engineer of Fagersta Ironworks from 1882 to 1903, where his most original scientific work was conducted. Chief engineer of Jernkontoret (iron industry association) from 1903 to 1914. Chairman of the board of Fagersta from 1915 to 1923.
Instruments_Notes: Developed apparatus for testing material hardness, first displayed at the 1900 Paris Exposition. Uses a hardened steel ball (10 mm diameter) pressed under heavy load (up to 3,000 kg) to create an indentation; hardness number calculated by dividing load by indentation area. Procedure remains widely used with minimal modification.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Swedish Academy of Science; Iron and Steel Institute
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of the Swedish Academy of Science and the British Iron and Steel Institute.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Studied jurisprudence at Lund University from 1750 to 1757. No degree is named in the source.
Education_Locations: Lund, Unknown, Sweden, 1750, 1757
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Algebra; Geometry; Mathematical Analysis; Astronomy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Composed eight volumes of manuscript work on algebra, geometry, mathematical analysis, and astronomy. Principal achievement was reducing a general fifth-degree equation to trinomial form x⁵+px+q=0 using a transformation with coefficients defined by equations of not higher than third degree, published in Meletemata (1786). This result, later independently obtained by Jerrard and recognized through Hermite's work with elliptic modular functions, became foundational for solving higher-degree equations using transcendental functions.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Reader at Lund University from 1762; professor from 1779. Taught history at the university, though his principal interest was mathematics.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: None

Education_Notes: Educated at Woodbridge Grammar School and privately with Mr. Tilney of Harleston. Attended Caius College, Cambridge, graduating as senior wrangler and first Smith's Prizeman in 1788. Received M.A. at Cambridge in 1791 and D.D. from Dublin in 1806.
Education_Locations: Woodbridge, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Cambridge, Unknown, England, Unknown, 1788
Religion_Notes: Ordained a priest at Lincoln in 1791. Later elevated to bishop of Cloyne in 1826 after numerous ecclesiastical preferments.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal contributions were researches into stellar parallaxes and the detection of annual parallax in fixed stars. Published Elements of Plane Astronomy (1808) and ten mathematical papers. Conducted investigations into astronomical refractions, obliquity of the ecliptic, polar distances of fixed stars, and precession of the equinoxes.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed Andrews professor of astronomy at Dublin University in 1790, a position he held throughout his career. Received ecclesiastical preferments culminating in his elevation to bishop of Cloyne in 1826.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed to his professorship upon the personal recommendation of N. Maskelyne. Elevated to bishop of Cloyne by ecclesiastical authority.
Instruments_Notes: Acquired an eight-foot meridian circle in 1808, which he used to conduct his celebrated parallax observations of fixed stars.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Royal Irish Academy; Astronomical Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected Fellow of the Royal Society in 1803. Awarded the Conyngham Medal of the Royal Irish Academy in 1817 for his essay on the mean motion of the lunar perigee. Awarded the Copley Medal of the Royal Society in 1824. President of the Royal Irish Academy from 1822 to 1835, vice-president of the Astronomical Society from 1825 to 1827, and president from 1831 to 1833.

Father_Notes: None

Education_Locations: Pavia, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1845
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Virtuoso in computation and algebraist; developed determinant theory and theory of forms; applied elliptic and hyperelliptic functions to solving polynomial equations; worked in differential equations, elliptic functions, and mechanics including statics, dynamics, hydrostatics, and hydrodynamics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of applied mathematics at University of Pavia (1852–1861); general secretary of the Ministry of Education (1861–1862); member of the Executive Council of the Ministry of Education (1870–1882); director and professor at the Istituto Tecnico Superiore in Milan (1863–1897); worked as a hydraulic engineer on major projects including regulation of the Po and Tiber rivers.
Patronage_Notes: Served as general secretary and executive council member of the Ministry of Education; senator from 1865.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: President of the Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei from 1884 until his death; organized the Accademia Scientifica-Letteraria in Milan.

Father_Notes: Auguste Briot was a merchant with considerable reputation in the tanning trade at St.-Hippolyte.
Education_Notes: Entered École Normale Supérieure in 1838, ranked second; completed the course in 1841 and received agrégation in mathematics with highest rank. Received doctorate of science in March 1842 with thesis on the movement of a solid body round a fixed point.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1838, 1841
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted mathematical studies on heat, light, and electricity based on the hypothesis of imponderable molecules in the ether. Linked crystalline medium studies to Pasteur's work on crystal dissymmetry. Advanced theories of elliptic and Abelian functions and simplified integral calculus methods. Stressed the relation between thermodynamics and rational mechanics in his teaching.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at Orléans Lycée, then University of Lyons. From 1851 taught mathématiques spéciales at Lycée Bonaparte and Lycée Saint-Louis in Paris; acted as substitute at École Polytechnique and Faculté des Sciences in mechanical engineering, surveying, calculus, and mechanics/astronomy. From 1864 professor at the Sorbonne and École Normale Supérieure.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Named a corresponding member of the Göttingen Academy in recognition of his work on heat, light, and electricity.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Early education under tutors at home; studied at Edinburgh University and Kensington Academy, where he attended lectures on astronomy and mathematics. Received honorary degrees from Edinburgh (1824), Oxford (1832), and Cambridge (1833).
Education_Locations: Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, Unknown, Unknown; London, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Practical astronomer and observer; skilled in use of astronomical instruments. Established and directed observatories at Paramatta and Makerstoun; conducted systematic observations of southern hemisphere stars and terrestrial magnetism.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Gazetted ensign in 1789, progressively advanced to general (1841); saw active service in Europe, West Indies, and Canada. Appointed governor of New South Wales (1821). Supported himself through personal wealth and military pay while funding observatories at his own expense.
Patronage_Notes: Served as governor of New South Wales (1821); received commissions from Duke of Wellington for astronomical tables (1818). Created baronet (1836) and made G.C.B. (1837).
Instruments: Transit Instrument; Mural Circle; Altitude and Azimuth Instrument; Equatorial; Sextant; Repeating Reflecting Circle
Instruments_Notes: Built and equipped observatories at Brisbane House (1808), Paramatta (1822), and Makerstoun (1826) with precision instruments by Troughton and others. Developed and used pocket sextant for observations during military campaigns; designed method for determining latitude by sextant or circle.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Royal Society of Edinburgh; Astronomical Society; Paris Institute; Royal Irish Academy
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of Royal Society (1810); corresponding member of Paris Institute (1816); vice-president of Astronomical Society (1827); president of Royal Society of Edinburgh (1833); honorary member of Royal Irish Academy (1836). Awarded gold medal of Astronomical Society (1828) and Keith Medal of Royal Society of Edinburgh (1848).

Father_Notes: Inspector of commerce and manufacture for the financial district of Lyons.

Education_Notes: Studied at the Collège Oratorien de Juilly; admitted to the École des Ponts et Chaussées in December 1793; became an instructor at the École Centrale des Travaux Publics (future École Polytechnique) in 1794, where he was highly regarded by Gaspard Monge; graduated and admitted to the Corps des Ponts et Chaussées in December 1796; completed professional training at the École des Ponts et Chaussées in May 1798.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialized in the design and construction of ship canals using descriptive geometry; applied functional calculus to partial differential equations and linear differential equations with finite differences; edited Monge's Géométrie descriptive and contributed chapters on shadows and perspective.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Remained in the Corps des Ponts et Chaussées throughout his career; served as civil engineer for the department of Doubs; collaborated on major canal and dike construction projects (1802–1814); appointed professor of stereometry and construction at the École des Ponts et Chaussées in 1820; became inspector of the school from 1821 and secretary of the Conseil Royal des Ponts et Chaussées from 1824.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Presented reports on partial differential equations to the Académie des Sciences; his 1823 report was discussed before the Academy in 1825 and approved by Cauchy.

Father_Notes: Mathurin Brisson was named président des traites at Fontenay in 1726. The family belonged to the legal nobility of Poitou and was related to the naturalist Réaumur.
Education_Institution: Collège de Fontenay; Collège de Poitiers; St.-Sulpice Seminary
Education_Notes: Completed early studies at Collège de Fontenay (1737–1738), studied philosophy at Collège de Poitiers, and passed his baccalaureate in theology in 1744. Continued theological studies at St.-Sulpice Seminary in Paris from 1745 but renounced his vocation in 1747.
Education_Locations: Fontenay-le-Comte, Unknown, France, 1737, 1738; Poitiers, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, 1745, 1747
Religion_Notes: Took minor orders and studied theology; renounced his vocation for the subdiaconate in 1747.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Began as Réaumur's collaborator in natural history, publishing the Règne animal (1756) and the six-volume Ornithologie (1760), which described 1,500 bird species. Later devoted himself to experimental physics under Nollet's influence, publishing the Dictionnaire raisonné de physique (1781), Pesanteur spécifique des corps (1787), and Traité élémentaire ou Principes de physique (1789). Conducted research on density, refraction, burning mirrors, barometers, magnetism, and atmospheric electricity.
Means_of_Support_Notes: From 1749 served as caretaker and demonstrator of Réaumur's collection at 600 livres annually, funded by the Académie des Sciences. In 1768 became deputy professor and successor to Nollet's chair of experimental physics at Collège de Navarre. In 1770 appointed master of physics and natural history to the children of France. From 1796 taught experimental physics and chemistry at Collège des Quatre Nations and held a professorship at Lycée Bonaparte (1805).
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by Réaumur as his principal collaborator and demonstrator. Later supported by Nollet, who arranged his succession to the chair at Collège de Navarre and his appointment as master of physics to the royal children, which put him in touch with the royal family.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected adjoint fellow in botany in 1759, associate member in 1779, supernumerary pensioner in 1782, and pensioner of the section of general physics in 1785. Appointed resident member of the experimental physics section, first class, of the Institut National in December 1795. Member of the Academy commission for the metric system (1792–1793, reinstated after Thermidor).

Father_Notes: Father was Jean Sebastien Brocard; mother was Elizabeth Auguste Liouville Brocard. No siblings recorded.
Education_Institution: Lycée of Marseilles; Lycée and Academy of Strasbourg; École Polytechnique
Education_Notes: Early education at the lycée of Marseilles and the lycée and academy of Strasbourg. Attended École Polytechnique from 1865 to 1867. No university degree is named.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Chiefly known for work in the geometry of the triangle, particularly the Brocard configuration and Brocard circle. Also active as a meteorologist; co-founder of the Meteorological Institute at Algiers and served on meteorological commissions. Prolific contributor to mathematical and scientific journals.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Joined the Corps of Engineers of the French army after 1867; devoted much of his army career to teaching and research. Taught at Montpellier after graduation from École Polytechnique. Served on government meteorological commissions at Montpellier, Grenoble, and Bar-le-Duc. Retired from the army in 1910 as a lieutenant colonel.
Instruments_Notes: In retirement, made astronomical observations with a small telescope in the garden behind his house in Bar-le-Duc.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Life member of Société Mathématique de France (1873) and Association Française pour l'Avancement des Sciences (1875). Life member of Société Météorologique de France (1875). Member of Society of Letters, Sciences, and Arts of Bar-le-Duc (1894); served as librarian of this society.

Father_Notes: Cornelio Brocchi; family was cultured and well-to-do; father had enthusiasm for hunting.
Education_Notes: Educated in classics and literature; sent to Padua to study law but preferred botanical garden and botany lectures by Bonato; studied art and monuments of antiquity in Rome for six months; devoted himself to literature, especially Dante, for two years. No degree is named.
Education_Locations: Padua, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines: Geology; Paleontology; Natural History; Mineralogy; Zoology; Botany
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Major contributions to geology and paleontology, especially through Conchiologia fossile subappennina (1814), which surveyed Italian paleontological studies and compared Subapennine fossils with living Mediterranean fauna and Paris Basin species. Also published on mineralogy, zoology (insect eye anatomy, infusoria), botany, and conducted experiments on malaria transmission. Described volcanic rocks, tuffs, and ash beds around Rome and Naples.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Instructor in natural history at Gymnasium in Brescia from 1802; inspector of mines at Milan from 1808, allowing extensive travel and specimen collection; position lost in 1814 when Lombardy returned to Austria but restored in 1821; accepted invitation from viceroy of Egypt to survey mineral resources and organize mining industry, sailing from Trieste in fall of 1822.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed inspector of mines by Austrian government at Milan (1808); invited by viceroy of Egypt to conduct mineral survey and organize mining industry (1822).
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: None

Geological work focused on Alpine geology. Directed the preparation of France's first comprehensive geological map from 1825 until his death.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Engineer in the Agence des Mines from 1800; editor of Journal des mines from 1801; professor of geology and mineralogy at École des Mines from 1804; director of the glass factory at St. Gobain; inspector general of mines.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed professor at École des Mines by the state; held government posts as engineer and inspector general of mines.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member of the Académie des Sciences.

Alt_Name: B. C. Brodie; Sir Benjamin Brodie
Father_Notes: Rector of Winterslow parish; died in March 1804, leaving the family in difficult circumstances.
Education_Institution: Windmill Street School of Anatomy; St. George's Hospital
Education_Notes: Educated at home by his father alongside his siblings. At eighteen went to London to study medicine, attending anatomy lectures of John Abernethy at St. Bartholomew's Hospital. Entered Windmill Street School of Anatomy in 1802 and became surgical pupil of Everard Home in 1803. Enrolled at St. George's Hospital in June 1804. Admitted member of Royal College of Surgeons in October 1805. No university degree is named.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, 1802, 1803; London, Unknown, England, 1804, 1805
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted experimental research on animal heat production and the role of the nervous system, publishing six papers in Philosophical Transactions (1809–1814) that challenged contemporary chemical theories of respiration and heat. Pioneered conservative surgical treatment of joint diseases, advocating limb preservation over amputation and recognizing hysterical origins of some afflictions. Authored influential textbook Diseases of the Joints (1818–1850).
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lectured on surgery at Windmill Street School of Anatomy (1808–1830). Practiced as a surgeon and leading surgical consultant, building a flourishing private practice. Appointed house surgeon at St. George's Hospital (1805), assistant surgeon (1808), and personal surgeon to King George IV (1828). President of Royal College of Surgeons (1844).
Patronage_Notes: Personal surgeon to King George IV from 1828. Knighted in 1834. Supported early in career by his uncle Thomas Denman, a distinguished obstetrician, who introduced him to prominent London medical men.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Society for Promoting Knowledge of Animal Chemistry
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected Fellow of the Royal Society in February 1810 at age twenty-six. Awarded Copley Medal in 1811, the youngest recipient ever. Croonian Lecturer in 1810 and 1813. Elected president of Royal Society in 1858, the first surgeon to hold the post. Member of Society for Promoting Knowledge of Animal Chemistry, which published his experimental papers.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Investigated waxes and discovered cerotic acid, cerotin, and melissic acid. Examined graphite and discovered graphitic acid. Developed an alternative symbolic calculus for chemistry independent of atomic theory, treating chemical operations as applied algebra on space.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Waynflete Professor of Chemistry at Oxford from 1855 to 1873.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected Fellow of the Royal Society in 1849. Presented his calculus of chemical operations to the Royal Society in 1866.

Father_Notes: Anton Wilhelm Brøgger was a well-known book publisher.
Education_Notes: Received baccalaureate in 1869; took examen philosophicum at University of Oslo in 1870; initially studied zoology, then transferred to mineralogy and geology under Theodor Kjerulf.
Education_Locations: Oslo, Unknown, Norway, 1870, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines: Geology; Mineralogy; Petrology; Paleontology; Stratigraphy; Tectonics; Zoology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in magmatic differentiation theory; major contributions to Permian eruptive rocks of Oslo district, pegmatite minerals, carbonatite-containing rocks, Cambro-Silurian stratigraphy and paleontology, Quaternary geology, and tectonic geology. Published numerous geological maps.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant at mineralogical institute and Geological Survey of Norway from 1876; professor at Stockholms Høgskola (University of Stockholm) from 1881; professor at University of Oslo from 1890 to 1917; rector of University of Oslo.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Norwegian Academy of Science in Oslo; Geological Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: President of Norwegian Academy of Science for many years; received Wollaston Medal in 1911 from Geological Society of London.

Alt_Name: Maurice de Broglie; Maurice, Le Duc de Broglie
Father_Notes: Member of an ancient aristocratic family long prominent in French military, diplomatic, and political service. Family wealth enabled him to establish and maintain a private laboratory.
Education_Institution: École Navale; Marseilles University; Meudon Observatory; Collège de France
Education_Notes: Attended École Navale (1893–1895) with distinction. Studied at schools in Toulon and Marseilles University, receiving the licence ès sciences in 1900. Later studied spectroscopy at the Meudon Observatory under Deslandres and at the Collège de France under Paul Langevin, defending a thesis on ionic mobilities in 1908.
Education_Locations: Brest, Unknown, France, 1893, 1895; Marseilles, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1900; Meudon, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1908
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; X-ray Spectroscopy; Optics; Nuclear Physics; Cosmic Radiation
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal research on X-ray emission and absorption spectra, including the rotating crystal method and discovery of the third L absorption edge. Investigated ionic mobilities, Brownian motion, ionization mechanisms, photoelectric spectra, and the Compton effect. Later directed laboratory work in nuclear physics and cosmic radiation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Maintained a private, well-equipped laboratory in the family mansion where he conducted research throughout his career. Served in the French Navy (1895–1908), including work on wireless communications. Later directed a private laboratory that attracted students and became a center for French experimental physics.
Instruments_Notes: Improved X-ray generation apparatus and developed the rotating crystal method for X-ray spectroscopy, which eliminated spurious spectral lines and became a standard technique.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Académie Française; Académie de Marine; Institut Océanographique
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1924 and the Académie Française in 1934. Member of the French Atomic Energy Commission. Participated in the Solvay Congresses.

Father_Notes: Olof Bromelius was a prominent physician and botanist in Göteborg; Magnus inherited part of his father's natural history cabinet.

Father_Notes: Father was a woolen draper.
Education_Notes: Entered Cambridge as a pensioner of Saint John's College in October 1892 and graduated three years later as senior wrangler in 1895, in a class with E. T. Whittaker and J. H. Grace. Obtained fellowship in 1897. Received Sc.D. in 1909.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Described by Hardy as the best pure mathematician among applied mathematicians and best applied mathematician among pure mathematicians. Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Royal Society in 1906. Active in the London Mathematical Society, serving as secretary (1911–1919) and vice-president (1919, 1920).

Father_Notes: His father was Alexandre Brongniart, an eminent geologist who trained him and collaborated with him from an early age.
Education_Notes: Registered for courses in medicine in 1818; passed his agrégation in medicine before age 27. Trained by his father and initiated into science through early collaboration and original research.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of paleobotany as a distinct science; developed comparative morphology of living and fossil plants; made fundamental contributions to plant classification, anatomy, and the study of fossil plant genera; research on plant fertilization and embryology; later focused on Neo-Caledonian flora and systematic botany.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Succeeded Desfontaines as professor of botany at the Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle in 1833; conducted original research throughout his career.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Joined U.S. Geological Survey as geologist and petrographer in 1894; placed in charge of Alaska Branch in 1903 and retained that position until his death in 1924. Vice-chairman of Alaska Railroad Commission (1912). Appointed to American Commission to Negotiate Peace after World War I.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by U.S. Geological Survey throughout his career; appointed to Alaska Railroad Commission by Congress (1912); assigned to American Commission to Negotiate Peace after World War I.

Education_Notes: Graduated from Williams College in 1870. Attended the Anderson School of Natural History on Penikese Island in summer 1873, where he met Louis Agassiz. Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed associate in biology at Johns Hopkins University in 1875 under H. Newell Martin. Spent his entire academic career at Johns Hopkins, rising to biology department chairmanship in 1894, a position he held until his death.

Father_Notes: Father was a clergyman; Brooks delivered astronomical lectures in his father's church.
Education_Notes: Self-taught in observational astronomy and mechanical construction; no formal institutional education is recorded.
Education_Locations: None
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Observational astronomer specializing in comet discovery; discovered twenty-seven comets between 1881 and 1888. Also constructed telescopes and delivered popular astronomical lectures.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as a commercial photographer briefly in 1870; took charge of Smith Observatory in Geneva from 1888; professor of astronomy at Hobart College from 1900 and William Smith College from 1908. Supported by the Smith Observatory founder's endowment.
Patronage_Notes: Smith Observatory was newly established and endowed; Brooks was appointed to direct it in 1888.
Instruments_Notes: Built his first telescope in 1858; constructed a two-inch refractor and reflectors of five and nine inches aperture for his Red House Observatory; used portable apparatus for comet discovery.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Astronomical Society; Liverpool Astronomical Society; American Association for the Advancement of Science; British Astronomical Association; Astronomical Society of the Pacific
