Father_Notes: John Broom was a designer of calicoes and Paisley shawls engaged in business in Glasgow; an enthusiastic amateur botanist who encouraged Robert's interest in natural history and taught him drawing.
Education_Institution: Hutcheson's Grammar School; University of Glasgow
Education_Notes: Attended Hutcheson's Grammar School in Glasgow; entered University of Glasgow in 1883, where he assisted in the chemistry laboratory and was influenced by botanist F. O. Bower and anatomist John Cleland. Received medical degree in 1889.
Education_Locations: Glasgow, Unknown, Scotland, Unknown, Unknown; Glasgow, Unknown, Scotland, 1883, 1889
Religion_Notes: Retained strong religious beliefs throughout his life; sought to explain organic evolution as the result of cosmic intelligence or plan. Mother belonged to Plymouth Brethren; father held liberal religious viewpoint.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Major contributions to the study of mammalian origins and skull structure, evolutionary history and classification of Permian and Triassic reptiles, and discovery and interpretation of earliest human fossils. Conducted extensive embryological investigations of mammalian development and wrote on evolution, zoology, anthropology, and medicine.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced medicine throughout his life, frequently in remote rural communities in Australia and South Africa. Held professorship of zoology and geology at Victoria College (now Stellenbosch University) from 1903 to 1910. Served as curator of paleontology at Transvaal Museum from 1934 until his death.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Invited to deliver the Croonian lecture in 1913; elected to fellowship in 1920. Received numerous honorary doctorates and honorary fellowships in distinguished academies.

Father_Notes: Sir William Brouncker, created Viscount of Castle Lyons, Ireland, in September 1645; died November 1645.
Education_Notes: Entered Oxford University at age sixteen; showed proficiency in mathematics, languages, and medicine; received Doctor of Physick degree in 1647.
Education_Locations: Oxford, Unknown, England, 1636, 1647
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Major work in mathematics, particularly infinite series, continued fractions, and solutions to Diophantine equations. Calculated π to ten decimal places using continued fractions. Solved the quadrature of a rectangular hyperbola and recognized the result as proportional to log 2. Improved methods for rectifying curves and attempted proofs of the isochronous property of the cycloidal pendulum.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Member of Parliament for Westbury in 1660; president of Gresham College from 1664 to 1667; commissioner for the navy from 1664 to 1668; comptroller of the treasurer's accounts from 1668 to 1679; master of St. Catherine's Hospital from 1681 to 1684.
Patronage_Notes: King's nominee for president of the Royal Society; appointed without opposition and reappointed annually; served as president until his resignation in 1677.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: President of the Royal Society from his appointment (date not specified) until his resignation in 1677; succeeded by Sir Joseph Williamson. Enthusiastic supporter of the society's experimental bias and energetic in suggesting and assessing experimental work.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as a naval surgeon; entered the Service de Santé Militaire; became professor at Val de Grâce; won a chair at the Faculty of Medicine in Paris through government influence after the 1830 revolution; held the rank of inspector general in the Service de Santé Militaire.

Father_Notes: François Broussounet (des Terrasses) was a physician and taught at Montpellier's school of medicine.

Patronage_Notes: Supported by Sir Joseph Banks, who provided specimens and financial assistance. Jean Chaptal, minister of the interior and relative, secured his professorship at Montpellier and supported his botanical garden improvements.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Royal Society in London (1780). Elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1785 following presentation of ichthyological notes. Elected to the Institut in 1796.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in chemical structure notation and graphical formulas for representing molecular bonds; developed the double-bond symbol still in use. Father_Notes: Rev. James Brown, a Scottish Episcopalian clergyman of strong independent views; the son inherited his intellectual honesty and sturdiness of character but lost his uncompromising religious faith.
Education_Notes: Studied at Marischal College, Aberdeen, and the University of Edinburgh, where he completed his medical studies. No degree is named in the source.
Education_Locations: Aberdeen, Unknown, Scotland, Unknown, Unknown; Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Born into Scottish Episcopalian family but lost his uncompromising religious faith; no specific affiliation stated in the entry.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in plant taxonomy and classification, particularly of Australian flora. First to investigate Brownian movement of particles in fluids. Recognized the nucleus as essential to living cells. Demonstrated the distinction between gymnosperms and angiosperms through study of ovule structure. Contributed to understanding of pollen tubes, floral development, and plant relationships through microscopic observation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as naturalist aboard HMS Investigator (1801–1805) at £420 salary. Clerk, Librarian and Housekeeper of the Linnean Society of London (1806–1822). Librarian and curator at Soho Square under Sir Joseph Banks (1810–1820). Head (underlibrarian) of the botanical department at the British Museum (1827–1858).
Patronage_Notes: Recommended by Sir Joseph Banks to the Admiralty for the Investigator voyage. Banks appointed him librarian and curator at Soho Square and bequeathed him an annuity of £200 and life tenancy of his house. The Admiralty funded his work describing Australian plants after the voyage.
Instruments_Notes: Extensively used the microscope in his botanical investigations, particularly in studying pollen grains, cell nuclei, and plant structures. His microscopical observations led to the discovery of Brownian movement.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Linnean Society of London; Royal Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Fellow of the Linnean Society from 1822; president from 1849 to 1853. Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1810. Honored with foreign membership by numerous academies, including the Munich Academy of Sciences.

Father_Notes: Thomas Browne senior was a mercer (silk merchant) in London who died when his son was eight, leaving ample means for the boy's education.
Education_Institution: Winchester College; Broadgates Hall; University of Montpellier; University of Leiden
Education_Notes: Attended Winchester College for eight years from 1615, receiving a sound classical education. Matriculated at Broadgates Hall (later Pembroke College), Oxford, where he took his M.A. in philosophy in 1629. Studied medicine at Montpellier and Leiden, defending his thesis and receiving his M.D. from Leiden in December 1633. Completed required apprenticeship with an established physician before taking his M.D. by incorporation at Oxford on 10 July 1637.
Education_Locations: Winchester, Unknown, England, 1615, 1623; Oxford, Unknown, England, 1623, 1629; Montpellier, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Leiden, Unknown, Netherlands, Unknown, 1633
Religion_Notes: Educated at Winchester College, an Anglican and Royalist school. His Religio medici describes the religion and philosophy of a tolerant, humorous, and latitudinarian mind.
Scientific_Disciplines: Medicine; Natural History; Physics; Anatomy; Biology; Comparative Anatomy; Electricity; Embryology; Archaeology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Practiced medicine as his profession while pursuing natural history and science as serious pursuits. Conducted experiments in physics, electricity (a term he coined), biology, and comparative anatomy, dissecting animals, birds, fishes, reptiles, worms, and insects. Became an acknowledged authority on the plants, animals, birds, and fishes of East Anglia. Investigated bubbles, coagulation, freezing, and other properties of matter. Deeply interested in archaeology, particularly Roman antiquities. His major works Pseudodoxia epidemica and Hydriotaphia demonstrate wide-ranging inquiry into natural history, medicine, embryology, and antiquarian subjects.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Established himself as a physician in Norwich in 1637 and practiced medicine throughout his life. Elected a fellow of the College of Physicians.
Patronage_Notes: Knighted in 1671 by King Charles II, who was visiting Norwich and wished to honor its most distinguished citizen.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected a fellow of the College of Physicians. Never a fellow of the Royal Society of London, though he corresponded with several fellows including Henry Oldenburg (secretary), John Ray, Christopher Merrett, and John Evelyn, and occasionally sent communications through his son Edward.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: Not Specified; Not Specified; University of Leiden
Education_Notes: Apprenticed to a physician in Whitehaven before 1733; studied in London; obtained doctorate in medicine from Leiden in 1737.
Education_Locations: Whitehaven, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; London, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Leiden, Unknown, Netherlands, Unknown, 1737
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Investigated gases from coal mines (firedamp and chokedamp); demonstrated identity of gas from mineral springs with carbon dioxide; advanced understanding of gas properties and handling techniques; first trained European scientist to examine platinum specimens.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced medicine in Whitehaven from 1737; conducted experimental investigations supported by patronage and Royal Society fellowship.
Patronage_Notes: Sir James Lowther, owner of Whitehaven collieries, encouraged investigations into mine damps and arranged for firedamp to be piped to Brownrigg's laboratory; married into the Spedding family, stewards of the Lowther estates.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in May 1742 following communication of papers on damps; received the Copley Medal for work on mineral waters and carbon dioxide.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by E. L. Scott. Father_Notes: American naval officer; died before Brown-Séquard's birth.
Education_Notes: Received M.D. from Paris on 3 January 1846. Became protégé of Pierre Rayer and worked at La Charité hospital. Conducted original experiments on gastric digestion and spinal cord function as a student.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1846
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of endocrinology and experimental physiology. Discovered the Brown-Séquard syndrome (crossing of nervous pathways in spinal cord). Demonstrated vasoconstrictive nerves, adrenal gland function, and internal secretion. Investigated epilepsy, spinal shock, and nervous inhibition. Conducted controversial rejuvenation experiments with testicular extracts.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced medicine in Philadelphia, New York, Boston, and London. Held professorships at Virginia Medical College (1854), Royal College of Surgeons (1858), Harvard Medical School (1864–1867), and Collège de France (1878–1894). Physician at National Hospital for the Paralysed and Epileptics in London (1860–1863). Founded and edited three scientific journals.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Académie des Sciences; Société de Biologie
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to Royal Society in 1861. Elected to Académie des Sciences in 1886. Active member and presenter to Société de Biologie.

Articles in Comptes rendus de la Société de biologie and Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences. Father_Notes: Jakub Brożek was an educated landowner who taught his son writing and geometry.
Education_Institution: University of Krakow; University of Padua
Education_Notes: Primary school in Kurzelow; baccalaureate at University of Krakow (March 1605) under professors Stanislaw Jacobeius and Walenty Fontanus; magister rank (March 1610); ordained priest (1611); studied medicine at Padua (June 1620–June 1624), receiving doctorate in medicine (1624); baccalaureate in theology; master of theology (1648); doctor of theology (February 1650).
Education_Locations: Krakow, Unknown, Poland, Unknown, 1605; Padua, Unknown, Italy, 1620, 1624
Religion_Notes: Ordained priest in 1611; became canon of St. Anne's church (1629) after receiving higher ecclesiastical orders; also held canonry of St. Florent church. Despite his loyalty to the Catholic Church, his primary allegiance was to the University of Krakow.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Greatest Polish mathematician of his time; published Arithmetica integrorum introducing logarithms to schools; wrote on perfect numbers and amicable numbers, contributing results later known as Fermat's theorem; defended Aristotle and Euclid against Petrus Ramus; collected Copernican documents and wrote on Copernicus; held chair of astrology at University of Krakow; studied medicine and served as physician to the bishop of Krakow.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor at Collegium Minus (1614, chair of astrology) and Collegium Maius (1619) of University of Krakow; professor of rhetoric (1625–1630); professor of theology; director of library of Collegium Maius (April 1631–December 1638); physician to bishop of Krakow (1624–autumn 1625); canon of St. Anne's church (1629) and St. Florent church; rector of University of Krakow (1652).
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: David Bruce emigrated from Edinburgh to Australia during the gold rush to install a crushing plant in a Victoria goldfield, indicating substantial means.
Education_Notes: Attended high school in Stirling until age fourteen; worked briefly in Manchester; gained admission to University of Edinburgh in 1876 and completed first year as medalist in natural history before switching to medicine; graduated M.B., C.M. in 1881.
Education_Locations: Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, 1876, 1881
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Discovered the bacterial cause of Malta fever (Micrococcus melitensis, later Brucella); conducted extensive researches on trypanosomiasis, identifying Trypanosoma brucei and establishing the tsetse fly as vector of nagana and sleeping sickness; introduced experimental bacteriological methods to Army Medical School.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Commissioned surgeon captain in Army Medical Service in 1883 and served throughout his career, attaining rank of surgeon general; taught pathology at Army Medical School at Netley; maintained medical practice and research alongside military service; commandant of Royal Army Medical College 1914–1919.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by the Royal Society, which elected him fellow in 1899 and organized commissions he headed (Sleeping Sickness Commission 1903, continuing commission 1908–1910, Nyasaland commission 1911); Foreign Office sponsored sleeping sickness investigations.
Instruments_Notes: Purchased a microscope in Malta to investigate Malta fever; his wife Mary acquired the latest microscopy techniques during his leave in Koch's laboratory.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Royal College of Physicians of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1899; fellow of the Royal College of Physicians of London; honorary memberships in several foreign academies and societies.

Father_Notes: David Bruce of Kinnaird; family was wealthy and landowning.

Education_Locations: None
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Explored Ethiopia and the Nile region; brought back drawings of buildings, fauna, and flora; collected seeds; kept precise meteorological and astronomical records.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as consul-general at Algiers from March 1763 to summer 1765; supported by family wealth as a landowning heir.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Began studies at Berlin in 1838; became assistant to physiologist Johannes Müller in 1843; graduated as doctor of medicine and surgery in 1842 on the basis of his dissertation De diffusione humorum per septa mortua et viva.
Education_Locations: Berlin, Unknown, Germany, 1838, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines: Physiology; Anatomy; Optics; Microscopy; Physiology of Digestion; Physiological Chemistry; Physiological Optics; Nerve and Muscle Physiology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in physical physiology and enzyme research; discovered ciliary muscle; investigated optical media, stereoscopic vision, and luminescence in animal eyes; studied digestive tract microscopically and recognized Peyer's glands; introduced terms achroödextrin and erythrodextrin; conducted experiments on peptic digestion and electric stimulation of muscles; investigated protoplasm and cell function; published 143 works across physics, plant physiology, microscopic anatomy, and experimental physiology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of physiology at University of Königsberg from 1848; moved to Vienna in 1849 where he founded a school for physiologists and taught until his death in 1892.
Instruments_Notes: Used labiograph to measure length of accented syllables in verse; conducted extensive microscopic investigations of physiological structures and cellular function.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Imperial Academy of Sciences in Vienna
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Published work in Proceedings of the Imperial Academy of Sciences in Vienna; received honors from numerous academies including highest Prussian order and Austrian ennoblement.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Trained as a locksmith; came to Berlin in 1851 and worked as a mechanic while developing mathematical skills. Recognized by Encke at the Berlin Observatory for mathematical talent. After one year of calculations, became assistant at the observatory. Graduated from the University of Berlin in 1856 with a dissertation on minor planets.
Education_Locations: Berlin, Unknown, Germany, 1855, 1856
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early work centered on theoretical astronomy under Encke's influence, including observations with equatorial and meridian circle. In Leipzig, shifted toward observational astronomy and related fields. Conducted longitude determinations between major European observatories. Organized uniform worldwide weather observations in cooperation with Buys-Ballot and Jellinek. Published Atlas der Astronomie and historical works on astronomical refraction and biographies of Humboldt and Encke.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lecturer in astronomy at University of Berlin from 1859; assistant professor at University of Leipzig from 1861, becoming professor in 1868. Director of the Leipzig Observatory from 1860 until his death. Rector of the university in 1877–1878.
Instruments_Notes: Used equatorial and meridian circle for observations in Berlin. Oversaw replacement of antiquated observatory tower equipment with new well-equipped facility at Leipzig outskirts.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Astronomische Gesellschaft; Kommission für Mitteleuropäische Gradmessung; Preussisches Geodätisches Institut
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Active member of the Astronomische Gesellschaft. Served on the Commission for Central European Arc Measurement and held chair in the astronomical section of the Prussian Geodetic Institute. Initiated and equipped the first German astronomical expeditions.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by H. C. Freiesleben. Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Began career as preparateur at Paris Faculté des Sciences in 1895; received doctorate in science in 1906 and M.D. thesis on mycetomas in 1906; passed agrégation in 1907.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1895, 1906
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Originator of medical parasitology in France. Demonstrated developmental phases of trypanosomes in leeches (1904) and in tsetse flies (1911); described complete life cycle of Trypanosoma cruzi and transmission of Chagas' disease through feces (1912). Studied all parasite groups including Piroplasma, filariae, Bilharzia, and vectors. Proved nonpathogenic amoeba species distinction (1923). Brought Plasmodium gallinaceum strain from Ceylon (1935) for malaria chemotherapy research.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant professor at Faculté de Médecine from 1906; full professor in chair of parasitology from 1919. Practiced as physician and conducted experimental research.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member of Académie de Médecine in 1919.

Father_Notes: Ser Brunellesco di Lippo Lapi was a notary; the family was of comfortable circumstances. Mother Giuliana was a member of the noble Spini family.
Education_Notes: Abandoned formal education early but apprenticed to a goldsmith, where he gained knowledge of stone-setting, niello work, and the mechanics of weights and wheels. Learned geometry from Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli in Florence, possibly between 1402 and 1418; may also have learned principles of perspective from Toscanelli.
Education_Locations: None
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in mathematical perspective and conical projection; demonstrated knowledge of vanishing points through his optical experiments. Designed and constructed engineering devices including remarkable clocks. Applied mathematical proportion to architectural design. Invented technique for building the cathedral dome without scaffolding.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as an architect and engineer on major commissions including the cathedral dome (1420–1446), secular buildings such as the Ospedale degli Innocenti, and military fortifications. Engaged in the intellectual exchange of ideas among Florence's artists and scientists.
Patronage_Notes: Commissioned for military fortifications by the Sforzas (Milan fortress), the city of Florence (cathedral dome, Ponte a Mare, fortress of Vicopisano), and other state authorities (Pisa citadel, port of Pesaro).
Instruments_Notes: Made remarkable clocks, demonstrating mechanical knowledge gained from his goldsmith apprenticeship.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Father was a cooper; mother's name unknown.

Education_Notes: Received early education locally; earned master of arts degree at University of Mainz in 1508/1509. Entered Carthusian monastery in Strasbourg in 1509, remaining until 1521. Received doctor of medicine degree from University of Basel in late 1532.
Education_Locations: Mainz, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1509; Strasbourg, Unknown, Germany, 1509, 1521; Basel, Unknown, Switzerland, Unknown, 1532
Religion_Notes: Fled the Carthusian monastery and Catholic faith in 1521 with aid of Ulrich von Hutten, a principal defender of Luther. Served as pastor in Steinau 1521–1524 and engaged in theological controversy.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of botanical emancipation from medieval herbalism; authored Herbarum vivae eicones (1530–1536), the first printed botanical book with scientific value in its illustrations. Edited and translated medical texts; compiled medical bibliographies and pharmacological reference works including Reformation der Apotecken.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Opened his own school in Strasbourg in 1524. Appointed town physician in Bern on 3 October 1533 for a six-year term. Active as editor, translator, and author of medical, botanical, and theological texts; worked closely with printer Johann Schott.

Father_Notes: Father Julien was a professor of physics; older brother Bernard was also a professor of physics.
Education_Notes: Entered École Normale Supérieure in 1889; graduated in 1892 and passed the agrégation in history and geography under adviser Vidal de la Blache. On Thiers Foundation scholarship from 1892 to 1896, took courses in law, mining, and agriculture. Defended thesis on irrigation in Iberian Peninsula and North Africa in 1902.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1889, 1892
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of human geography in France. Géographie humaine (1910) presented first systematic coordination of geographical phenomena resulting from human activities, illustrated with photographs. Argued against geographic determinism, emphasizing human agency and choice within natural possibilities.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of general geography at University of Fribourg from 1896; appointed to teach human geography at University of Lausanne in 1908; held chair of human geography at Collège de France from 1912.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences Morales et Politiques

Education_Notes: Entered University of Giessen in 1842 and studied physics, chemistry, botany, mineralogy, and philosophy. Later studied medicine and passed examinations in 1848, graduating with a dissertation on the excitomotor nervous system. Further studies in Würzburg with Rudolf Virchow and in Vienna.

Religion_Notes: Materialist philosopher opposed to dogmatic metaphysics and religious orthodoxy. Founded the Deutschen Freidenkerbund (German Freethinkers' League) in 1881.
Scientific_Disciplines: Medicine; Philosophy; Natural Philosophy; Physics; Chemistry; Botany; Zoology; History of Science
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed a consistent materialism grounded in empirical natural science. Championed Darwin's theory and the elimination of the barrier between inorganic and organic chemistry. Wrote extensively on the relationship between force and matter, and on the application of natural-scientific methods to philosophy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Academic lecturer in Tübingen from 1854, teaching physical diagnosis, medical encyclopedia, and forensic medicine; served as assistant physician at the university clinic. Later practiced medicine in Darmstadt. Published numerous works disseminating natural science, many translated into multiple languages.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Founded the Deutschen Freidenkerbund (German Freethinkers' League) in 1881.

Education_Notes: Trained under his stepfather Voigt and uncle W.H.S. Bucholz, both pharmaceutical chemists. Apprenticed to Karl Wilhelm Fiedler in Kassel from 1784, where he also taught himself languages and natural science. Received doctorate in pharmacy from University of Rinteln in 1808 and Ph.D. from University of Erfurt in 1809.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted detailed investigations of sulfur compounds, molybdenum, tungsten, and tin salts; extracted uranium compounds from pitchblende; distinguished strontium and barium oxides from hydroxides; investigated separation methods for metal pairs and mineral analyses; identified camphoric acid. Published over one hundred articles in German chemical and pharmaceutical journals and several books.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Inherited and operated a pharmacy in Erfurt from 1794; appointed Assessor at the College of Medicine, University of Erfurt in 1809 and made professor at the University of Erfurt in 1810.

Father_Notes: None

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in dimensional analysis and dimensional theory; authored influential treatise on thermodynamics (1900); conducted research on soil physics, properties of gases, blackbody radiation, steam turbine and propeller design, and developed the pi-theorem for reducing independent variables in experimental design.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught physics at Harvard, Bryn Mawr College, and University of Wisconsin between 1891 and 1901. Entered government service as assistant physicist in Bureau of Soils in 1902; employed by National Bureau of Standards from 1905 until retirement in 1937. Lectured at Naval Postgraduate School at Annapolis (1911–1912) and in National Bureau of Standards graduate program (1912–1913).
Patronage_Notes: Served as technical expert on Council of National Defense during World War I; associate scientific attaché with United States Embassy in Rome (1918–1919); frequently consulted by Navy Department on steam turbine and propeller research.

Father_Notes: Charles Buckland was rector of Templeton and Trusham; had a taste for ammonites and related shells.
Education_Institution: Winchester School; Corpus Christi College, Oxford
Education_Notes: Attended Winchester School, where he became familiar with chalk formations. Won a competitive scholarship to Corpus Christi College, Oxford in 1801 and graduated in 1804 with a very good examination. Continued in residence supporting himself on his scholarship and by taking pupils. Elected fellow of his college and admitted to holy orders in 1809.
Education_Locations: Winchester, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Oxford, Unknown, England, 1801, 1804
Religion_Notes: Admitted to holy orders in 1809. Took religion seriously and maintained an independent theological position within the Anglican Church, defending geology against evangelical and Tractarian opposition. Emphasized natural theology and the unity of the Deity.
Scientific_Disciplines: Geology; Paleontology; Mineralogy; Conchology; Stratigraphy; Petrography
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in British geology who redefined geological explanation through detailed local stratigraphic and dynamic analysis combined with paleontological evidence. Major contributions to understanding fossil animals (hyenas, bears, ichthyosaurs, megatherium), cave deposits, valley formation, Alpine structure, and glaciation. Emphasized use of modern analogies to interpret past phenomena.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Reader in mineralogy from 1813, then reader (styled as professor) in geology from 1818 at Oxford, giving two sets of lectures yearly until 1849. Accepted a country parsonage in 1825 and was appointed canon of Christ Church, Oxford, one of the richest ecclesiastical rewards. Became dean of Westminster in 1845.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed dean of Westminster in 1845 by Tory prime minister Robert Peel, an admirer of his work. Received Copley Medal of the Royal Society in 1822 for cavern researches. Nominated in 1830 to write the geological work in the Bridgewater treatise series stemming from the will of the eighth earl of Bridgewater.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Geological Society of London; Royal Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Geological Society of London in 1813. President of the Geological Society in 1824–1825 and again in 1840–1841. Member of the Council of the Royal Society from 1827 to 1849. Active participant in the British Association for the Advancement of Science, serving as president and host of its second meeting in 1832.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Initially destined for the bar by his father but abandoned jurisprudence for medicine. Became docteur-régent at the Faculty of Medicine in Paris in 1770.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1770
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Natural History; Medicine; Botany; Physiology; Anatomy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered integration of chemistry with natural history and medicine. Conducted experimental work on gases, particularly carbon dioxide (fixed air), and modified apparatus for gas investigation. Published detailed accounts of mineral and plant chemistry. Collaborated with Lavoisier on fundamental chemical experiments and was among the first to teach Lavoisier's theory.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of pharmacy at the Faculty of Medicine, Paris (1775–1777); elected to the chair of chemistry in 1776 following Augustin Roux's death; gave public and private chemistry courses from 1777 until ill health forced him to cease in autumn 1779. Also gave courses in botany, physiology, anatomy, hygiene, and medicine.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Société Royale de Médecine; Academy of Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected associate of the Société Royale de Médecine in February 1777; appointed adjoint-chimiste at the Academy of Sciences in Paris on 14 January 1778, succeeding Sage.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Independent discoverer of the rule of Budan and Fourier, which gives necessary conditions for determining the number of real roots of a polynomial equation between two given real numbers. Developed mechanical arithmetic methods for solving numerical equations without appeal to calculus or finite differences.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held the post of inspector general of studies at the University of Paris for over twenty years. Also held the degree of doctor of medicine.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Read a paper on his rule to the Institut de France in 1803; presented a proof of his rule to the Institute in 1811.

Father_Notes: Samuel Budd was a surgeon who had inherited landed property from his grandfather, an Anglican clergyman, and could afford to send all nine sons to good universities.
Education_Institution: École de Médecine; Middlesex Hospital; University of Edinburgh
Education_Notes: Studied at the École de Médecine in Paris intermittently from October 1828 to September 1837 under Broussais, Cruveilhier, Lisfranc, Louis, Orfila, and Ricord; attended Middlesex Hospital, London in winter 1835–1836; completed M.D. requirements at Edinburgh University and graduated August 1838.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1828, 1837; London, Unknown, England, 1835, 1836; Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, 1837, 1838
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer epidemiologist and precursor of germ theory of disease. Investigated over eighty cases of typhoid at North Tawton in 1839–1840. Demonstrated that specific infective agents determine epidemic phenomena of communicable diseases including typhoid, cholera, diphtheria, scarlet fever, and tuberculosis. Applied principles to animal diseases including sheep-pox, rinderpest, and hog cholera.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed assistant physician to the Dreadnought, Seaman's Hospital at Greenwich; physician to St. Peter's Hospital, Bristol (1842); lecturer in medicine at Bristol Medical College (1845); physician to Bristol Royal Infirmary (1847). Maintained general medical practice.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Royal College of Physicians of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1871. Founded the Bristol Microscopical and Pathological societies. Served ten years as councillor of the Bath and Bristol branch of the Provincial Medical and Surgical Association, becoming its president in 1855–1856; played active part on the Council of the British Medical Association until 1866.

Alt_Name: Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon; Leclerc
Father_Notes: Benjamin-François Leclerc became lord of Buffon and Montbard in 1717 and served as Conseiller to the Burgundian parliament; the family's wealth derived from Anne Marlin's relation to a rich financier.

Education_Notes: Attended Collège des Jésuites in Dijon from 1717 to 1723, where he showed aptitude for mathematics. Studied law in Dijon between 1723 and 1726. In 1728 studied medicine, botany, and mathematics at Collège de l'Oratoire in Angers under Père de Landreville. Became friendly with mathematician Gabriel Cramer in 1727.
Education_Locations: Dijon, Unknown, France, 1717, 1723; Dijon, Unknown, France, 1723, 1726; Angers, Unknown, France, 1728, 1730
Religion_Notes: Raised in Catholic France; no conflict with religious authority except for posthumous condemnation of some writings on cosmogony and earth history.
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural History; Zoology; Botany; Geology; Paleontology; Physics; Optics; Mathematics; Astronomy; Chemistry; Physiology; Anatomy; Mineralogy; Geography; Philosophy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal work was the 36-volume Histoire naturelle, a comprehensive natural history combining zoology, botany, geology, and mineralogy. Made major contributions to paleontology through study of giant fossils. Developed theories of earth history (cosmogony and cooling), animal reproduction and classification, and the unity of human species. Conducted microscopic research on animal reproduction and experiments on cooling of globes. Translated Newton's Method of Fluxions and Hales's Vegetable Statics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Intendant of the Jardin du Roi from 1739, a position he held for fifty years, during which he doubled its area and enriched its collections. Administered his estates at Montbard each summer. Inherited and significantly increased his personal wealth through landholdings and pensions from the crown.
Patronage_Notes: Minister Maurepas requested his early works on timber and sponsored his admission to the Académie Royale des Sciences in 1734 and his appointment as intendant of the Jardin du Roi in 1739. Louis XV made him Comte de Buffon and commissioned a bust by sculptor Augustin Pajou. Catherine II bestowed gifts upon him.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie Royale des Sciences; Académie Française; Royal Society of London; Academy of Berlin; Academy of St. Petersburg
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Admitted to Académie Royale des Sciences as adjoint-méchanicien on 9 January 1734; became académicien-associé in June 1739 and transferred to the botanical section. Elected to Académie Française, Royal Society of London, and academies of Berlin and St. Petersburg.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Lecturer and demonstrator in botany at University of Birmingham (1901–1904); professor of botany at University of Manitoba (1904–1936). Conducted independent research at Birmingham, Kew Gardens, and Winnipeg.
Patronage_Notes: Royal Society of Canada sponsored posthumous publication of Researches on Fungi, Volume VII (1950). National Research Council of Canada subsidized later volumes of Researches on Fungi.

Father_Notes: John Bulloch, an accountant; the family was plain-living and scholarly, with literary talent and interests in history and genealogy.

Education_Notes: Attended Aberdeen Grammar School until 1884, then King's College Aberdeen for two years. Enrolled in medicine at Marischal College, graduating in 1890 with highest honors. Studied pathology at Aberdeen, Leipzig, and other European medical centers. Presented prize-winning M.D. thesis at Aberdeen in 1894. Took courses in bacteriology at the Pasteur Institute under Émile Roux, Élie Metchnikoff, and Émile Duclaux. Brief assistantship to Victor Horsley at University College London. Received honorary LL.D. from Aberdeen in 1920.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in early development of medical bacteriology in Britain. Conducted research on diphtheria toxin, anaerobic bacteria, bacterial filters, antitoxin assay, opsonins, vaccine therapy for tuberculosis, and the Wassermann test. After 1910 shifted focus to historical and review work, particularly on hereditary diseases including hemophilia. Published authoritative monographs on diphtheria and surgical catgut, and his masterwork The History of Bacteriology (1938).
Means_of_Support_Notes: Took charge of serum laboratories at the British (later Lister) Institute of Preventive Medicine in July 1895. Appointed bacteriologist to London Hospital in 1897 and lecturer on bacteriology and pathological chemistry to its medical school. Became Goldsmith's professor of bacteriology at the University of London in 1919. Officially retired in 1934 but served as consulting bacteriologist and emeritus professor. Also held lectureships: Horace Dobell (Royal College of Physicians, 1910), Tyndall (Royal Institution, 1922), and Heath Clark (University of London, 1937).
Instruments_Notes: Described a new anaerobic jar and bacterial filter in his publications; these were among his technical contributions to bacteriological methodology.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1913. Served on various technical advisory committees and was chairman of the Lister Institute's board of governors in 1932.

Father_Notes: Chief librarian and professor of modern languages at the University of Göttingen. Ancestors on the paternal side held public office in Arolsen, frequently as master of the mint.
Education_Institution: Gymnasium at Holzminden; University of Göttingen
Education_Notes: Studied chemistry, physics, mineralogy, and mathematics at the University of Göttingen under Friedrich Stromeyer. Received doctorate in 1830 with a thesis in physics on hygrometers. Toured Europe from 1830 to 1833 visiting laboratories and factories, studying under Gay-Lussac in Paris and Heinrich Rose in Berlin.
Education_Locations: Holzminden, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1828; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1830
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Inorganic Chemistry; Analytical Chemistry; Physics; Geology; Spectroscopy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in analytical chemistry and gas analysis. Developed spectroscopic methods for elemental analysis and discovery. Conducted extensive geological research on volcanic rocks and geysers in Iceland. Early work in organic chemistry, particularly cacodyl compounds, before focusing on inorganic chemistry. Contributions to photochemistry and electrochemistry.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Privatdozent at University of Göttingen from 1833. Succeeded Wöhler at Polytechnic School in Kassel in 1836. Professor extraordinarius at University of Marburg from 1838, professor ordinarius from 1842. Succeeded Gmelin at University of Heidelberg in 1852, remaining there until retirement in 1889. Government of Baden constructed a laboratory for him, completed in 1855.
Patronage_Notes: Aided by a grant from the Hanoverian government for his European tour (1830–1833). Government of Baden constructed a laboratory for him at Heidelberg. Conducted government-sponsored study of mineral water of Baden with Victor Meyer.

Instruments_Notes: Designed and improved numerous pieces of laboratory equipment. Skilled glassblower who frequently made his own glassware. Created the Bunsen battery with carbon as the negative pole in 1841. Devised a sensitive ice calorimeter for measuring specific heats of rare elements. Constructed a filter pump for washing precipitates.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted extensive studies in natural sciences, particularly the observation of shells and lower animals using a three-lens microscope. Made detailed illustrations of insects including flies, lice, mites, fleas, and mosquitoes. Engaged in the spontaneous generation controversy, arguing against Redi's conclusions on oviparous generation. Developed a rational classification system for shells.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught mathematics at the Collegium Romanum from 1680, succeeding Kircher. Appointed curator of the Kircherian Museum in 1698. Member of the Jesuit order.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by the Jesuit order and the Collegium Romanum; his position as curator of the Kircherian Museum was an ecclesiastical institutional appointment.
Instruments_Notes: Constructed his own microscope with three lenses following Tortona's system, described as an ingenious mechanism for continual observation. The design and specifications are detailed in his Micrographia curiosa (1691).

His work on embryonic development indirectly influenced modern embryology.

Tsego Manteifel's surgical clinic in 1903. After presenting his doctoral thesis in 1909, studied surgical methods in Germany and Switzerland under August Bier, O. Hildebrandt, F. Krause, and Hermann Oppenheim. Studied anatomy, histology of the central nervous system, and neurological surgery under Constantin von Monakow in Zurich.

Scientific_Disciplines: Medicine; Neurology; Surgery; Anatomy; Physiology; Biochemistry; Histology; Pathology; Oncology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of Soviet neurosurgery and founder of an important school emphasizing experimental surgery. Early research focused on physiology of the liver, duodenum, stomach, and pancreas. Later work encompassed anatomy, physiology, biochemistry, histology, and pathology. Made contributions to oncology of the central nervous system, vegetative nervous system, blood circulation, brain edema, and operative treatment of nervous system conditions. Authored over 300 articles on clinical and theoretical medicine.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant professor of surgery at Yuriev University (after 1910), adjunct professor of surgery and anatomy, and professor ordinarius at the surgical clinic (from 1917). Headed the Voronezh Medical Institute's surgical clinic (1918–1923). Appointed to the chair of anatomy and surgery at Moscow State University Institute (1923). Organized the neurological department from 1924 onward. Director of the neurological clinic of the Health Ministry's roentgenology institute (after 1929) and the Central Neurosurgical Institute (founded 1934). Served as Chairman of the Board of Directors of the U.S.S.R. College of Surgeons (after 1939) and Chairman of the Medical Sciences Council of the U.S.S.R. Ministry of Health (after 1937).
Patronage_Notes: Appointed to leadership positions within Soviet state medical institutions and the U.S.S.R. Ministry of Health. Served as first president of the U.S.S.R. Academy of Medical Sciences and as a deputy to the Supreme Soviet of the U.S.S.R.

Education_Locations: Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, 1847, 1851; Paris, Unknown, France, 1851, 1852
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer experimental investigations of contagious diseases and infective processes; demonstrated the particulate nature of the infective agent in cattle plague (1865) and confirmed the inoculability of tuberculosis in animals (1867). Conducted extensive electrophysiological investigations, notably on the Venus's-flytrap leaf, discovering the electrical current accompanying leaf closure. Established physiology as an independent discipline in England.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Medical registrar and lecturer at St. Mary's Hospital (1853–1862); medical officer of health for Paddington parish (1856–1867); inspector for the medical department of the Privy Council (1860–1865); professor of practical physiology and histology at University College, London (1870–1874); Jodrell professor of human physiology at University College (1874–1882); Waynflete professor of physiology at Oxford University (1882–1895); Regius professor of medicine at Oxford (1895–1905). Also served on staffs of Brompton Hospital for Consumption and Middlesex Hospital.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1867; delivered the Croonian lecture three times (1867, 1877, 1899); awarded the Royal Medal in 1883. Elected fellow of the Royal College of Physicians in 1871; appointed Harveian orator in 1878; awarded the Baly Medal in 1880. President of the British Association for the Advancement of Science in 1893.

Cooperated in the survey of Austria and was coeditor of Viennese ephemerides with Triesnecker.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Prolific Aristotelian commentator on logic and natural philosophy; major contributions to medieval logic theory, particularly through De puritate artis logicae (two versions, ca. 1324 and 1325–1328), which engaged with Ockham's logic. In natural philosophy, wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle's Physics, De anima, and other works; developed influential theories on the nature of motion, intension and remission of forms, and first and last instants in temporal processes. Also wrote on moral philosophy and history of philosophers.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Master of arts and fellow at Merton College, Oxford; regent in arts at Oxford; studied and taught theology in Paris; appointed envoy of Edward III to the papal court in 1327; acquired a rectory in Kent in 1344.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed envoy of Edward III to the papal court in 1327; maintained intermittent official connections with English public figures thereafter.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed The Sacred Theory of the Earth, combining Cambridge Platonist idealism with Scripture and geological explanation of earth's surface features. Theory addressed earth's origin from chaos, the universal deluge, conflagration, and consummation. Emphasized the importance of the Deluge and mountain formation in geological thought.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Fellow of Christ's College, Cambridge (1657–1678), serving as proctor from 1667. Master of the Charterhouse from 1685 until his death. Chaplain in ordinary to King William III and clerk of the closet.
Patronage_Notes: Served as governor to the young earl of Wiltshire and traveled with the grandson of the duke of Ormonde, the earl of Orrery. Received the Charterhouse position at the recommendation of the duke of Ormonde. Dedicated Archaelogiae philosophicae to William III.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Graduated from Thetford Academy; self-trained amateur astronomer with no formal astronomical education. Received M.A. from Yale in 1878 and Sc.D. from Northwestern in 1915, both likely honorary recognitions of his astronomical work.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering observer of double stars; discovered numerous visual binary systems and measured their separation and position angles. Compiled comprehensive catalogues of northern double stars and proper motion stars. Designed improved filar micrometer for precise measurements.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked full-time as a shorthand reporter in law courts until retirement at age sixty-four in 1902. From 1897 to 1914 served as professor of practical astronomy at Yerkes Observatory, commuting from Chicago to Williams Bay two nights weekly.
Instruments_Notes: Designed and used a filar micrometer with greatly improved bright-wire illumination for measuring difficult binary pairs. Conducted observations with the forty-inch refractor at Yerkes Observatory and excellent telescope lenses figured by Alvan Clark & Sons.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Astronomical Society; Académie des Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of Royal Astronomical Society from 1874, associate from 1898, awarded Gold Medal in 1894. Received Prix Lalande from Académie des Sciences in 1904.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant astronomer at Copenhagen University observatory 1893–1898; lectured on practical mathematics at Copenhagen University 1906–1912; worked as an actuary for most of his career.

Education_Notes: Medical education at St. Thomas' and St. Bartholomew's hospitals; became member of the Royal College of Surgeons in 1832.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal work on Bryozoa (Polyzoa), for which he formulated the first scientific arrangement in 1856; paleontological studies including fossil polyzoa; craniometry and fossil identification; anthropological research including the Gibraltar cranium (Neanderthal type, 1868); early observations on scurvy and fasciolopsiasis.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Surgeon to the Seaman's Hospital Society from 1832, serving on the hospital ship Dreadnought at Greenwich until 1854; Hunterian professor of comparative anatomy at the Royal College of Surgeons (1856–1859); editor of multiple scientific journals (Microscopic Journal, Quarterly Journal of Microscopic Science, Natural History Review, Journal of the Ethnological Society); member of the Senate of London University; treasurer of the Royal Institution.

Religion_Notes: Benedictine monk at Abbaye de St.-Antoine; forced to leave the monastery in 1562 during the Wars of Religion.

Treated mathematical aspects of jurisprudence including land division and inheritance.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lived as a Benedictine monk at Abbaye de St.-Antoine from ca. 1508; served as abbot for two years. Taught mathematics in Paris under Oronce Fine in 1522.

Father_Notes: Mikhail Vasilievich Butlerov was a retired lieutenant colonel; the family owned part of Butlerovka village.
Education_Notes: Attended private boarding school, then gymnasium in Kazan, and studied at Kazan University from 1844 to 1849. Received candidate of natural sciences degree for thesis on butterflies. Defended master's dissertation in 1851 and doctoral dissertation at Moscow University in 1854, both on chemical topics, though both remained in manuscript form until 1953.

Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Organic Chemistry; Physical Chemistry; Inorganic Chemistry; Entomology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of structural theory of organic chemistry; synthesized hexamethylenetetramine and first complete synthesis of a sacchariferous substance; predicted and proved positional and skeletal isomerism; studied polymerization reactions, valency, and organometallic compounds. Early work in entomology on Volga-Ural butterflies.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught chemistry at Kazan University from 1849, initially part-time then as official assistant, and as professor from 1852 to 1868. Professor of chemistry at St. Petersburg University from 1868 to 1885, then retired on pension but continued special lecture courses. Also practiced as a physician and conducted agricultural research.
Patronage_Notes: Served as rector of Kazan University twice (1860–1861 and 1862–1863). Elected junior scientific assistant of St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences in 1870, associate member in 1871, and full member in 1874.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of Chemical Society of Paris from 1857; Russian Chemical Society from 1869; chairman of chemistry section of Russian Physics and Chemistry Society from 1878 to 1882; honorary or foreign member of multiple international chemical societies from 1876 onward.

Education_Notes: Studied mineralogy, chemistry, and paleontology at Karlsruhe Polytechnic Institute; completed doctorate in mineralogy with minors in zoology and chemistry at Heidelberg in 1868. Advanced study in zoology at Leuckart's laboratory in Leipzig after military service in 1869.
Education_Locations: Karlsruhe, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Heidelberg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1868; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, 1869, 1869

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in cytology, particularly cell division, fertilization, and ciliate conjugation. Developed the alveolar theory of protoplasm and conducted extensive studies on protozoans. Later work examined colloidal structures in organic and inorganic materials, and mineral structures of biological origin. Returned to comparative anatomy in his final years.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant to paleontologist Karl von Zittel (1865–1866); assistant to taxonomist Möbius at Kiel (two years after 1869); Privatdozent at Karlsruhe Polytechnic Institute (1876); professor of zoology and paleontology at Heidelberg from age thirty until retirement in 1918.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Started as a chemist with interests in molecular structure and properties of matter; shifted to meteorology after his chemical speculations were poorly received. Formulated Buys Ballot's law relating wind direction to pressure gradient (1857). Also taught mathematics and physics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lecturer in mineralogy and geology at Utrecht (1845); added theoretical chemistry (1846); appointed professor of mathematics (1847); professor of physics (1867–1888). Founded and directed the Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute (K.N.M.I.) from 1854 until death.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to Royal Academy of Sciences of Amsterdam in 1855 and to Royal Belgian Academy. Served as chairman of the International Meteorological Committee from its founding at Vienna Congress in 1873 until 1879.
